Title: Ensure SSL/TLS encryption is implemented and HTTPS is enforced on the website
Issue: • Absence of HTTPS exposes data transmitted between users and government servers. • Users observe “Not Secure” warnings or missing padlock icons in the browser. • This increases risk of data interception, erodes public trust, and violates mandated government security norms.
Advice: • Implement valid SSL/TLS certificates across all URLs. • Enforce HTTPS for both desktop and mobile web. • Redirect all HTTP traffic to HTTPS automatically.
Examples – Pass: • URL starts with https:// and shows a secure padlock icon. • No mixed-content warnings across pages.
Examples – Fail: • Website loads over http://. • Browser displays “Not Secure” warnings. • Mixed HTTP/HTTPS assets present.
Accessibility Consideration: • Secure connections ensure assistive-technology users can safely submit personal data without security interruptions. • Reduces anxiety and abandonment caused by browser security alerts.
Rationale: SSL/TLS encryption is a foundational security requirement for government digital services to protect data integrity and confidentiality. Enforcing HTTPS prevents man-in-the-middle attacks, reassures citizens through visible security indicators, and ensures compliance with nationally mandated standards such as GIGW. Failure to implement HTTPS undermines trust, exposes sensitive data, and creates systemic security risk across the platform.

Title: Ensure ownership and management information is clearly displayed on the website
Issue: • Missing or unclear ownership details prevent users from identifying the responsible authority. • Users question authenticity when department or organisation details are not visible. • This reduces trust and violates mandatory government identification norms.
Advice: • Display owning and managing department/organisation clearly. • Place ownership details on homepage and footer. • Include basic official identifiers alongside ownership information.
Examples – Pass: • Department/organisation name clearly shown in footer. • Homepage includes ownership information.
Examples – Fail: • No ownership details on homepage or footer. • Ownership buried in PDFs or inaccessible pages.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear ownership indicators reduce cognitive load and help users quickly validate official sources.
Rationale: Visible ownership disclosure establishes authenticity, accountability, and trust in government digital services. It is a mandated requirement under national governance standards to help citizens quickly verify that a service is official and reliable.

Title: Display official state emblems and ownership identification on mobile app splash screens
Issue: • Absence of official emblems and ownership labels on app launch creates authenticity doubts. • Users may mistrust or abandon apps that do not appear officially endorsed. • This undermines trust and violates branding and identity standards.
Advice: • Display DBIM-compliant logo lockups on splash screens. • Show state emblem with correct ratio and colors. • Include ownership information in Hindi and English.
Examples – Pass: • Splash screen shows state emblem and department name correctly. • Branding follows DBIM specifications.
Examples – Fail: • Splash screen lacks official emblem or ownership details. • Incorrect or distorted emblem usage.
Accessibility Consideration: • Properly labelled emblems with alternate text support screen reader users during app launch.
Rationale: First-launch identification is critical for establishing trust in government mobile applications. Prominent display of official emblems and ownership ensures authenticity, legal compliance, and citizen confidence from the first interaction.

Title: Ensure clear and accessible contact details are provided on the website
Issue: • Missing or hidden contact details prevent users from seeking help. • Users feel unsupported when email or phone information is unavailable. • This reduces transparency and trust in government services.
Advice: • Display official email address and phone number clearly. • Place contact details in footer and on a dedicated contact page.
Examples – Pass: • Footer displays official email and phone number. • Dedicated contact page available.
Examples – Fail: • No visible contact details. • Contact information only in downloadable documents.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear contact details help users with disabilities seek assistance without additional navigation effort.
Rationale: Accessible contact information is a core trust and transparency requirement for citizen-facing services. It reassures users that support and accountability mechanisms are in place, as mandated by governance standards.

Title: Obtain explicit user consent before collecting or storing personal data
Issue: • Data is collected without explicit user consent. • Users are unaware of data storage or usage practices. • This creates legal, trust, and compliance risks.
Advice: • Implement clear opt-in consent mechanisms. • Use consent banners or forms before data collection. • Clearly link consent to stated purposes.
Examples – Pass: • Cookie or data consent banner with opt-in action. • Clear consent language linked to data usage.
Examples – Fail: • Data collected automatically without consent. • Pre-checked or hidden consent mechanisms.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear consent flows help all users, including assistive-technology users, understand and control data usage.
References: GIGW 3.0 – 2.6.3, BIS IS 17428:2020, DBIM, DPDP Act 2023
Rationale: Explicit consent is a legal and ethical requirement for government digital services. Obtaining informed, purpose-specific consent protects citizen rights, builds trust, and ensures compliance with national data protection and governance laws.

Title: Clearly inform users about what data is collected and how it is used
Issue: • Users are not informed about the types of data being collected. • Users do not understand the purpose of data usage. • This creates trust erosion and legal non-compliance risks.
Advice: • Clearly disclose data types collected. • Explain purposes of data usage in simple language. • Present disclosures before or at the point of data collection.
Examples – Pass: • Privacy notice lists data types and purposes clearly. • Disclosure visible before form submission.
Examples – Fail: • Data collected without disclosure. • Vague or generic privacy statements.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear disclosures support cognitive accessibility and informed consent for assistive-technology users.
References: GIGW 3.0 – 2.6.3, BIS IS 17428:2020, DBIM, DPDP Act 2023
Rationale: Transparent data disclosure is a mandatory requirement for citizen trust and lawful data processing. Clearly informing users about data collection and usage supports informed decision-making and ensures compliance with governance and data protection standards.

Title: Display the National Emblem prominently in the website or app header
Issue: • Absence or poor placement of the National Emblem reduces perceived authenticity. • Users may doubt whether the platform is an official government service. • This weakens trust and violates identity standards.
Advice: • Place the National Emblem prominently in the header. • Follow official size, color, and placement guidelines.
Examples – Pass: • National Emblem visible in header on homepage. • Correct emblem proportions and placement.
Examples – Fail: • Emblem missing, distorted, or placed inconsistently.
Accessibility Consideration: • Proper emblem display supports visual recognition for users with cognitive disabilities.
Rationale: The National Emblem serves as a primary visual indicator of official government authority. Proper display establishes legitimacy, reinforces trust, and ensures compliance with national identity and branding standards.

Title: Implement trusted government login systems for user authentication
Issue: • Absence of trusted login systems weakens authentication assurance. • Users face fragmented or insecure login experiences. • This increases security and trust risks.
Advice: • Integrate trusted login systems such as Meri Pehchan. • Ensure secure and consistent authentication flows.
Examples – Pass: • Login via Meri Pehchan available. • Secure government-backed authentication flow.
Examples – Fail: • Only local or insecure login mechanisms present.
Accessibility Consideration: • Standardized login flows improve accessibility and reduce cognitive effort for users.
Rationale: Trusted login systems standardize authentication, reduce security risks, and improve user confidence. Their use aligns with national digital identity and secure access initiatives.

Title: Provide a clear grievance redressal mechanism for users
Issue: • Users cannot easily submit complaints or feedback. • Lack of grievance mechanisms reduces accountability. • This undermines trust and service quality.
Advice: • Provide a visible grievance or feedback mechanism. • Place access links prominently (e.g., footer).
Examples – Pass: • Dedicated grievance form or feedback link available.
Examples – Fail: • No grievance or feedback mechanism present.
Accessibility Consideration: • Accessible grievance channels support inclusive participation for all users.
Rationale: Grievance redressal mechanisms are essential for accountability and responsive governance. They empower citizens to raise concerns and support continuous service improvement.

Title: Allow users to track the status of submitted grievances
Issue: • Users cannot track grievance resolution status. • Lack of updates increases follow-ups and dissatisfaction. • This reduces transparency and trust.
Advice: • Provide grievance tracking using reference numbers or login. • Display status updates clearly.
Examples – Pass: • Users can view complaint status online.
Examples – Fail: • No tracking or status visibility provided.
Accessibility Consideration: • Status tracking supports clarity for users with cognitive or memory impairments.
Rationale: Complaint tracking improves transparency, reduces uncertainty, and demonstrates responsive governance by keeping citizens informed throughout resolution.

Title: Communicate grievance resolutions clearly to users
Issue: • Users are not informed when their grievances are resolved. • Lack of resolution communication causes uncertainty and repeat follow-ups. • This reduces trust and perceived responsiveness of the system.
Advice: • Notify users when grievances are resolved. • Communicate outcomes via status updates, messages, or notifications.
Examples – Pass: • User receives resolution status or message. • Resolution details visible in grievance history.
Examples – Fail: • No notification or update after grievance submission.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear resolution messages support users with cognitive and memory impairments.
Rationale: Communicating grievance resolutions is essential for transparent and responsive governance. Timely updates close the feedback loop, reduce user anxiety, and demonstrate accountability in service delivery.

Title: Provide a system for users to submit feedback, reviews, and ratings
Issue: • Users cannot easily share feedback or ratings. • Lack of feedback channels limits service improvement. • This weakens participation and accountability.
Advice: • Provide feedback forms or rating widgets. • Make feedback mechanisms easily accessible.
Examples – Pass: • Feedback form or rating widget available.
Examples – Fail: • No feedback or review mechanism present.
Accessibility Consideration: • Multiple feedback options support inclusive participation for diverse users.
Rationale: Feedback systems enable citizen participation and continuous service improvement. They support transparency, accountability, and user-centric governance practices.

Title: Inform users before redirecting them to external websites
Issue: • Users are redirected without prior notice. • Unexpected redirection reduces trust and perceived security. • This violates transparency requirements.
Advice: • Display external link warnings or indicators. • Inform users before navigating away from the site.
Examples – Pass: • External link warning or confirmation shown.
Examples – Fail: • Immediate redirection without notice.
Accessibility Consideration: • Warnings help screen-reader users understand navigation context changes.
Rationale: Advance notification of external redirection maintains transparency and protects user trust by clearly signalling context changes and security boundaries.

Title: Minimize external redirects and outbound links in mobile applications
Issue: • Excessive external redirects expose users to security risks. • Users lose trust when leaving the app frequently. • This weakens app security posture.
Advice: • Prefer deep linking and in-app flows. • Restrict and secure necessary external links.
Examples – Pass: • Services open via deep links or in-app views.
Examples – Fail: • Frequent redirection to external browsers.
Accessibility Consideration: • In-app navigation reduces cognitive load and context loss.
Rationale: Reducing external redirects in mobile apps limits security exposure and preserves user trust by keeping interactions within controlled, authenticated environments.

Title: Ensure Privacy Policy and Terms & Conditions are available on the website
Issue: • Users cannot access legal and policy information. • Missing policies create legal and trust risks. • This violates mandatory compliance requirements.
Advice: • Publish Privacy Policy and Terms & Conditions pages. • Ensure links are easily accessible from footer or key pages.
Examples – Pass: • Footer links to Privacy Policy and Terms pages.
Examples – Fail: • Policies missing or inaccessible.
Accessibility Consideration: • Accessible policy pages support informed decision-making for all users.
Rationale: Availability of legal policies is a foundational compliance requirement. Clear access to Privacy Policy and Terms builds trust, supports informed consent, and ensures legal transparency.

Title: Ensure privacy policies and terms are accessible before users access core functionality
Issue: • Users access core features without reviewing legal policies. • Consent is obtained after functionality use begins. • This results in uninformed consent and legal non-compliance.
Advice: • Present Privacy Policy and Terms before authentication or feature access. • Require explicit acknowledgement prior to data collection.
Examples – Pass: • Pre-auth screen displays policies with mandatory acknowledgment.
Examples – Fail: • Policies accessible only after login or data submission.
Accessibility Consideration: • Pre-access policy viewing supports informed decision-making for all users, including cognitive accessibility needs.
Rationale: Providing access to legal documents before functionality ensures informed, lawful consent and protects citizens’ data rights. It aligns with lifecycle governance requirements and prevents retroactive or invalid consent collection.

Title: Ensure legal documents are consistently accessible from profile and navigation menus
Issue: • Users cannot easily locate legal documents during usage. • Inconsistent access creates transparency gaps. • This weakens trust and compliance perception.
Advice: • Provide persistent access to policies from profile and side menu. • Maintain clear navigation to legal documents at all times.
Examples – Pass: • Legal section accessible from profile and menu.
Examples – Fail: • Policies hidden deep within app flows.
Accessibility Consideration: • Persistent navigation supports users with memory or orientation challenges.
Rationale: Continuous access to legal information reinforces transparency and empowers users to review rights and obligations at any stage of interaction.

Title: Provide a clearly visible “Contact Us” link on the website
Issue: • Users struggle to find support or contact options. • Missing contact access increases frustration. • This reduces transparency and trust.
Advice: • Display a visible “Contact Us” link. • Place it consistently in header, footer, or navigation.
Examples – Pass: • “Contact Us” link visible on homepage and footer.
Examples – Fail: • Contact link missing or hidden.
Accessibility Consideration: • Consistent placement supports navigation predictability for assistive-technology users.
Rationale: Clear contact access demonstrates openness and accountability. It reassures users that assistance is available and supports transparent governance practices.

Title: Distribute mobile applications through official government and recognised app stores
Issue: • Apps distributed through unofficial channels reduce trust. • Users question authenticity and security. • This increases security and compliance risks.
Advice: • Publish apps on gov.in app store and recognised commercial stores. • Maintain consistent metadata and certification compliance.
Examples – Pass: • App listed on gov.in app store and Google Play / App Store.
Examples – Fail: • App distributed via unofficial links or APKs.
Accessibility Consideration: • Official stores provide accessibility and security assurances for all users.
Rationale: Official distribution channels validate authenticity, ensure security vetting, and protect users from fraudulent or tampered applications.

Title: Implement mandated security protocols and obtain required government cybersecurity certifications
Issue: • Required security controls and certifications are missing. • Systems are exposed to cybersecurity threats. • This creates severe legal and operational risks.
Advice: • Obtain mandated certifications (CERT-In, STQC). • Implement secure SDLC and continuous security practices.
Examples – Pass: • Valid cybersecurity certifications present. • Regular audits and security updates implemented.
Examples – Fail: • No certification or outdated security practices.
Accessibility Consideration: • Secure systems protect vulnerable users relying on digital services.
Rationale: Strong cybersecurity posture is essential for protecting citizen data and maintaining trust in government digital systems. Compliance with mandated certifications ensures resilience against threats and legal adherence.
Metrics Affected: Security risk, Legal risk, User trust

Title: Provide a comprehensive and transparent “About Us” section in the application
Issue: • Users cannot easily understand who operates the application. • Missing version, ownership, or legal details reduce transparency. • This weakens trust and compliance perception.
Advice: • Include organisation details, ownership, version metadata, and legal links. • Keep information structured, searchable, and up to date.
Examples – Pass: • About Us page shows organisation name, version number, legal links, and support contacts.
Examples – Fail: • About Us page missing ownership or version information.
Accessibility Consideration: • Structured information supports users with cognitive disabilities and screen-reader navigation.
Rationale: A well-structured “About Us” section acts as a transparency anchor for government applications. It enables users to verify authenticity, understand accountability, and access critical legal and support information.

Title: Apply visual brand identity consistently across all application interfaces
Issue: • Inconsistent colours, typography, or logos create fragmented brand perception. • Users may question authenticity due to visual inconsistency. • This weakens trust and recognition.
Advice: • Apply DBIM colour, typography, and logo standards consistently. • Maintain a unified design system across screens.
Examples – Pass: • Consistent colours, fonts, and logos across screens.
Examples – Fail: • Mixed colour palettes or typography styles.
Accessibility Consideration: • Consistent visuals improve readability and reduce cognitive load.
Rationale: Consistent visual identity reinforces authenticity, recognisability, and professionalism of government digital services. It reduces cognitive friction and strengthens trust signals.

Title: Implement mandatory data security controls across the application
Issue: • Data is insufficiently protected at rest or in transit. • Weak authentication or access control exposes systems to breaches. • This creates severe legal and operational risks.
Advice: • Implement encryption, secure authentication, and access control. • Conduct regular audits and follow secure coding practices.
Examples – Pass: • Encrypted storage and secure authentication in place. • Regular security audits conducted.
Examples – Fail: • Plaintext data storage or weak authentication mechanisms.
Accessibility Consideration: • Secure systems protect vulnerable users dependent on digital services.
Rationale: Strong data security controls are essential to protect citizen information and maintain trust. Compliance with mandated cybersecurity requirements reduces breach risks and ensures regulatory adherence.
Metrics Affected: Security risk, Legal risk, User trust

Title: Transparently communicate data practices and user rights through clear notices and consent
Issue: • Users are unaware of how their data is collected or used. • Consent mechanisms are unclear or insufficient. • This leads to mistrust and non-compliance risks.
Advice: • Provide clear privacy notices and granular consent controls. • Enable users to manage rights such as access, correction, and deletion.
Examples – Pass: • Clear privacy notice with consent options available. • Privacy dashboard accessible to users.
Examples – Fail: • Vague or missing data practice disclosures.
Accessibility Consideration: • Plain-language notices improve understanding for all users, including those with cognitive disabilities.
Rationale: Transparent communication of data practices empowers users, ensures informed consent, and aligns with privacy-by-design principles mandated for government digital services.

Title: Explain complex features using plain, easy-to-understand language
Issue: • Complex feature explanations use jargon or technical terms. • Users with low or varied literacy struggle to understand functionality. • This leads to confusion, abandonment, and misuse of features.
Advice: • Use plain language (6th–8th grade reading level). • Keep sentences short and action-oriented. • Introduce complexity progressively with contextual help.
Examples – Pass: • Walkthrough text uses simple words and short sentences. • Tooltips explain unavoidable technical terms.
Examples – Fail: • Dense paragraphs with technical jargon. • Long sentences explaining multiple concepts at once.
Accessibility Consideration: • Supports users with cognitive disabilities and low literacy by reducing comprehension effort.
Rationale: Plain language reduces cognitive barriers and ensures inclusive access to digital services. It enables users across literacy levels to understand functionality, supporting equitable service adoption.

Title: Limit cognitive load through focused and well-structured walkthrough content
Issue: • Walkthrough screens contain excessive or unfocused information. • Users feel overwhelmed and skip onboarding. • This reduces feature understanding and completion rates.
Advice: • Present one primary concept per screen. • Use chunking and progressive disclosure. • Remove decorative or redundant content.
Examples – Pass: • Screens contain a single task or concept. • Content grouped into clear sections.
Examples – Fail: • Screens overloaded with text and multiple actions.
Accessibility Consideration: • Reduced cognitive load benefits users with attention and memory limitations.
Rationale: Managing cognitive load is essential for effective onboarding. Focused information presentation improves comprehension and reduces abandonment during walkthroughs.

Title: Use graphics and animations purposefully to support understanding
Issue: • Decorative or excessive animations distract users. • Graphics lack accessibility alternatives. • This impairs comprehension and accessibility compliance.
Advice: • Use graphics only when they clarify concepts. • Respect reduced-motion preferences. • Provide text alternatives for visuals.
Examples – Pass: • Illustrations clarify steps. • Animations respect reduced-motion settings.
Examples – Fail: • Auto-playing animations with no control. • Missing alt text for graphics.
Accessibility Consideration: • Supports users with motion sensitivity and screen reader users.
Rationale: Purposeful visuals enhance comprehension when used sparingly and accessibly. Accessible animations support understanding without excluding users sensitive to motion or non-text content.

Title: Introduce features progressively to avoid overwhelming users
Issue: • Too many features are introduced at once. • Users skip or abandon walkthroughs. • This reduces onboarding effectiveness.
Advice: • Use step-by-step onboarding with progress indicators. • Allow skipping and revisiting steps.
Examples – Pass: • Walkthrough limited to 3–4 focused steps. • Progress indicators visible.
Examples – Fail: • Long walkthroughs with dense information per screen.
Accessibility Consideration: • Step-by-step flows support users with cognitive processing difficulties.
Rationale: Progressive disclosure aligns feature introduction with user readiness, improving comprehension and walkthrough completion rates.

Title: Clearly communicate the core value proposition during walkthroughs
Issue: • Walkthroughs focus on features without explaining benefits. • Users do not understand why the app is valuable. • This reduces motivation to continue.
Advice: • Highlight core benefits early. • Visually emphasize high-value features.
Examples – Pass: • Benefits stated clearly on first walkthrough screen.
Examples – Fail: • Feature lists without explaining user value.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear benefits help users with cognitive limitations grasp purpose quickly.
Rationale: Clear value communication helps users quickly understand relevance and encourages continued engagement with the application.

Title: Ensure walkthrough text meets accessibility standards for readability
Issue: • Text size, contrast, or spacing is insufficient. • Users struggle to read walkthrough content. • This creates accessibility violations and exclusion.
Advice: • Use minimum font sizes and contrast ratios. • Support text scaling and system fonts. • Maintain readable spacing.
Examples – Pass: • Text meets contrast and size requirements. • Text scales up to 200% without loss.
Examples – Fail: • Low contrast text. • Fixed font sizes that do not scale.
Accessibility Consideration: • Essential for users with low vision or reading impairments.
Rationale: Readable text is a foundational accessibility requirement. Compliance ensures that all users, including those with visual impairments, can access onboarding content.

Title: Implement comprehensive screen reader support with semantic structure
Issue: • Screen readers cannot correctly interpret walkthrough content. • Focus order is illogical or elements are unlabeled. • This prevents non-visual users from completing onboarding.
Advice: • Add semantic labels and roles to all UI elements. • Ensure logical focus order and announce dynamic changes. • Provide alternative navigation paths.
Examples – Pass: • TalkBack/VoiceOver reads elements in correct order. • All icons and images have meaningful labels.
Examples – Fail: • Unlabeled buttons. • Focus jumps unpredictably.
Accessibility Consideration: • Essential for blind and low-vision users relying on assistive technologies.
Rationale: Full screen reader support is a foundational accessibility requirement. Proper semantics and focus management ensure that visually impaired users can independently understand and complete onboarding flows.

Title: Keep onboarding sequences concise while ensuring comprehension
Issue: • Onboarding has too many screens or excessive content. • Users rush or skip without understanding. • This reduces feature adoption.
Advice: • Limit onboarding to optimal screen count. • Focus on essential concepts only. • Validate comprehension through testing.
Examples – Pass: • 3–4 focused onboarding screens.
Examples – Fail: • Long, repetitive onboarding flows.
Accessibility Consideration: • Short sequences benefit users with cognitive or attention limitations.
Rationale: Concise onboarding respects user time and attention while improving understanding. Optimized sequences reduce drop-offs and improve early engagement.

Title: Allow users to skip onboarding and access it later
Issue: • Users are forced through onboarding. • No way to revisit guidance later. • This causes frustration and missed learning.
Advice: • Provide skip option on all onboarding screens. • Allow access to walkthroughs later from settings or help.
Examples – Pass: • Visible “Skip” button present. • Tutorial accessible from menu later.
Examples – Fail: • No skip option. • Walkthrough inaccessible after first use.
Accessibility Consideration: • User control benefits users with anxiety or slower processing speed.
Rationale: Optional onboarding respects user autonomy while preserving learning access when needed.

Title: Maintain consistent brand voice and communication style during onboarding
Issue: • Inconsistent tone across walkthrough screens. • Conflicting terminology confuses users. • This weakens brand trust.
Advice: • Apply a consistent content style guide. • Use uniform terminology and tone across screens.
Examples – Pass: • Same tone and terminology across all steps.
Examples – Fail: • Mixed formal and informal language.
Accessibility Consideration: • Predictable language benefits users with cognitive disabilities.
Rationale: Consistent brand voice builds familiarity, credibility, and confidence, especially for first-time users.

Title: Use supportive and confidence-building language in onboarding
Issue: • Language feels intimidating or overly technical. • Users feel anxious or unsure. • This discourages engagement.
Advice: • Use encouraging, friendly language. • Avoid negative or commanding phrasing.
Examples – Pass: • Encouraging microcopy (“You’re almost done”).
Examples – Fail: • Threatening or directive language.
Accessibility Consideration: • Positive tone supports users with anxiety or low confidence.
Rationale: Supportive language reduces anxiety and increases confidence, leading to better onboarding completion and engagement.

Title: Support Indian languages with culturally appropriate localization
Issue: • Onboarding content is only in one language. • Cultural or language barriers prevent understanding. • This excludes large user groups.
Advice: • Support scheduled Indian languages. • Adapt content culturally and linguistically. • Ensure correct language tagging and RTL support if applicable.
Examples – Pass: • Language switch available with localized content.
Examples – Fail: • Only English onboarding provided.
Accessibility Consideration: • Critical for users with limited proficiency in English.
Rationale: Multilingual and culturally adapted onboarding ensures inclusivity and equitable access for India’s diverse user base.

Title: Ensure core content and primary functionality are accessible on mobile screens
Issue: • Core content or key actions are hidden or truncated on mobile. • Users must zoom, scroll excessively, or switch devices. • This leads to task failure and poor mobile adoption.
Advice: • Prioritize core content and actions for mobile view. • Use responsive layouts and touch-friendly elements. • Ensure parity of functionality between mobile and desktop.
Examples – Pass: • Navigation, forms, and services fully usable on mobile.
Examples – Fail: • Key actions unavailable or broken on mobile.
Accessibility Consideration: • Reduces barriers for users with motor or visual impairments relying on mobile devices.
Rationale: Mobile access is the primary entry point for many citizens. Ensuring full access to core functionality on mobile is foundational to equitable service delivery and compliance with mobile compatibility standards.

Title: Implement responsive layouts using flexible grids, fluid images, and media queries
Issue: • Layouts break or overflow on different screen sizes. • Content requires horizontal scrolling. • This degrades usability and accessibility.
Advice: • Use flexible grids and fluid media. • Apply media queries for breakpoints. • Test across device sizes and orientations.
Examples – Pass: • Layout adapts cleanly across screen sizes.
Examples – Fail: • Fixed-width layouts cause overflow.
Accessibility Consideration: • Reflow prevents loss of content for users who zoom or resize text.
Rationale: Responsive design ensures consistent access across devices and orientations, preventing layout-related barriers and supporting scalable digital services.

Title: Design touch targets with adequate size for reliable interaction
Issue: • Touch targets are too small or tightly packed. • Users make accidental taps. • This increases errors and frustration.
Advice: • Ensure minimum touch target size (48×48px). • Add padding around icons. • Use clear visual affordances.
Examples – Pass: • Buttons meet size guidelines and are easy to tap.
Examples – Fail: • Small icons without padding.
Accessibility Consideration: • Improves usability for users with motor impairments.
Rationale: Adequately sized touch targets are critical for error-free interaction on mobile, especially for users with limited motor control or larger fingers.

Title: Provide sufficient spacing between interactive elements to prevent accidental taps
Issue: • Interactive elements are placed too close together. • Users trigger unintended actions. • This increases error rates.
Advice: • Maintain adequate spacing (8–12px or more). • Use grouping and visual separation. • Avoid dense layouts.
Examples – Pass: • Buttons clearly separated and easy to target.
Examples – Fail: • Links clustered too closely.
Accessibility Consideration: • Supports users with tremors or limited dexterity.
Rationale: Proper spacing reduces accidental interactions and improves comfort and accuracy on touch interfaces.

Title: Use mobile-friendly navigation patterns aligned with platform conventions
Issue: • Navigation relies on desktop or hover-based patterns. • Users struggle to find or reach destinations. • This increases abandonment.
Advice: • Use hamburger menus or bottom navigation. • Limit primary options to 3–5 items. • Pair icons with text labels.
Examples – Pass: • Bottom navigation with labeled icons.
Examples – Fail: • Hover-based menus on mobile.
Accessibility Consideration: • Consistent navigation supports screen reader and keyboard users.
Rationale: Familiar mobile navigation patterns reduce learning effort and improve discoverability, especially for first-time users.

Title: Minimize loading time using efficient coding and performance practices
Issue: • Pages load slowly, exceeding acceptable thresholds on mobile. • Users wait or abandon before content becomes usable. • This degrades usability and increases drop-offs.
Advice: • Compress images and media (WebP/SVG). • Prioritize critical resources and defer non-essential assets. • Continuously test and optimize performance.
Examples – Pass: • First meaningful paint occurs quickly and core content is usable under ~2 seconds.
Examples – Fail: • Heavy assets block rendering and delay interaction.
Accessibility Consideration: • Faster loading benefits users on low bandwidth and assistive technologies sensitive to delays.
Rationale: Fast load times are critical for mobile usability and equitable access. Performance optimization reduces abandonment, supports assistive technologies, and aligns with mandated governance standards.

Title: Implement lazy loading for non-critical images and resources
Issue: • Non-essential resources load upfront. • Initial page load is delayed. • Users perceive the site as slow.
Advice: • Lazy load below-the-fold assets. • Use skeletons or placeholders to manage expectations. • Preserve functionality and focus order.
Examples – Pass: • Above-the-fold content loads immediately; below-the-fold assets load on demand.
Examples – Fail: • All media loads at once, delaying first interaction.
Accessibility Consideration: • Proper lazy loading avoids focus jumps and supports keyboard and screen reader users.
Rationale: Lazy loading improves perceived and actual performance by prioritizing essential content, enhancing mobile experience without compromising accessibility.

Title: Allow users to expand sections to view additional details when needed
Issue: • Long content overwhelms users on mobile. • Important actions are pushed out of view. • Users struggle to focus on primary tasks.
Advice: • Use accordions or expandable sections. • Clearly label expand/collapse controls. • Keep primary content visible by default.
Examples – Pass: • Collapsible sections reveal details on tap.
Examples – Fail: • Long uninterrupted content blocks scrolling.
Accessibility Consideration: • Expandable sections help users with attention and cognitive limitations.
Rationale: Progressive disclosure reduces cognitive load on mobile while preserving access to detailed information when required.

Title: Make language selection easily accessible on mobile
Issue: • Language switch is hidden or hard to access. • Users cannot easily change language. • This limits inclusivity.
Advice: • Place language selector prominently in header or mobile menu. • Use clear labels and touch-friendly controls. • Apply selection globally.
Examples – Pass: • Language switch visible and usable on mobile.
Examples – Fail: • Language option buried or inaccessible.
Accessibility Consideration: • Supports users who rely on regional languages for comprehension.
Rationale: Easy access to language selection ensures multilingual inclusivity and equitable access for diverse users.

Title: Provide clear validation and error handling to guide form completion
Issue: • Users encounter errors without guidance. • Forms are abandoned due to unclear feedback. • This increases frustration and failure rates.
Advice: • Implement inline validation with clear messages. • Explain how to fix errors. • Use consistent visual cues for states.
Examples – Pass: • Inline error messages explain fixes clearly.
Examples – Fail: • Generic or missing error feedback.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear error messaging supports users with cognitive and visual impairments.
Rationale: Effective validation and error handling reduce user frustration, prevent data loss, and support accessible form completion across devices.

Title: Ensure the homepage presents a professional and trustworthy first impression
Issue: • Homepage layout appears cluttered or visually unpolished. • Users perceive the site as unofficial or unreliable at first glance. • Poor first impression reduces trust and willingness to engage.
Advice: • Use clean layout with adequate whitespace. • Apply consistent colours, typography, and official symbols. • Limit unnecessary visual noise.
Examples – Pass: • Clean layout with balanced spacing and consistent branding. • Official symbols used correctly.
Examples – Fail: • Overcrowded layout with inconsistent styles. • Poor spacing and visual clutter.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clean layouts reduce cognitive overload and improve readability for all users.
Rationale: The homepage forms the first and most influential trust signal for a government website. A professional visual presentation reassures citizens of authenticity and encourages continued engagement with public services.

Title: Establish a clear visual hierarchy to guide user attention on the homepage
Issue: • Important information is not visually prioritised. • Users struggle to identify what to notice first. • This causes confusion and slower decision-making.
Advice: • Prioritise key content using size, contrast, and placement. • Use headings, spacing, and alignment consistently.
Examples – Pass: • Key actions and messages are visually prominent. • Headings and sections clearly structured.
Examples – Fail: • All elements appear equal in importance. • No clear focus areas on the page.
Accessibility Consideration: • Proper hierarchy improves screen-reader structure and visual scanning.
Rationale: Clear visual hierarchy helps users quickly understand content importance and navigation paths. It improves comprehension, reduces effort, and supports efficient exploration of government services.

Title: Present valuable content on the homepage or within one click
Issue: • Important content requires multiple steps to access. • Users feel effort is high to find useful information. • This reduces engagement and increases abandonment.
Advice: • Place critical content directly on the homepage. • Ensure high-value content is reachable within one click.
Examples – Pass: • Key services and information visible on homepage. • Important content accessible within one click.
Examples – Fail: • Users must navigate through multiple layers to reach core content.
Accessibility Consideration: • Reduced navigation depth benefits users with cognitive or motor impairments.
Rationale: Easy access to valuable content improves engagement and demonstrates user-centric design. Minimising navigation effort increases confidence and encourages continued use of government services.

Title: Reveal homepage information progressively to avoid cognitive overload
Issue: • Homepage presents too much information at once. • Users feel overwhelmed and struggle to identify priorities. • This increases cognitive load and abandonment risk.
Advice: • Show key information first. • Use progressive disclosure for secondary content. • Reveal details on interaction (expand, scroll, navigate).
Examples – Pass: • Key sections visible initially with expandable details.
Examples – Fail: • Long pages with dense content blocks visible at once.
Accessibility Consideration: • Reduces cognitive load for users with attention or memory limitations.
Rationale: Progressive disclosure improves scannability and comprehension, especially on mobile and low-attention contexts. It helps users focus on primary information before engaging with deeper content.

Title: Highlight primary tasks clearly for immediate discovery on the homepage
Issue: • Key user tasks are not visually prominent. • Users must search or scroll excessively to act. • This causes confusion and task failure.
Advice: • Identify top user tasks. • Place them prominently above the fold. • Use clear labels and buttons.
Examples – Pass: • Primary actions clearly visible on page load.
Examples – Fail: • Tasks buried under banners or dense content.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear task grouping supports screen reader navigation and quick access.
Rationale: Clear task prioritization enables faster orientation and action, especially for first-time or low-literacy users accessing government services.

Title: Display recent content with access to archival information
Issue: • Homepage appears static or outdated. • Users cannot find older announcements easily. • This reduces trust and discoverability.
Advice: • Show latest updates prominently. • Provide a clear link to archives or past items.
Examples – Pass: • “Latest Updates” section with archive link.
Examples – Fail: • No recent content or missing archive access.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear content grouping supports users with cognitive limitations.
Rationale: Balancing fresh content with easy archival access signals activity, transparency, and reliability in government communication.

Title: Use visuals to convey meaning rather than decoration
Issue: • Images and icons are decorative without purpose. • Visual clutter distracts users and slows pages. • Content meaning is unclear.
Advice: • Use visuals to explain, guide, or reinforce content. • Remove purely decorative media.
Examples – Pass: • Images support content meaning with alt text.
Examples – Fail: • Stock images unrelated to content purpose.
Accessibility Consideration: • Meaningful visuals support non-text comprehension for screen reader and low-literacy users.
Rationale: Purpose-driven visuals enhance understanding, reduce text dependency, and prevent unnecessary performance and cognitive overhead.

Title: Motivate users to browse and explore further from the homepage
Issue: • Homepage lacks cues that encourage further exploration. • Users do not perceive the site as engaging or active. • Low motivation leads to early exits and shallow engagement.
Advice: • Use inviting layouts, clear section labels, and previews of deeper content. • Highlight pathways to key sections and services.
Examples – Pass: • Homepage includes clear navigation cues, featured sections, or content previews.
Examples – Fail: • Static homepage with no directional cues or engaging elements.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear cues and labels reduce cognitive effort and support predictable navigation.
Rationale: Encouraging exploration increases user engagement and perceived value of government websites. A motivating homepage signals relevance, activity, and usefulness, helping users discover services with less effort.

Title: Clearly communicate the website’s value proposition on the homepage
Issue: • Users cannot quickly understand the purpose of the website. • Absence of a clear message causes disorientation. • This reduces trust and willingness to explore further.
Advice: • Display a concise welcome message or tagline near the top of the page. • Clearly state what the site offers and who it serves.
Examples – Pass: • Homepage displays a clear tagline or purpose statement.
Examples – Fail: • No introductory message or unclear messaging.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear messaging benefits screen-reader users and users with cognitive disabilities.
Rationale: A clear value proposition or welcome message orients users immediately and sets expectations. It reinforces professionalism and helps users decide whether the site is relevant to their needs.

Title: Use descriptive page titles, link text, and semantic labels to improve clarity and discoverability
Issue: • Page titles or links are vague or generic. • Users and search engines struggle to understand link purpose. • This reduces clarity and findability.
Advice: • Use descriptive page titles. • Place key terms at the start of links. • Apply ARIA labels and alt text where required.
Examples – Pass: • Links clearly describe destination (e.g., “Apply for Permit”). • Pages have meaningful titles.
Examples – Fail: • Generic links like “Click here”. • Missing or vague page titles.
Accessibility Consideration: • Descriptive links and titles support screen-reader navigation and comprehension.
Rationale: Descriptive titles and links improve usability, accessibility, and search discoverability. Clear semantics help users quickly understand navigation options and page context.

Title: Group organisational or departmental information into a dedicated section
Issue: • Organisational information is scattered or mixed with services. • Users struggle to locate background or ownership details. • This reduces clarity and perceived credibility.
Advice: • Create a dedicated “About Us” or equivalent section. • Group institutional information separately from services.
Examples – Pass: • “About Us” section clearly groups organisational details.
Examples – Fail: • Organisational information mixed randomly across the homepage.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear sectioning improves navigation for screen-reader and keyboard users.
Rationale: Clear grouping of organisational information improves scannability and transparency. Dedicated sections allow users to quickly verify credibility without cluttering primary service content.

Title: Use a clear, meaningful URL that reflects the website’s purpose
Issue: • URL is cryptic, generic, or unrelated to the site’s purpose. • Users are unsure if they are on the correct or official site. • This reduces trust and increases navigation errors.
Advice: • Use human-readable, descriptive URLs. • Align domain/subdomain names with the service purpose. • Avoid unnecessary parameters or abbreviations.
Examples – Pass: • URL clearly references the service or department name.
Examples – Fail: • Random strings or unrelated abbreviations in the URL.
Accessibility Consideration: • Descriptive URLs help users with cognitive impairments understand context and destination.
Rationale: A clear and meaningful URL acts as an identity signal for government websites. It improves memorability, reduces user error, and strengthens trust by helping citizens quickly validate the legitimacy and intent of the service.

Title: Maintain consistent branding across devices and screen sizes
Issue: • Logos, colors, or fonts vary across devices. • Inconsistent branding confuses users. • This weakens perceived authenticity.
Advice: • Use consistent logos, color palette, and typography. • Follow DBIM branding standards across breakpoints.
Examples – Pass: • Same logo, colors, and fonts on desktop and mobile.
Examples – Fail: • Different branding elements across views.
Accessibility Consideration: • Consistent visuals help users with cognitive disabilities recognize familiar patterns.
Rationale: Visual consistency reinforces official identity and trust. Consistent branding ensures users recognize the service regardless of device, reducing doubt and cognitive friction.

Title: Position navigation controls within thumb-zone reach on mobile
Issue: • Navigation controls are hard to reach with one hand. • Users struggle with repeated stretching or mis-taps. • This reduces mobile usability.
Advice: • Place navigation within thumb-zone reach. • Use platform-standard patterns and adequate target sizes. • Provide visual feedback on interaction.
Examples – Pass: • Menu easily reachable with one thumb.
Examples – Fail: • Navigation placed outside comfortable reach zones.
Accessibility Consideration: • Supports users with limited motor reach or dexterity.
Rationale: Thumb-zone-aware navigation improves one-handed usability on mobile devices, reducing physical strain and interaction errors, especially for frequent tasks.

Title: Provide centralized service discovery from the homepage
Issue: • Users cannot easily find all available services. • Services are fragmented or hidden behind deep navigation. • This increases task time and abandonment.
Advice: • Present a centralized service directory on the homepage. • Group services logically and prioritize high-use services. • Support search and deep linking.
Examples – Pass: • Homepage lists all major services with clear entry points.
Examples – Fail: • Services scattered without a single discovery view.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear service grouping supports users with cognitive limitations and first-time visitors.
Rationale: Centralized service discovery enables citizens to quickly understand the full scope of services offered and access them efficiently, supporting transparency and task-oriented navigation.

Title: Provide guided assistance for advanced or multi-step features on the homepage
Issue: • Advanced or multi-step features lack contextual guidance. • Users are unsure how to start or proceed with complex tasks. • This increases confusion and abandonment.
Advice: • Provide contextual tours, tooltips, or guided walkthroughs. • Trigger assistance on first visit and allow re-access. • Ensure guidance is skippable and non-blocking.
Examples – Pass: • Contextual tour highlights key features with clear steps. • “Help” or “Take a Tour” option available.
Examples – Fail: • Complex features presented with no guidance.
Accessibility Consideration: • Guided tours with clear labels and focus management support screen reader and cognitive accessibility.
Rationale: Guided assistance reduces learning friction for complex features, helping users build confidence and complete tasks efficiently without overwhelming the interface.

Title: Structure homepage information to support rapid scanning and comprehension
Issue: • Content hierarchy is unclear or inconsistent. • Labels are vague or non-descriptive. • Users struggle to locate information quickly.
Advice: • Apply clear visual hierarchy and descriptive headings. • Use semantic markup and consistent labels. • Organize content into scannable sections.
Examples – Pass: • Clear headings and grouped sections visible at a glance.
Examples – Fail: • Dense content blocks with unclear labels.
Accessibility Consideration: • Semantic structure and headings improve navigation for screen reader users.
Rationale: A scannable information architecture enables users to quickly orient, identify relevant sections, and act—critical for high-traffic government homepages.

Title: Clearly define the organisation’s purpose, mission, vision, and values
Issue: • Purpose, mission, or vision is missing or vaguely stated. • Users cannot quickly understand why the organisation exists. • This reduces credibility and clarity of intent.
Advice: • Add a concise “Our Purpose” section. • Clearly list Mission, Vision, and Values in simple language. • Place prominently and link from navigation/footer.
Examples – Pass: • About Us page clearly lists Mission, Vision, and Values in dedicated sections.
Examples – Fail: • About Us page contains generic text with no clear purpose or mission.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear structure supports screen readers and users with cognitive disabilities by improving comprehension.
Rationale: Clearly articulating purpose and values builds trust, transparency, and alignment with citizen expectations, which is foundational for government digital services.

Title: Provide a clear organisational overview describing background and mandate
Issue: • Organisation background and mandate are unclear or missing. • Users cannot identify who operates the service. • This weakens transparency and accountability.
Advice: • Add a structured organisational overview. • Use headings such as “Who We Are” and “Our Journey”. • Include concise supporting visuals if relevant.
Examples – Pass: • About Us page explains organisational background and mandate clearly.
Examples – Fail: • Only generic or marketing text with no organisational detail.
Accessibility Consideration: • Structured headings and semantic sections improve navigation for assistive technologies.
Rationale: Providing organisational context establishes legitimacy and accountability, which are critical for citizen-facing governance platforms.

Title: Clearly outline the organisation’s core values
Issue: • Core values are missing or buried in text. • Users cannot understand guiding principles. • This reduces perceived ethics and trustworthiness.
Advice: • Add a dedicated “Our Core Values” section. • List 3–5 concise values with short descriptions. • Place near mission and vision.
Examples – Pass: • Clearly labelled “Core Values” section with short descriptions.
Examples – Fail: • Values implied indirectly or not stated at all.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear labels and contrast support readability for low-vision and cognitive users.
References: GIGW 3.0 – Section 3.1.4; DBIM; WCAG 2.1 SC 2.4.6; BIS IS 17428:2020
Rationale: Explicitly stating values communicates ethics, accountability, and intent, strengthening institutional trust.

Title: Introduce key leaders and team members with roles and responsibilities
Issue: • Leadership information is missing or unclear. • Users cannot identify responsible authorities. • This weakens transparency and accountability.
Advice: • Add a “Our Leadership” or “Who’s Who” section. • Include names, roles, and brief bios. • Place logically within About Us.
Examples – Pass: • Leadership section lists key members with roles and short bios.
Examples – Fail: • No mention of leadership or responsible officials.
Accessibility Consideration: • Proper headings and structured bios support screen reader navigation.
Rationale: Leadership visibility reinforces accountability and helps users associate services with responsible authorities.

Title: Highlight significant achievements and milestones
Issue: • Key achievements or milestones are missing or hard to find. • Users cannot assess impact or credibility. • Trust and transparency are weakened.
Advice: • Add a clearly labeled “Achievements” or “Milestones” section. • Use a simple timeline or grid with dates and outcomes. • Keep content concise and verifiable.
Examples – Pass: • Timeline showing milestones like awards, scale reached, or major launches.
Examples – Fail: • Achievements buried in long paragraphs or not present at all.
Accessibility Consideration: • Structured headings and clear labels support screen readers and users with cognitive disabilities.
References: GIGW 3.0 – Section 3.1.4; DBIM Public Accountability Guidelines; WCAG 2.1 SC 2.4.6
Rationale: Showcasing achievements builds institutional credibility and reassures users of legitimacy and impact.

Title: Include a brief history of the organisation
Issue: • Organisational background is missing. • Users lack context on origin and evolution. • Identity and trust signals are weakened.
Advice: • Add a short history section with key dates. • Use a lightweight visual timeline. • Place near achievements or overview.
Examples – Pass: • “Our Journey” section summarizing key phases with dates.
Examples – Fail: • No historical context or only vague statements.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear structure and readable text support comprehension for assistive technology users.
References: GIGW 3.0 – Section 3.1.4; DBIM Organisational Identity Guidelines
Rationale: A concise history provides context, continuity, and legitimacy for citizen-facing services.

Title: Use authentic images or videos to humanize the organisation
Issue: • About Us page feels impersonal. • Users cannot visually connect with the organisation. • Perceived authenticity is reduced.
Advice: • Include real images or short videos of team or workplace. • Use captions and consistent layout. • Ensure media is inclusive and relevant.
Examples – Pass: • Team photos with captions and alt text.
Examples – Fail: • Stock images unrelated to the organisation or no media at all.
Accessibility Consideration: • Alt text and captions ensure non-text content is accessible to screen reader users.
References: GIGW 3.0 – Section 3.1.4; DBIM Visual Identity & Engagement Guidelines
Rationale: Authentic visuals humanize the organisation, increasing trust and emotional connection.

Title: Provide links to related sections to encourage exploration
Issue: • Users reach a dead end on About Us. • Related information is not discoverable. • Engagement opportunities are missed.
Advice: • Add a small “Explore More” section with relevant links. • Ensure links are clearly labeled and accessible. • Place logically at the end of the page.
Examples – Pass: • Visible links to Careers, News, or Press pages.
Examples – Fail: • No outbound links or vague “Click here” links.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear link purpose supports keyboard and screen reader navigation.
Rationale: Cross-linking improves discoverability, engagement, and task continuation across the site.

Title: Follow recognized scanning patterns (F-pattern / Z-pattern)
Issue: • Layout does not align with natural reading and scanning behavior. • Important content is placed outside common visual scan paths. • Users miss key information or actions.
Advice: • Arrange content to follow F-shaped or Z-shaped scanning patterns. • Place critical headings, CTAs, and links along primary scan paths.
Examples – Pass: • Key information appears along top and left-aligned scan areas.
Examples – Fail: • Important actions placed randomly or far from scan paths.
Accessibility Consideration: • Predictable visual flow helps users with cognitive and attention limitations process content efficiently.
References: GIGW 3.0 – Section 2.2.5; DBIM; BIS IS 17428:2020; WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.3
Rationale: Aligning layouts with natural scanning behavior reduces cognitive effort, improves discoverability, and supports efficient task completion.

Title: Make webpage content easy to scan without cognitive overload
Issue: • Content appears dense and difficult to scan. • Lack of hierarchy makes it hard to locate information quickly. • Users feel overwhelmed and disengage.
Advice: • Use clear headings, short paragraphs, and grouped content. • Apply strong visual hierarchy and whitespace.
Examples – Pass: • Page uses headings, bullets, and spacing to guide scanning.
Examples – Fail: • Large text blocks with no hierarchy or spacing.
Accessibility Consideration: • Improved scanability supports users with cognitive disabilities and low literacy.
Rationale: Scan-friendly layouts reduce mental load and help users find information quickly, improving usability and confidence.

Title: Ensure screen density is appropriate for target users and tasks
Issue: • Content is too dense or too sparse for user needs. • Readability and task efficiency suffer. • Interface feels cluttered or inefficient.
Advice: • Adjust spacing, font size, and content chunking based on user context. • Maintain clean hierarchy and adequate whitespace.
Examples – Pass: • Layout balances readability and information density for target users.
Examples – Fail: • Overcrowded screens or excessive empty space.
Accessibility Consideration: • Proper density benefits users with visual, motor, or cognitive limitations.
Rationale: Appropriate screen density improves readability, reduces errors, and supports diverse user groups across devices.

Title: Use legible fonts and font sizes to ensure readability and accessibility
Issue: • Fonts are too small or hard to read. • Poor contrast or spacing reduces legibility. • Users struggle to read content.
Advice: • Use readable sans-serif fonts with minimum 16px body text. • Ensure sufficient contrast and line spacing. • Support text resizing up to 200%.
Examples – Pass: • Text is clearly readable with proper size, spacing, and contrast.
Examples – Fail: • Small fonts, low contrast, or cramped text.
Accessibility Consideration: • Essential for users with low vision, dyslexia, or cognitive impairments.
Rationale: Legible typography is foundational for accessibility, comprehension, and inclusive design across all digital services.

Title: Guide users’ focus toward the next action using clear visual cues
Issue: • Page layout does not clearly indicate the next step. • Users hesitate or miss the primary action. • This increases friction and task abandonment.
Advice: • Use strong visual hierarchy and directional cues. • Highlight the primary CTA with color, size, and placement. • Apply progressive disclosure to sequence actions logically.
Examples – Pass: • A prominent “Continue” or “Next” CTA appears after completing a step.
Examples – Fail: • Multiple CTAs compete equally with no clear priority.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear focus order and prominent CTAs help screen reader and cognitive users identify the intended next step.
Rationale: Guiding user focus reduces decision fatigue and supports intuitive task progression, improving completion rates and user confidence.

Title: Provide a clear visual starting point on every page
Issue: • Pages lack a clear entry point or focal element. • Users are unsure where to begin. • This increases orientation time and confusion.
Advice: • Introduce a prominent heading, hero, or key CTA at the top. • Maintain consistent entry-point patterns across pages.
Examples – Pass: • Page opens with a clear heading or hero guiding attention.
Examples – Fail: • Page begins with dense content and no focal point.
Accessibility Consideration: • Strong entry points support users with cognitive impairments by improving orientation and predictability.
Rationale: A clear starting point orients users quickly, reducing cognitive load and improving navigation efficiency.

Title: Maintain consistent layout across all pages and devices
Issue: • Layout patterns vary across pages or platforms. • Users must relearn navigation repeatedly. • This reduces trust and usability.
Advice: • Use shared layout templates and a design system. • Keep navigation, headers, and footers consistent.
Examples – Pass: • Pages follow the same structural layout across the site/app.
Examples – Fail: • Different pages use inconsistent layouts and patterns.
Accessibility Consideration: • Consistency benefits screen reader users and users with cognitive disabilities by reducing learning effort.
Rationale: Consistent layouts reinforce familiarity, reduce cognitive load, and support efficient navigation across journeys.

Title: Place high-priority information above the first screen
Issue: • Important features are hidden below the fold. • Users must scroll to access frequent actions. • This reduces efficiency.
Advice: • Position commonly used features above the fold. • Prioritize key actions and content in the first screen.
Examples – Pass: • Login, search, or primary services visible on page load.
Examples – Fail: • Key actions only visible after scrolling.
Accessibility Consideration: • Above-the-fold placement benefits users with motor or cognitive limitations by reducing effort.
Rationale: Surfacing high-priority content early improves efficiency and supports task-oriented user behavior, especially on mobile.

Title: Make clickable elements clearly recognizable as interactive
Issue: • Clickable elements lack visual affordances. • Users fail to recognize buttons or links. • This causes hesitation, errors, and task abandonment.
Advice: • Use consistent visual cues (shape, color, underline, hover/focus states). • Differentiate buttons from static content. • Maintain consistent styles across pages and devices.
Examples – Pass: • Buttons have solid fills or outlines with hover/focus states; links are underlined and color-distinct.
Examples – Fail: • Clickable text styled like body copy; buttons indistinguishable from cards or labels.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear affordances and focus states support keyboard and screen reader users in identifying actionable elements.
Rationale: Clear interactivity cues are foundational to predictable navigation and task completion, reducing cognitive load and preventing user errors.

Title: Avoid false visual affordances on non-clickable elements
Issue: • Non-interactive items visually resemble clickable elements. • Users attempt interactions that do nothing. • This causes confusion and loss of trust.
Advice: • Ensure only interactive elements look clickable. • Remove underlines, hover states, shadows, or button styling from static content.
Examples – Pass: • Headings and labels appear as plain text with no hover or underline.
Examples – Fail: • Static text styled like a button or link.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear affordances reduce confusion for users with cognitive disabilities and screen reader users relying on role clarity.
Rationale: Preventing false affordances ensures predictable interaction and reduces user errors, which is essential for trustworthy government interfaces.

Title: Use interactive components appropriately and label actions clearly
Issue: • Interactive controls are unclear or ambiguously labeled. • Non-interactive items resemble controls. • Users are unsure what actions are possible.
Advice: • Use standard components (buttons, checkboxes, radios) for actions. • Apply clear, action-oriented labels. • Avoid styling static items as controls.
Examples – Pass: • Buttons labeled “Submit Form” or “Download Report”.
Examples – Fail: • Vague labels like “Click Here” or decorative elements styled as controls.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear labeling and component roles support screen reader users and reduce cognitive load.
Rationale: Proper use of interactive components improves action clarity and prevents errors, supporting predictable and accessible interactions.

Title: Make hyperlinked text visually distinguishable
Issue: • Links are visually indistinguishable from body text. • Users miss available navigation paths. • This reduces discoverability.
Advice: • Style links using consistent cues (underline, color contrast). • Avoid hover-only link visibility.
Examples – Pass: • Links are underlined and color-distinct from body text.
Examples – Fail: • Links appear identical to normal text.
Accessibility Consideration: • Distinct link styling benefits low-vision users and keyboard users navigating by links.
Rationale: Clearly identifiable links are essential for navigation efficiency and accessibility compliance.

Title: Use standard and intuitive icons and graphics
Issue: • Icons are custom or ambiguous. • Users misinterpret meaning. • This increases cognitive load.
Advice: • Use widely recognized icons. • Prefer established icon libraries. • Pair icons with labels where needed.
Examples – Pass: • Magnifying glass icon used for search.
Examples – Fail: • Abstract or decorative icons with unclear meaning.
Accessibility Consideration: • Standard icons improve comprehension for cognitive and low-literacy users.
Rationale: Recognizable icons reduce learning effort and support faster comprehension across diverse user groups.

Title: Use a consistent font style across the webpage
Issue: • Multiple font families used inconsistently. • Visual inconsistency increases cognitive load. • Brand perception weakens.
Advice: • Use a single primary font family across pages. • Limit variations to weight and size only.
Examples – Pass: • One font family (e.g., Noto Sans) used consistently.
Examples – Fail: • Multiple unrelated fonts used across sections.
Accessibility Consideration: • Consistent typography improves readability for users with dyslexia and cognitive impairments.
References: BIS IS 17428:2020 Clause 8.2.3; DBIM Typography Guidelines
Rationale: Consistent typography reduces visual noise, strengthens brand identity, and improves comprehension across pages and languages.

Title: Use color to group and organize content for clear visual hierarchy
Issue: • Content lacks visual grouping. • Users struggle to identify relationships and priorities. • Page appears flat or cluttered.
Advice: • Apply a consistent color palette for grouping. • Use color to differentiate primary, secondary, and background elements.
Examples – Pass: • Related sections grouped using background color or accents.
Examples – Fail: • Random or inconsistent color usage with no grouping logic.
Accessibility Consideration: • Color-based grouping must not be the sole indicator; pair with spacing or labels for accessibility.
Rationale: Strategic color usage improves scannability, hierarchy recognition, and faster comprehension of page structure.

Title: Maintain a harmonious, accessible color scheme with sufficient contrast
Issue: • Low contrast text reduces readability. • Busy or distracting backgrounds hinder comprehension. • Accessibility standards are violated.
Advice: • Use harmonious color palettes. • Ensure WCAG contrast ratios (4.5:1 normal text; 3:1 large text). • Avoid textured or busy backgrounds.
Examples – Pass: • Dark text on light background meeting contrast ratios.
Examples – Fail: • Low-contrast text over patterned backgrounds.
Accessibility Consideration: • Essential for users with low vision, color blindness, or aging-related vision loss.
Rationale: Accessible color schemes are foundational to inclusive design, ensuring content is perceivable by all users.

Title: Provide print-friendly pages or printable versions
Issue: • Printed pages include navigation and clutter. • Content is hard to read when printed. • Users waste time formatting manually.
Advice: • Apply print-specific CSS styles. • Remove non-essential elements. • Offer a dedicated “Print Version” where relevant.
Examples – Pass: • Clean print layout with only essential content.
Examples – Fail: • Printed page includes menus, ads, and backgrounds.
Accessibility Consideration: • High-contrast, simplified print layouts benefit users relying on physical copies.
Rationale: Print-friendly layouts support offline access, documentation needs, and accessibility for users preferring physical records.

Title: Avoid italics and reserve underlining only for hyperlinks
Issue: • Italicized text reduces readability. • Underlining used for non-links misleads users. • Users confuse static text with interactive elements.
Advice: • Use bold text for emphasis instead of italics. • Restrict underlining strictly to hyperlinks.
Examples – Pass: • Emphasis shown using bold text; only links are underlined.
Examples – Fail: • Long italic paragraphs; underlined headings that are not links.
Accessibility Consideration: • Improves readability for users with dyslexia and low vision; prevents false affordances for assistive technology users.
Rationale: Clear and consistent text styling prevents confusion, improves readability, and maintains predictable interaction patterns.

Title: Use a grid system for structured and aligned layouts
Issue: • Content lacks alignment and visual balance. • Pages appear cluttered or inconsistent. • Scanning becomes inefficient.
Advice: • Apply a consistent grid system (e.g., 12-column). • Align text, images, and components both horizontally and vertically.
Examples – Pass: • Cards, text, and images align cleanly within a grid.
Examples – Fail: • Elements appear misaligned or arbitrarily placed.
Accessibility Consideration: • Structured layouts improve navigation for screen reader users and users with cognitive limitations.
Rationale: Grid-based layouts ensure visual order, predictability, and responsive consistency across devices.

Title: Group related information and functions for efficient scanning
Issue: • Related content and actions are scattered. • Users must jump across the page to complete tasks. • Cognitive load increases.
Advice: • Group related items using cards, sections, or containers. • Use spacing and headings to reinforce grouping.
Examples – Pass: • Filters grouped with search; form fields grouped with submit action.
Examples – Fail: • Related controls placed far apart with no visual grouping.
Accessibility Consideration: • Logical grouping improves comprehension for users with cognitive and memory impairments.
Rationale: Logical grouping reduces mental effort and enables faster task execution and scanning.

Title: Structure pages section-by-section to aid element discovery
Issue: • Page content lacks clear sections. • Users struggle to locate information. • Navigation feels chaotic.
Advice: • Use clear sectioning with headings (H1–H3). • Apply semantic landmarks (nav, main, footer).
Examples – Pass: • Page divided into clear sections with descriptive headings.
Examples – Fail: • Long unbroken pages with no structural cues.
Accessibility Consideration: • Semantic structure improves screen reader navigation and keyboard accessibility.
Rationale: Well-structured pages improve findability, orientation, and accessibility for all users.

Title: Maintain consistent logo placement across all pages
Issue: • Logo placement varies across pages. • Brand recognition weakens. • Users lose a familiar navigation anchor.
Advice: • Place logo consistently (typically top-left). • Link logo to homepage on all pages.
Examples – Pass: • Logo appears in the same position on every page and links home.
Examples – Fail: • Logo position changes or is missing on some pages.
Accessibility Consideration: • Consistent logo placement supports cognitive predictability and quick orientation.
Rationale: Consistent logo placement reinforces brand identity and provides a reliable navigation reference point.

Title: Ensure clicking the logo navigates to the homepage
Issue: • Logo does not link to the homepage. • Users lose a common navigation shortcut. • Orientation and trust are reduced.
Advice: • Link the logo to the homepage on all pages. • Keep placement consistent and avoid decorative-only usage.
Examples – Pass: • Logo at top-left links to homepage across all pages.
Examples – Fail: • Logo is static or links to a non-home destination.
Accessibility Consideration: • Predictable logo behavior supports cognitive accessibility and keyboard navigation.
Rationale: Linking the logo to the homepage aligns with user expectations and provides a reliable navigation anchor.

Title: Use attention-grabbing elements sparingly and purposefully
Issue: • Excessive animation or bright colors distract users. • Visual noise overwhelms content. • Accessibility risks increase.
Advice: • Apply motion, color, and size changes only to emphasize critical items. • Keep animations subtle and WCAG-compliant.
Examples – Pass: • Subtle animation highlights a primary CTA only.
Examples – Fail: • Multiple flashing elements competing for attention.
Accessibility Consideration: • Reduces risk for users sensitive to motion or visual overload.
Rationale: Controlled use of emphasis preserves usability, focus, and accessibility while still guiding attention.

Title: Align UI components with overall theme and branding
Issue: • Components appear visually inconsistent. • Brand coherence is weakened. • User confidence decreases.
Advice: • Use design system components. • Match colors, typography, and styles to brand guidelines.
Examples – Pass: • Search bar and controls match brand palette and typography.
Examples – Fail: • Third-party or mismatched components break visual unity.
Accessibility Consideration: • Consistent theming improves recognition for users with cognitive impairments.
References: DBIM Branding & UI Guidelines; GIGW 3.0 Quality; WCAG 2.1 SC 1.4.3, 3.2.4
Rationale: Brand-aligned components create a cohesive experience and reinforce legitimacy.

Title: Provide access to underlying data for graphs and charts
Issue: • Charts convey information only visually. • Users cannot access exact values. • Non-visual users are excluded.
Advice: • Add data labels, tooltips, or tables alongside charts. • Ensure keyboard and screen reader access.
Examples – Pass: • Bar chart includes numeric labels or accessible data table.
Examples – Fail: • Chart without labels or alternative data access.
Accessibility Consideration: • Ensures non-text content is perceivable to screen reader users.
Rationale: Providing data access ensures equitable understanding and meets non-text content accessibility requirements.

Title: Apply visual hierarchy to guide attention and information flow
Issue: • Content lacks clear hierarchy. • Users struggle to identify priorities. • Information flow is unclear.
Advice: • Use size, color, spacing, and positioning to establish hierarchy. • Follow scanning patterns and contrast requirements.
Examples – Pass: • Headings, CTAs, and primary content clearly stand out.
Examples – Fail: • Uniform sizing and color make priorities unclear.
Accessibility Consideration: • Strong hierarchy aids users with cognitive and visual impairments in understanding structure.
Rationale: Visual hierarchy directs attention efficiently, reducing cognitive load and improving task success.

Title: Apply a systematic typography scale for readability and comprehension
Issue: • Inconsistent font sizes, weights, or spacing across headings and body text. • Poor readability and comprehension. • Visual hierarchy breaks down.
Advice: • Implement a defined type scale across headings and body text. • Maintain consistent line height, letter spacing, and paragraph spacing. • Support responsive and scalable typography.
Examples – Pass: • H1/H2/H3/body follow a documented scale with consistent spacing and contrast.
Examples – Fail: • Arbitrary font sizes and spacing used across screens.
Accessibility Consideration: • Consistent spacing and scalable text support low-vision users and users relying on text resizing.
References: WCAG 2.1 SC 1.4.8, 1.4.12; WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.11; DBIM Typography; GIGW 3.0 – 5.2
