Rationale: Systematic typography improves readability, hierarchy clarity, and inclusive comprehension across devices.

Title: Apply a consistent visual identity system across all touchpoints
Issue: • Colors, typography, icons, or logos are inconsistently applied. • Brand coherence weakens. • User trust is reduced.
Advice: • Use DBIM-defined colors, icons, typography, and logo lockups. • Enforce consistency via templates and audits.
Examples – Pass: • All screens follow DBIM palette, typography, and icon style.
Examples – Fail: • Mixed icon styles, fonts, or color palettes across screens.
Accessibility Consideration: • Consistent identity improves recognition for users with cognitive impairments.
Rationale: A consistent visual identity reinforces trust, legitimacy, and usability across digital touchpoints.

Title: Maintain comprehensive design system documentation
Issue: • Reusable components and rules are undocumented. • Inconsistent implementation occurs across teams. • Accessibility rules are missed.
Advice: • Document components, tokens, patterns, and accessibility rules. • Provide usage guidelines and handoff specs.
Examples – Pass: • Centralized design system with components, tokens, and accessibility notes.
Examples – Fail: • Ad-hoc designs recreated without guidance.
Accessibility Consideration: • Documented accessibility rules support consistent inclusive implementation.
References: GIGW 3.0 – 5.1; DBIM Component Library & UX Kit
Rationale: Design system documentation ensures scalability, consistency, and governance across teams and releases.

Title: Manage information density using grouping and progressive disclosure
Issue: • Screens present too much information at once. • Users feel overwhelmed. • Key content is hard to locate.
Advice: • Group related content into cards or sections. • Use accordions, tabs, and “Show more” patterns. • Apply adequate whitespace.
Examples – Pass: • Content grouped into cards with expandable sections.
Examples – Fail: • Long unstructured lists and dense screens.
Accessibility Consideration: • Progressive disclosure benefits users with cognitive or attention limitations.
Rationale: Controlled information density reduces cognitive load and improves scanability and task success.

Title: Ensure interface affordances clearly communicate functionality
Issue: • Interactive elements lack clear affordances. • Users cannot predict what is clickable. • Errors and hesitation increase.
Advice: • Use clear shapes, colors, icons, and states for interactivity. • Provide hover, focus, active, and disabled states. • Meet minimum touch target sizes.
Examples – Pass: • Buttons have clear depth, states, and labels; links are distinct.
Examples – Fail: • Interactive items look like static content.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear affordances and states support keyboard and screen reader users.
Rationale: Clear affordances are foundational to predictable interaction and efficient task completion.

Title: Use rich media purposefully to enhance understanding without clutter
Issue: • Rich media is overused or decorative without informational value. • Media causes clutter, distraction, or accessibility barriers. • Performance and comprehension are negatively impacted.
Advice: • Use images, videos, audio, and animations only when they aid understanding. • Provide alt text, captions, transcripts, and user controls. • Respect reduced-motion preferences and optimize performance.
Examples – Pass: • Images have meaningful alt text, videos include captions, animations are subtle and optional.
Examples – Fail: • Decorative images without alt text, autoplay videos, excessive animations.
Accessibility Consideration: • Non-text alternatives, captions, audio controls, and reduced motion support users with visual, auditory, or vestibular impairments.
Rationale: Purposeful rich media improves comprehension while avoiding cognitive overload, accessibility violations, and performance degradation.

Title: Implement platform-specific design patterns while maintaining unified brand identity
Issue: • Native platform conventions are ignored. • Interfaces feel unfamiliar or inconsistent with OS expectations. • Brand identity becomes fragmented across platforms.
Advice: • Follow iOS HIG and Material Design guidelines per platform. • Use native components and gestures. • Maintain DBIM colors, typography intent, and branding consistently.
Examples – Pass: • iOS uses tab bars and SF symbols; Android uses Material components, both retaining DBIM branding.
Examples – Fail: • Same UI patterns forced across iOS and Android without adaptation.
Accessibility Consideration: • Native components improve accessibility support provided by the operating system.
Rationale: Respecting platform conventions reduces learning effort while a unified brand system preserves trust and recognition.

Title: Maintain consistent branding across all screen sizes
Issue: • Logos, colours, or fonts change across breakpoints. • Brand recognition weakens on smaller screens. • Visual trust is reduced.
Advice: • Use reusable branding components and a unified style guide. • Lock logo placement, colour tokens, and font families across breakpoints.
Examples – Pass: • Logo, colours, and fonts remain identical on desktop and mobile views.
Examples – Fail: • Logo disappears or colours/fonts change on mobile view.
Accessibility Consideration: • Consistent branding improves recognition for users with cognitive impairments and reduces disorientation.
References: GIGW 3.0 – 2.1.4; DBIM Branding Guidelines; BIS IS 17428:2020; BIS IS 17802:2022
Rationale: Branding consistency across responsive layouts reinforces trust, legitimacy, and recognition for government services.

Title: Design touch-friendly elements with adequate spacing
Issue: • Buttons and links are too small or too close. • Accidental taps occur. • Mobile usability degrades.
Advice: • Maintain minimum 48×48px touch targets. • Keep 8–12px spacing between interactive elements. • Design for finger ergonomics.
Examples – Pass: • Buttons are large, well-spaced, and easy to tap on mobile.
Examples – Fail: • Small, tightly packed buttons cause mis-taps.
Accessibility Consideration: • Adequate target size and spacing support users with motor impairments.
Rationale: Proper touch spacing reduces errors, frustration, and task failure on touch devices.

Title: Optimize images and media for responsive resizing
Issue: • Images do not resize correctly across screens. • Layout breaks or content overflows. • Performance suffers.
Advice: • Use responsive images with srcset. • Compress media and prevent fixed dimensions. • Ensure images reflow correctly.
Examples – Pass: • Images resize fluidly without distortion across breakpoints.
Examples – Fail: • Images overflow containers or appear cropped on small screens.
Accessibility Consideration: • Responsive images support zoom and reflow for low-vision users.
Rationale: Responsive media preserves visual integrity, performance, and accessibility across devices.

Title: Optimize performance for mobile devices
Issue: • Heavy files and scripts slow mobile loading. • Users abandon pages. • Battery and data usage increase.
Advice: • Minify CSS/JS, compress media. • Lazy-load non-critical content. • Prioritize above-the-fold resources.
Examples – Pass: • Pages load quickly on mobile under typical network conditions.
Examples – Fail: • Long load times due to large scripts and media.
Accessibility Consideration: • Faster performance benefits users with limited bandwidth or assistive technologies.
Rationale: Mobile performance optimization directly impacts usability, retention, and service completion.

Title: Use responsive containers to maintain layout structure
Issue: • Fixed widths break layout on different screens. • Content alignment becomes inconsistent.
Advice: • Use container-based layouts with breakpoints. • Avoid hardcoded widths. • Apply adaptive spacing.
Examples – Pass: • Layout scales proportionally across screen sizes.
Examples – Fail: • Fixed-width layouts cause horizontal scrolling.
Accessibility Consideration: • Proper reflow supports users who zoom or use small screens.
References: DBIM Responsive Design Guidelines; WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.10; GIGW 3.0 Layout Consistency
Rationale: Responsive containers ensure structural consistency and predictable navigation across devices.

Title: Implement a flexible, adaptive grid layout across devices
Issue: • Layout does not adapt smoothly across screen sizes. • Alignment breaks on smaller devices.
Advice: • Use a responsive grid (e.g., 12-column) with CSS Grid/Flexbox. • Define gutters and responsive breakpoints.
Examples – Pass: • Grid reflows correctly across desktop, mobile view, and app screens.
Examples – Fail: • Fixed columns cause overlap or horizontal scroll.
Accessibility Consideration: • Proper reflow supports zoom and small screens without loss of content.
Rationale: Adaptive grids preserve structure and predictability across devices, reducing usability errors.

Title: Adjust text size and line height for readable content across devices
Issue: • Text is too small or dense on some screens. • Users must zoom to read.
Advice: • Use relative units (rem/em). • Maintain line height 1.4–1.6 and optimal line length.
Examples – Pass: • Text remains readable without zoom on all devices.
Examples – Fail: • Fixed px fonts cause cramped or tiny text on mobile.
Accessibility Consideration: • Supports text resizing and readability for low-vision users.
Rationale: Responsive typography improves comprehension and reduces visual strain.

Title: Use CSS media queries to adapt styles by screen size
Issue: • Styles do not adapt at breakpoints. • Layout and spacing feel inconsistent.
Advice: • Apply CSS media queries for layout, spacing, and typography. • Prefer CSS over JS for resizing.
Examples – Pass: • Breakpoints adjust layout and spacing cleanly.
Examples – Fail: • Single static stylesheet across all screens.
Accessibility Consideration: • Proper reflow and contrast at breakpoints aid accessibility.
References: WCAG 2.1 SC 1.4.10; GIGW 3.0 Responsive Web Design
Rationale: Media queries enable predictable, accessible adaptation across viewports.

Title: Create fluid layouts using relative units
Issue: • Fixed units prevent smooth resizing. • Visual hierarchy breaks across screens.
Advice: • Use %, vw, rem for widths and spacing. • Avoid fixed pixel layouts.
Examples – Pass: • Layout scales proportionally across devices.
Examples – Fail: • Fixed-width containers cause overflow.
Accessibility Consideration: • Fluid layouts support zoom and varied device sizes.
Rationale: Fluid layouts ensure continuity and adaptability across form factors.

Title: Include viewport meta tag for proper mobile rendering
Issue: • Pages render zoomed-out or broken on mobile. • Touch interaction is impaired.
Advice: • Add viewport meta tag with device width and initial scale.
Examples – Pass: • Page renders correctly on mobile browsers.
Examples – Fail: • Mobile page appears tiny and requires zoom.
Accessibility Consideration: • Enables proper reflow and zoom behavior on mobile devices.
References: GIGW 3.0 Responsive Web Design; DBIM Mobile Guidelines; BIS IS 17802:2022 Part 1 – 7.4.4; WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.10
Rationale: Viewport configuration is foundational for responsive and accessible mobile rendering.

Title: Allow exploration of key content without login
Issue: • Users are forced to log in before understanding value. • Early trust and discoverability are reduced.
Advice: • Keep informational content, FAQs, guides, and eligibility openly accessible. • Gate only user-specific actions.
Examples – Pass: • Users can browse services, FAQs, and guides without authentication.
Examples – Fail: • Login wall blocks all content at entry.
Accessibility Consideration: • Open access supports users with cognitive load sensitivity and reduces anxiety.
References: GIGW 3.0 UX Discoverability; DBIM Section 3.3; BIS IS 17802:2022 Clause 8.3.1
Rationale: Allowing exploration before login builds trust, clarity, and informed decision-making before commitment.

Title: Provide teaser or preview of premium features
Issue: • Users cannot assess value before signing up. • Engagement motivation is low.
Advice: • Show limited previews, blurred data, or demo states for premium features.
Examples – Pass: • Demo dashboards and sample results visible pre-login.
Examples – Fail: • No indication of premium value until after signup.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear previews reduce uncertainty and cognitive friction.
References: DBIM 3.3; GIGW 3.0 Engagement Design; BIS IS 17802:2022 Clause 8.3.3
Rationale: Teasers balance transparency with controlled access, improving conversion without misleading users.

Title: Restrict interactive actions for non-logged-in users
Issue: • Sensitive or data-modifying actions are exposed. • Security and data integrity risks arise.
Advice: • Allow browsing but restrict actions like apply, comment, or submit to logged-in users.
Examples – Pass: • “Apply” or “Save” requires login, browsing remains open.
Examples – Fail: • Anonymous users can submit forms or modify data.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear gating prevents accidental data submission and confusion.
References: GIGW 3.0 Security 2.3, 3.5.1; DBIM 4.3; BIS IS 17802:2022 Clause 6.2.4
Rationale: Separating exploration from action ensures usability without compromising security.

Title: Integrate single sign-on (SSO) for seamless authentication
Issue: • Users face repeated or complex login flows. • Drop-offs occur at authentication.
Advice: • Integrate government-approved SSO for unified access across services.
Examples – Pass: • User logs in once and accesses multiple services seamlessly.
Examples – Fail: • Separate credentials required for each service.
Accessibility Consideration: • SSO reduces cognitive effort and repetitive input for users.
Rationale: SSO improves continuity, efficiency, and trust in government digital ecosystems.

Title: Provide offline access to previously viewed content
Issue: • Users lose access in low-connectivity scenarios. • Critical information becomes unavailable.
Advice: • Cache static and viewed content using service workers or local storage.
Examples – Pass: • FAQs and guides accessible offline after first view.
Examples – Fail: • No content available without connectivity.
Accessibility Consideration: • Offline access benefits users in low-bandwidth or rural areas.
Rationale: Offline access increases resilience and inclusivity in real-world usage conditions.

Title: Prompt login when accessing restricted features
Issue: • Users are blocked without explanation. • Abrupt interruptions cause frustration.
Advice: • Show contextual login/signup prompts when restricted actions are attempted.
Examples – Pass: • Inline or modal prompt appears when user clicks “Save” or “Apply.”
Examples – Fail: • Hard redirect to login without context.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear prompts reduce confusion for assistive technology users.
Rationale: Contextual access gating preserves flow while enforcing authentication rules.

Title: Provide accessible and discoverable search for guest users
Issue: • Guest users cannot find content efficiently. • Search is hidden, limited, or unavailable without login. • Users struggle with typos or vague queries.
Advice: • Expose search without authentication. • Support autocomplete, spell correction, filters, and sorting. • Ensure keyboard and screen reader accessibility.
Examples – Pass: • Persistent search bar visible pre-login with suggestions, filters, and accessible results.
Examples – Fail: • Search hidden behind login or returns poor/no results for common queries.
Accessibility Consideration: • Proper ARIA roles, keyboard navigation, and clear result structure support screen reader and keyboard users.
Rationale: Search is a primary discovery mechanism; making it accessible pre-login significantly improves findability and task success.

Title: Enable content sharing via social media and copy links
Issue: • Users cannot easily share useful content. • Outreach and awareness are limited.
Advice: • Provide contextual social sharing buttons and copy-link options without clutter.
Examples – Pass: • Articles and service pages include share buttons (e.g., WhatsApp, X, copy link).
Examples – Fail: • No sharing options or intrusive, cluttered share controls.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clearly labeled share controls support assistive technology users.
Rationale: Easy content sharing increases reach, transparency, and citizen awareness without forcing registration.

Title: Communicate registration value proposition clearly and voluntarily
Issue: • Users do not understand why registration is beneficial. • Registration feels forced or unclear.
Advice: • Clearly explain benefits of registration. • Keep opt-in voluntary. • Avoid dark patterns and blocking critical services.
Examples – Pass: • Guest users see clear benefits like saved history, personalization, and faster services before signing up.
Examples – Fail: • Registration required without explanation or incentives.
Accessibility Consideration: • Transparent messaging reduces anxiety and supports informed consent for all users.
Rationale: Clear value communication increases voluntary sign-ups while maintaining trust and ethical onboarding.

Title: Integrate government-approved SSO API for seamless authentication
Issue: • Users must create separate credentials per service. • Login friction and drop-offs increase. • Identity trust is fragmented.
Advice: • Integrate Meri Pehchaan SSO API with approved IDPs (DigiLocker, Parichay, e-Pramaan). • Ensure seamless login across services.
Examples – Pass: • User logs in once via Meri Pehchaan and accesses multiple services without re-authentication.
Examples – Fail: • Separate login systems per service with repeated credential creation.
Accessibility Consideration: • SSO reduces repetitive input and cognitive effort for users with accessibility needs.
References: GIGW 3.0 – GuDApps SSO Integration; UX4G Authentication Guidelines
Rationale: SSO is foundational to unified digital identity, reducing friction while increasing trust and adoption of government services.

Title: Follow official SSO integration documentation for secure implementation
Issue: • SSO is implemented inconsistently. • Security, consent, or token handling gaps exist.
Advice: • Follow official Meri Pehchaan documentation for token validation, encryption, consent flows, and callbacks.
Examples – Pass: • OAuth/OIDC flow implemented exactly as per MeitY documentation.
Examples – Fail: • Custom or incomplete SSO flows bypass official standards.
Accessibility Consideration: • Proper implementation ensures secure authentication flows for all users.
References: GIGW 3.0 – Cybersecurity Standards; MeitY SSO Guidelines; UX4G SSO Compliance
Rationale: Compliance with official SSO documentation ensures national security, interoperability, and audit readiness.

Title: Place login/sign-up entry points prominently and consistently
Issue: • Users cannot easily locate login option. • Navigation friction increases.
Advice: • Place login/sign-up button prominently (navbar/header or primary menu). • Maintain consistent placement across screens.
Examples – Pass: • Login button visible in navbar on all pages.
Examples – Fail: • Login buried in footer or hidden behind multiple steps.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear placement aids keyboard and screen reader navigation.
Rationale: Prominent login access reduces confusion and improves task efficiency for returning users.

Title: Maintain consistent official SSO branding across platforms
Issue: • SSO branding is altered or inconsistently applied. • User trust is reduced.
Advice: • Use Meri Pehchaan logo, colors, and labels exactly as specified. • Do not modify proportions or placement.
Examples – Pass: • Official Meri Pehchaan branding used consistently on all login screens.
Examples – Fail: • Modified logos or inconsistent branding across platforms.
Accessibility Consideration: • Consistent branding helps users recognize trusted login paths.
References: GIGW 3.0 – Branding & Identity; Meri Pehchaan Integration Handbook; UX4G Brand Consistency
Rationale: Official branding reinforces trust and recognisability of national authentication services.

Title: Enforce strong authentication security standards
Issue: • Weak authentication exposes user data. • Risk of impersonation or data leakage.
Advice: • Use HTTPS, encrypted tokens, secure session handling, CAPTCHA, and MFA where applicable. • Follow Meri Pehchaan security requirements strictly.
Examples – Pass: • OAuth/OIDC over HTTPS with MFA and CSRF protection enabled.
Examples – Fail: • Plain-text credentials or insecure session handling.
Accessibility Consideration: • Strong security protects all users, especially those unfamiliar with digital threats.
References: GIGW 3.0 – Authentication Security; Meri Pehchaan Security Guidelines; UX4G Handbook
Rationale: Robust authentication security is critical for protecting citizen data and maintaining platform integrity.

Title: Clearly communicate data privacy policies and terms of service
Issue: • Users are not informed how their data is collected, used, or protected. • Transparency and trust are compromised.
Advice: • Display clear Privacy Policy and Terms links on all login, signup, and data-collection screens. • Use plain, non-technical language to explain data usage and protection.
Examples – Pass: • Privacy Policy and Terms are visible and readable before submission on login/signup screens.
Examples – Fail: • Policies are hidden, vague, or accessible only after login.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear disclosure supports informed consent, especially for users with cognitive limitations.
References: GIGW 3.0 – Privacy & Transparency; UX4G Handbook Section 6.3
Rationale: Transparent privacy communication is foundational for user trust and legal compliance in government services.

Title: Obtain explicit user consent before initiating SSO
Issue: • Users are redirected to SSO without informed consent. • Data access expectations are unclear.
Advice: • Present a consent screen detailing data accessed and usage. • Use unticked checkboxes and clear options to proceed or decline.
Examples – Pass: • Consent screen clearly lists data fields and requires explicit confirmation.
Examples – Fail: • SSO initiates immediately without any consent explanation.
Accessibility Consideration: • Explicit consent flows benefit all users, including screen reader users, by clarifying intent.
References: GIGW 3.0 Section 5.3; DPDP Act 2023; UX4G Handbook Section 6.3
Rationale: Explicit consent is a legal and ethical requirement for identity and data-sharing processes.

Title: Allow seamless linking of existing accounts with SSO credentials
Issue: • Existing users lose data continuity when adopting SSO. • Multiple accounts are created unnecessarily.
Advice: • Provide secure, optional account linking during or after SSO login. • Preserve user data and preferences.
Examples – Pass: • User links existing account to Meri Pehchaan and retains history and settings.
Examples – Fail: • Users must create a new account, losing prior data.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear linking flows reduce confusion for users with memory or cognitive constraints.
Rationale: Account linking ensures continuity while enabling transition to national SSO infrastructure.

Title: Simplify login and signup UI to minimize steps
Issue: • Login/signup requires too many steps or fields. • Cognitive load and abandonment increase.
Advice: • Use minimal steps (e.g., OTP or single SSO CTA). • Apply progressive disclosure and clear labels.
Examples – Pass: • One-step OTP login or single “Continue with Meri Pehchaan” button.
Examples – Fail: • Multi-page forms with unnecessary fields.
Accessibility Consideration: • Simplified flows support users with cognitive or motor impairments.
References: GIGW 3.0 Usability; WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.8; UX4G Handbook Section 4.1
Rationale: Reducing steps improves completion rates and accessibility for diverse users.

Title: Conduct thorough testing of login and SSO integrations
Issue: • Login or SSO fails under edge cases (OTP errors, network issues). • Reliability and trust suffer.
Advice: • Test authentication across devices, browsers, networks, and failure states. • Include functional, security, and accessibility testing.
Examples – Pass: • SSO and OTP flows handle errors gracefully across conditions.
Examples – Fail: • Login breaks on slow networks or token expiry scenarios.
Accessibility Consideration: • Robust testing ensures reliable access for users relying on assistive technologies.
Rationale: Comprehensive testing prevents critical access failures in citizen-facing services.

Title: Keep SSO integration updated with latest APIs and security patches
Issue: • SSO integration becomes outdated. • Security vulnerabilities and authentication failures occur. • Compliance risk increases.
Advice: • Monitor Meri Pehchaan release notes, deprecations, and security advisories. • Apply updates and patches promptly. • Retest authentication flows after each update.
Examples – Pass: • SSO continues to function seamlessly after API upgrades with no user disruption.
Examples – Fail: • Login fails due to deprecated endpoints or outdated SDKs.
Accessibility Consideration: • Up-to-date integrations reduce unexpected failures that disproportionately affect assistive-technology users.
References: UX4G Handbook Section 6.7 – API Maintenance & Security Compliance
Rationale: Continuous maintenance of authentication integrations is essential for security, reliability, and citizen trust.

Title: Use trust indicators to reassure users during login
Issue: • Users are unsure about the legitimacy of the login process. • Anxiety increases during credential entry.
Advice: • Display government emblems, SSL indicators, and verified security badges near login areas. • Avoid decorative or misleading badges.
Examples – Pass: • Login screen shows official government emblem and secure connection indicators.
Examples – Fail: • Login screen lacks any reassurance signals or shows unofficial badges.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear trust indicators help users with cognitive concerns feel confident during sensitive actions.
References: GIGW 3.0 – Visual Identity; DBIM Co-branding & Identity; UX4G Handbook Section 6.9
Rationale: Trust signals reduce perceived risk and increase completion rates for authentication flows.

Title: Provide contextual error guidance and recovery mechanisms
Issue: • Users receive vague or technical error messages. • Recovery paths are unclear. • Frustration and abandonment increase.
Advice: • Show inline, specific error messages with actionable suggestions. • Provide recovery options (retry, reset, help). • Handle network and auth failures gracefully.
Examples – Pass: • Error message clearly explains issue and suggests next steps (e.g., retry OTP, reset password).
Examples – Fail: • Generic errors like “Something went wrong” with no guidance.
Accessibility Consideration: • WCAG-compliant error identification and suggestions support screen reader and keyboard users.
Rationale: Clear error guidance improves task recovery, reduces support burden, and enhances trust.

Title: Provide a search bar for large, exploration-heavy products
Issue: • Users struggle to locate content in large systems. • Navigation alone is insufficient for discovery.
Advice: • Include a visible search bar when content scale is large. • Keep search persistent and easy to access.
Examples – Pass: • Search bar visible on homepage and key screens for content-heavy portals.
Examples – Fail: • No search provided despite large information volume.
Accessibility Consideration: • Search supports alternative navigation paths for users with cognitive or memory limitations.
References: GIGW 3.0 – 2.2.12, 3.3.2; DBIM Search UI; WCAG 2.1 SC 2.4.5; BIS IS 17428:2020
Rationale: Persistent search is essential for efficient exploration in large government digital systems.

Title: Place search functionality prominently for quick access
Issue: • Search is hidden or requires scrolling. • Users fail to discover search quickly.
Advice: • Place search in the header or primary navigation. • Ensure it is visible above the fold and consistently positioned.
Examples – Pass: • Search bar visible at top of screen without scrolling.
Examples – Fail: • Search buried in menus or secondary screens.
Accessibility Consideration: • Prominent placement improves keyboard and screen reader navigation.
Rationale: Easy discoverability of search reduces friction and reliance on complex navigation.

Title: Provide auto-suggestions to improve search efficiency
Issue: • Users must type full queries. • Spelling errors and uncertainty reduce success.
Advice: • Implement auto-suggestions and predictive typing as users type.
Examples – Pass: • Suggestions appear dynamically based on partial input.
Examples – Fail: • No suggestions; users must guess exact terms.
Accessibility Consideration: • Suggestions aid users with cognitive or literacy challenges.
References: GIGW 3.0 – 3.3.3; DBIM Search Interaction; BIS IS 17428:2020
Rationale: Auto-suggestions reduce effort, errors, and uncertainty during search.

Title: Clearly indicate whether search is global or local
Issue: • Users are unsure of search scope. • Results feel unexpected or irrelevant.
Advice: • Label search scope clearly (global vs section-specific). • Use toggles or contextual labels.
Examples – Pass: • Search labeled “Search entire portal” or “Search this section”.
Examples – Fail: • No indication of search scope.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear scope labeling supports predictability for all users.
References: GIGW 3.0 Search UX; WCAG 2.1 SC 2.4.5; WCAG G161
Rationale: Explicit scope communication prevents confusion and improves trust in search results.

Title: Enable filtering and sorting of search results
Issue: • Large result sets overwhelm users. • Users cannot refine queries effectively.
Advice: • Provide filters (category, date, type) and sorting options. • Use collapsible or chip-based filters.
Examples – Pass: • Users refine results using filters and sort controls.
Examples – Fail: • Flat, unfiltered result lists only.
Accessibility Consideration: • Filters support manageable content blocks for assistive tech users.
Rationale: Filtering and sorting reduce cognitive load and improve efficiency in large result sets.

Title: Provide auto-complete suggestions while typing
Issue: • Users must type full queries manually. • Search effort and errors increase on mobile.
Advice: • Enable real-time auto-complete suggestions as users type. • Surface popular and matching queries instantly.
Examples – Pass: • Suggestions appear dynamically after 2–3 characters.
Examples – Fail: • Search input accepts text but provides no suggestions.
Accessibility Consideration: • Suggestions reduce cognitive and motor effort, especially for users with limited dexterity.
References: GIGW 3.0 Search UX; WCAG 2.1 / 2.2 SC 3.3.5, SC 3.2.2
Rationale: Auto-complete accelerates search, prevents errors, and improves overall discovery efficiency.

Title: Rank search results by relevance and importance
Issue: • Results appear unordered or random. • High-value content is buried.
Advice: • Implement relevance-based ranking using keywords, recency, and service priority. • Make ranking logic user-centric.
Examples – Pass: • Most relevant and official services appear first.
Examples – Fail: • Results displayed in arbitrary or chronological order only.
Accessibility Consideration: • Predictable ordering helps users with cognitive impairments locate content faster.
References: GIGW 3.0 Search Experience; WCAG 2.1 / 2.2 SC 3.3.5, SC 3.2.2
Rationale: Relevant ranking ensures trust, reduces scanning effort, and improves search success.

Title: Support voice search for hands-free interaction
Issue: • Users with motor or literacy constraints face barriers. • Mobile input is slower.
Advice: • Integrate voice search using supported APIs. • Allow natural language input.
Examples – Pass: • Users can tap a microphone icon and speak queries.
Examples – Fail: • Search is limited to text-only input.
Accessibility Consideration: • Voice input supports inclusive access and alternative input modalities.
Rationale: Voice search improves accessibility and usability, especially on mobile and assistive contexts.

Title: Provide fast-loading results with visible loading feedback
Issue: • Users experience uncertainty during result loading. • Slow response feels broken.
Advice: • Optimize search queries and show loading indicators during fetch. • Use spinners or skeletons.
Examples – Pass: • Results load quickly with clear loading feedback.
Examples – Fail: • Blank screen or frozen UI during search.
Accessibility Consideration: • Status indicators are required for screen reader users to understand system state.
Rationale: Feedback during latency maintains trust and prevents premature abandonment.

Title: Use lazy loading for large search result sets
Issue: • Initial result load is heavy and slow. • Users may not need all results immediately.
Advice: • Load only visible results initially. • Fetch additional results on scroll or pagination.
Examples – Pass: • Results load progressively as the user scrolls.
Examples – Fail: • Entire result set loads at once.
Accessibility Consideration: • Progressive loading reduces cognitive and performance load for all users.
Rationale: Lazy loading balances performance with accessibility in large datasets.

Title: Maintain consistent search placement and interaction across screens
Issue: • Search location changes across screens. • Users must re-learn where and how to search. • Increases cognitive load and errors.
Advice: • Keep search placement identical across all screens. • Use consistent styling, icons, animations, and interaction behavior.
Examples – Pass: • Search appears in the same header position with identical behavior on all screens.
Examples – Fail: • Search appears in header on one screen, footer or FAB on another.
Accessibility Consideration: • Consistent identification supports users with cognitive impairments and reduces navigation effort.
Rationale: Predictable placement builds familiarity, reduces mental effort, and improves task efficiency.
Metrics Affected: Cognitive load, Task efficiency, Navigation errors

Title: Align search bar visual styling with brand and design system
Issue: • Search bar styling feels inconsistent with brand. • Visual fragmentation reduces trust and coherence.
Advice: • Apply DBIM colors, typography, icons, spacing, and elevation consistently. • Match search styling to design system tokens.
Examples – Pass: • Search bar uses DBIM palette, Noto Sans, standard iconography, and approved dimensions.
Examples – Fail: • Search bar uses ad-hoc colors, fonts, or non-standard icons.
Accessibility Consideration: • Adequate contrast and consistent styling support readability and recognition for all users.
References: DBIM UI Standards Section 8; GIGW 3.0 Quality Guidelines 5.1
Rationale: Visual consistency reinforces brand trust and creates a cohesive user experience.

Title: Use consent-based personalisation to tailor content and features
Issue: • Personalisation uses user data without explicit consent. • Users cannot control or understand personalisation logic. • Risk of trust erosion and regulatory non-compliance.
Advice: • Clearly explain personalisation use cases before activation. • Obtain explicit opt-in consent. • Provide granular controls to enable, disable, or adjust personalisation from settings.
Examples – Pass: • User opts in to content recommendations and can manage preferences at any time.
Examples – Fail: • Personalised notifications enabled by default with no explanation or opt-out.
Accessibility Consideration: • Consent flows must be screen-reader accessible and avoid coercive patterns.
References: GIGW 3.0 – Functional Requirements & Privacy Principles; UX4G Handbook – Data-Driven UX; WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.4
Rationale: Consent-driven personalisation improves relevance while preserving trust, transparency, and compliance.

Title: Ensure personal data collection complies with government data protection regulations
Issue: • Excessive or unclear data collection. • Missing user control over shared data. • Risk of legal and ethical violations.
Advice: • Collect only necessary data. • Provide clear disclosures and privacy links. • Allow users to view, edit, and delete their data.
Examples – Pass: • Data collection is minimal, purpose-bound, and user-controlled.
Examples – Fail: • Collects personal data without disclosure or deletion options.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear labels and error prevention reduce accidental data submission.
References: GIGW 3.0 – Data Protection Compliance; UX4G Handbook – Privacy by Design; WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.1
Rationale: Privacy-by-design ensures lawful, ethical, and user-respectful personalisation.

Title: Provide theme options to support user visual comfort
Issue: • Users cannot adjust visual theme. • Fixed themes may cause eye strain or discomfort.
Advice: • Offer light and dark modes. • Ensure both modes meet contrast and branding standards.
Examples – Pass: • User can toggle light/dark mode with accessible contrast.
Examples – Fail: • Only one theme available regardless of environment or preference.
Accessibility Consideration: • Contrast ratios must meet WCAG requirements in all themes.
References: GIGW 3.0 – Accessibility & Usability; WCAG 2.1 SC 1.4.3; WCAG 2.2 SC 1.4.6
Rationale: Theme personalisation improves comfort and accessibility without altering functionality.

Title: Allow users to adjust typography and layout for readability
Issue: • Users cannot resize text or adjust spacing. • Fixed layouts break readability for low-vision or elderly users. • Risk of accessibility non-compliance.
Advice: • Respect browser/device text scaling. • Provide in-app font size and layout density controls. • Ensure UI integrity at 200% zoom.
Examples – Pass: • Text scales cleanly up to 200% without loss of content or functionality.
Examples – Fail: • Text overlaps, truncates, or breaks layout when zoomed.
Accessibility Consideration: • Must meet WCAG text resize and spacing requirements without assistive tech.
References: WCAG 2.1 SC 1.4.4; WCAG 2.1 SC 1.4.12; WCAG 2.1 SC 1.4.8; GIGW 3.0 Accessibility & Usability Practices
Rationale: Adjustable typography ensures inclusive access across age, vision, and literacy levels.

Title: Recommend relevant content based on user interests and interactions
Issue: • Content remains generic despite user history. • Over-personalisation risks content silos.
Advice: • Use preferences and past interactions to suggest content. • Allow users to modify or reset recommendations. • Preserve discovery paths.
Examples – Pass: • Recommended schemes adapt to user interests with reset option.
Examples – Fail: • Recommendations are opaque, irreversible, or overly narrow.
Accessibility Consideration: • Recommendations must not trigger unexpected context changes.
References: GIGW 3.0 Functional Requirements – Personalisation; WCAG 2.2 SC 3.2.2; UX4G Handbook – Content Recommendations
Rationale: Balanced personalisation improves relevance without limiting user autonomy.

Title: Provide location-based content with user control
Issue: • Location-specific information is unavailable or inaccurate. • Automatic geolocation without consent risks trust.
Advice: • Use geolocation or PIN-code input with explicit consent. • Allow manual override at all times.
Examples – Pass: • User selects location to view nearby services and schemes.
Examples – Fail: • Location detected silently with no opt-out or correction.
Accessibility Consideration: • Multiple ways to access location-based content must be provided.
References: GIGW 3.0 Functional Requirements – Context Awareness; WCAG 2.2 SC 2.4.5; UX4G Handbook – Location-Based UX
Rationale: Contextual relevance improves service discovery while respecting privacy and control.

Title: Allow users to customize notification preferences
Issue: • Users receive excessive or irrelevant notifications. • No control over frequency, type, or channel causes fatigue.
Advice: • Provide notification controls for category, frequency, and delivery medium. • Default to minimal alerts. • Ensure settings are easy to find and modify.
Examples – Pass: • User selects SMS for critical alerts and email for announcements with weekly frequency.
Examples – Fail: • All notifications are pushed automatically with no opt-out or frequency control.
Accessibility Consideration: • Notification settings must be keyboard accessible and clearly labelled.
References: GIGW 3.0 User-Centric Design; WCAG 2.2 SC 2.2.4; WCAG 2.2 SC 3.3.2; UX4G Handbook – Notification UX
Rationale: User-controlled notifications prevent overload and improve trust and engagement.

Title: Prioritize notifications based on importance and user behavior
Issue: • All notifications are treated equally. • Critical messages may be missed among routine alerts.
Advice: • Classify notifications by urgency. • Adapt delivery based on user behavior and preferences. • Allow users to downgrade or mute non-critical alerts.
Examples – Pass: • Application status alerts appear as banners; routine updates go to inbox.
Examples – Fail: • Promotional and critical alerts use identical visual priority.
Accessibility Consideration: • Status messages must be programmatically announced to assistive tech.
References: WCAG 2.2 SC 4.1.3; WCAG 2.1 SC 3.2.2; GIGW 3.0 Usability & Predictable UX
Rationale: Intelligent prioritization ensures important information is not overlooked.

Title: Synchronize personalization changes in real time
Issue: • Preference changes are delayed or inconsistently applied. • Users receive outdated content.
Advice: • Sync personalization updates in real time. • Provide immediate UI feedback and allow manual refresh. • Persist preferences across sessions.
Examples – Pass: • Content updates instantly after preference change without refresh.
Examples – Fail: • User must relaunch app to see updated personalized content.
Accessibility Consideration: • Updates must not cause unexpected context changes.
References: GIGW 3.0 API Integration Guidelines; UX4G Handbook – Personalization Systems
Rationale: Real-time sync reinforces user control and system reliability.

Title: Ensure ethical, transparent, and non-manipulative personalization
Issue: • Personalization logic is opaque. • Users are nudged without clear consent or control. • Risk of dark patterns.
Advice: • Explain why content is personalized. • Provide opt-out for all personalization. • Avoid manipulative UI patterns and respect user pacing.
Examples – Pass: • “Why am I seeing this?” explanation with opt-out toggle available.
Examples – Fail: • Hidden unsubscribe options or forced personalization.
Accessibility Consideration: • All changes must be user-initiated and reversible.
References: WCAG 2.1 SC 3.2.5; GIGW 3.0 Quality Guidelines 5.1; UX4G Ethical UX Principles
Rationale: Ethical personalization protects autonomy, trust, and regulatory compliance.

Title: Avoid irrelevant information to maintain task focus
Issue: • Pages contain unrelated or distracting content. • Users lose focus from primary task.
Advice: • Prioritize task-critical content. • Remove or de-emphasize unrelated banners, carousels, and links.
Examples – Pass: • Service page shows only eligibility, steps, CTA, and help.
Examples – Fail: • Homepage-style banners and unrelated promotions on task pages.
Accessibility Consideration: • Reduced cognitive load supports users with cognitive and reading difficulties.
References: WCAG 2.1 SC 3.1.5; GIGW 3.0 SC 3.6.2; DBIM Clause 4.1; BIS IS 17802:2022 Clause 7.3.3
Rationale: Task-oriented pages improve completion rates and reduce abandonment.

Title: Use multimedia only when it supports the task
Issue: • Overuse of scripts, videos, animations causes distraction.
Advice: • Use multimedia only when it adds clarity. • Avoid autoplay and decorative motion.
Examples – Pass: • Static image explaining a step; video plays only on user action.
Examples – Fail: • Autoplay videos or looping animations unrelated to task.
Accessibility Consideration: • Motion control prevents disorientation and distraction.
References: WCAG 2.1 SC 2.2.2; GIGW 3.0 SC 3.6.4; DBIM Clause 4.2; BIS IS 17802:2022 Clause 6.3.4
Rationale: Focused interfaces reduce cognitive overload and fatigue.

Title: Avoid unnecessary registration for primary tasks
Issue: • Users are forced to register before understanding or starting tasks.
Advice: • Allow guest access or preview. • Require registration only when essential.
Examples – Pass: • User can view eligibility and steps before sign-up.
Examples – Fail: • Mandatory login before viewing service details.
Accessibility Consideration: • Reduces input burden for users with cognitive or motor challenges.
References: WCAG 2.1 SC 3.3.6; GIGW 3.0 SC 3.5.4; BIS IS 17802:2022 Clause 6.3.2
Rationale: Removing premature barriers increases trust and task success.

Title: Minimize steps and screens to complete tasks
Issue: • Tasks require excessive clicks or screens.
Advice: • Combine related steps. • Use wizards or progressive sections.
Examples – Pass: • Single structured form with sections.
Examples – Fail: • Same information split across many screens unnecessarily.
Accessibility Consideration: • Fewer steps reduce fatigue and navigation errors.
References: GIGW 3.0 SC 3.6.2; DBIM Clause 4.1; BIS IS 17802:2022 Clause 6.3.1
Rationale: Efficient flows reduce cognitive load and errors.

Title: Align digital task flow with real-world order
Issue: • Digital steps do not match user mental models.
Advice: • Mirror familiar offline or logical task order.
Examples – Pass: • Apply → Review → Submit flow.
Examples – Fail: • Submit required before review or confirmation.
Accessibility Consideration: • Predictable order benefits all users, especially first-time users.
Rationale: Familiar sequencing reduces confusion and rework.

Title: Reduce manual effort through automated inputs
Issue: • Users must manually enter predictable data repeatedly. • Increased effort and error rates.
Advice: • Implement autofill and data inference (e.g., state/district from PIN code). • Use authoritative government APIs.
Examples – Pass: • Entering PIN code auto-fills city and state fields.
Examples – Fail: • User manually types city and state despite PIN code availability.
Accessibility Consideration: • Autofill must be editable and announced to assistive technologies.
Rationale: Automation reduces friction, errors, and task completion time.

Title: Enable comparison to support informed decisions
Issue: • Users cannot easily compare options. • Decision-making becomes error-prone.
Advice: • Provide side-by-side comparisons or comparison tables when applicable.
Examples – Pass: • Scheme comparison table showing benefits and eligibility.
Examples – Fail: • Users must navigate back and forth between items to compare.
Accessibility Consideration: • Comparison layouts must be readable and navigable via keyboard and screen readers.
References: GIGW 3.0 SC 3.4.11; BIS IS 17802:2022 SC 6.3.2; DBIM Clause 4.5
Rationale: Comparison aids reduce cognitive load and improve choice accuracy.

Title: Place frequently used features in easily accessible areas
Issue: • Important actions are hard to find. • Users spend extra effort locating controls.
Advice: • Position high-use actions prominently and consistently. • Use sticky or persistent placement where appropriate.
Examples – Pass: • Sticky “Accessibility” or “Apply Now” button visible at all times.
Examples – Fail: • Critical actions buried deep in menus or below the fold.
Accessibility Consideration: • Persistent controls must not obscure content or trap focus.
References: GIGW 3.0 SC 3.3.2; DBIM Clause 3.2; BIS IS 17802:2022 SC 6.2.3
Rationale: Easy access to frequent actions improves efficiency and satisfaction.

Title: Prevent repeated data entry across tasks
Issue: • Users re-enter the same information multiple times. • Leads to frustration and abandonment.
Advice: • Persist user data across sessions. • Pre-fill fields using profiles or session storage.
Examples – Pass: • Personal details auto-filled in subsequent forms.
Examples – Fail: • User retypes name, address, or ID in every step.
Accessibility Consideration: • Stored data must respect consent and privacy controls.
References: GIGW 3.0 SC 6.1.1; DBIM Clause 5.1; BIS IS 17802:2022 SC 7.3.2
Rationale: Eliminating repetition significantly reduces friction and errors.

Title: Show task progress and remaining steps clearly
Issue: • Users are unaware of progress in multi-step tasks. • Uncertainty leads to abandonment.
Advice: • Display all steps and current progress. • Allow review before submission.
Examples – Pass: • Progress bar shows “Step 2 of 5” with review screen.
Examples – Fail: • No indication of steps or progress until submission.
Accessibility Consideration: • Progress indicators must be perceivable by screen readers.
References: GIGW 3.0 SC 6.2.1; BIS IS 17802:2022 SC 7.3.4; DBIM Clause 5.2
Rationale: Transparency in progress builds confidence and completion.

Title: Support recognition over recall across sections
Issue: • Users must remember prior selections or context. • Increased cognitive load and errors when navigating between sections.
Advice: • Persist and visibly repeat key context (filters, selections, titles). • Maintain breadcrumbs and summaries across transitions.
Examples – Pass: • Selected scheme name and filters remain visible on next page.
Examples – Fail: • User must recall filters or category names after navigation.
Accessibility Consideration: • Persistent context reduces memory load for users with cognitive impairments.
References: WCAG 2.1 SC 3.3.7 (AAA); GIGW 3.0 SC 6.2.4; BIS IS 17802:2022 SC 6.5.1; DBIM SC 4.3
Rationale: Recognition over recall improves accuracy and reduces abandonment.

Title: Use familiar metaphors and culturally appropriate formats
Issue: • Users struggle to interpret unfamiliar formats or symbols.
Advice: • Apply culturally familiar formats (dates, currency) and metaphors. • Use recognizable icons and terminology.
Examples – Pass: • Dates shown as dd/mm/yyyy; currency shown as ₹.
Examples – Fail: • US date formats or unfamiliar symbols used for Indian users.
Accessibility Consideration: • Familiar conventions aid comprehension for multilingual users.
References: WCAG 2.1 SC 3.1.2; GIGW 3.0 SC 6.1.6; BIS IS 17802:2022 SC 7.3.1; DBIM SC 4.2
Rationale: Cultural alignment reduces confusion and improves trust.

Title: Hide system internals and avoid technical jargon
Issue: • Users are exposed to backend or technical terminology.
Advice: • Abstract technical processes into user-friendly language. • Use plain status messages.
Examples – Pass: • “Processing…” displayed during actions.
Examples – Fail: • “Calling API / Fetching token” shown to users.
Accessibility Consideration: • Plain language benefits screen reader and low-literacy users.
References: GIGW 3.0 SC 4.4.2; DBIM SC 4.3; BIS IS 17802:2022 SC 7.4.2
Rationale: Abstraction prevents confusion and cognitive overload.

Title: Provide recovery paths for critical errors
Issue: • Users cannot easily recover from mistakes. • High risk of irreversible errors.
Advice: • Provide previews, confirmations, drafts, and undo paths for high-stakes actions.
Examples – Pass: • Review screen before final submission; save as draft available.
Examples – Fail: • Immediate irreversible submission without confirmation.
Accessibility Consideration: • Error prevention mechanisms protect users with motor or cognitive challenges.
Rationale: Recovery paths reduce anxiety and prevent costly mistakes.

Title: Enable self-sufficiency for common tasks
Issue: • Users need external help to complete routine actions.
Advice: • Provide contextual help, tooltips, and onboarding cues.
Examples – Pass: • Inline tooltip explains form field on first use.
Examples – Fail: • No guidance; users must consult external help.
Accessibility Consideration: • Contextual help must be accessible and dismissible.
Rationale: Self-guided UX improves efficiency and reduces support burden.

Title: Allow users to resume tasks after interruption
Issue: • Users lose progress when exiting mid-task.
Advice: • Persist progress locally or in account sessions. • Prompt users to resume on return.
Examples – Pass: • “Resume where you left off” prompt appears on return.
Examples – Fail: • Task restarts from beginning after interruption.
Accessibility Consideration: • Progress persistence benefits users with intermittent access or disabilities.
Rationale: Task continuity improves completion and satisfaction.

Title: Provide sorting and filtering for content-heavy interfaces
Issue: • Users struggle to locate relevant items in large datasets. • Excessive scrolling and scanning required.
Advice: • Provide sortable columns and filter controls aligned to user intent (date, status, category).
Examples – Pass: • Scheme list sortable by eligibility, date, or department with filters.
Examples – Fail: • Long static list with no sorting or filtering.
Accessibility Consideration: • Filters must be keyboard accessible and programmatically associated with results.
Rationale: Sorting and filtering reduce effort and speed up task completion in data-heavy UIs.

Title: Ensure buttons and icons clearly reflect intended actions
Issue: • Ambiguous labels or icons confuse users about outcomes.
Advice: • Use clear, action-oriented labels and universally recognizable icons.
Examples – Pass: • “Download Certificate” button with download icon.
Examples – Fail: • “Click Here” with unrelated or decorative icon.
Accessibility Consideration: • Non-text content must have accessible labels and names.
Rationale: Clear affordances prevent errors and increase confidence in task execution.

Title: Warn users before automatic session timeout
Issue: • Users lose work due to unexpected logout.
Advice: • Display advance warning with countdown and options to extend session or save progress.
Examples – Pass: • Modal alert 2 minutes before timeout with “Extend Session” option.
Examples – Fail: • Sudden logout without warning.
Accessibility Consideration: • Timing adjustments support users with motor or cognitive impairments.
Rationale: Advance warnings prevent data loss and frustration during long tasks.

Title: Support both novice and expert users
Issue: • Interface favors only one user skill level.
Advice: • Provide guided help for beginners and shortcuts for expert users.
Examples – Pass: • First-time tour plus keyboard shortcuts for power users.
Examples – Fail: • Same verbose guidance forced on expert users.
Accessibility Consideration: • Help mechanisms must be accessible and dismissible.
Rationale: Adaptive UX improves efficiency without excluding new users.

Title: Allow users to edit provided information
Issue: • Users are locked out from correcting mistakes.
Advice: • Enable edits with confirmations or audit trails where required.
Examples – Pass: • User can update address before final processing.
Examples – Fail: • Submitted data cannot be edited at any stage.
Accessibility Consideration: • Editable fields reduce error impact for all users.
Rationale: Flexibility reduces support load and improves data accuracy.

Title: Provide step-by-step onboarding for new users
Issue: • New users feel lost or overwhelmed.
Advice: • Use optional walkthroughs, spotlights, or guided tours.
Examples – Pass: • First-time modal tour highlighting key features with skip option.
Examples – Fail: • No onboarding or forced walkthrough every visit.
Accessibility Consideration: • Onboarding must be skippable and accessible.
Rationale: Guided onboarding accelerates adoption and reduces early drop-off.

Title: Use buttons for commands and actions instead of links
Issue: • Users confuse navigation links with actions. • Accidental navigation during task execution.
Advice: • Use buttons for actions (submit, save, apply). • Reserve links for navigation only.
Examples – Pass: • “Submit Application” implemented as a <button> with clear visual affordance.
Examples – Fail: • Form submission triggered via underlined text link.
Accessibility Consideration: • Buttons must expose correct role, name, and state to assistive tech.
References: GIGW 3.0 SC 4.4.5; BIS IS 17802:2022 SC 7.3.5; DBIM SC 4.4
Rationale: Clear differentiation between actions and navigation reduces errors and improves predictability.

Title: Provide real-time validation for incorrect inputs
Issue: • Users discover errors only after submission. • High form abandonment.
Advice: • Validate inputs inline and show corrective guidance immediately.
Examples – Pass: • Inline message: “PIN code must be 6 digits” shown while typing.
Examples – Fail: • Error shown only after full form submission.
Accessibility Consideration: • Error messages must be programmatically associated and not rely on color alone.
Rationale: Immediate feedback reduces cognitive load and prevents repeated failures.

Title: Make primary call-to-action buttons prominent and distinct
Issue: • Users miss or misinterpret the main action.
Advice: • Visually prioritize primary CTAs using size, color, and placement.
Examples – Pass: • Primary “Apply Now” button in DBIM primary color, thumb-reachable.
Examples – Fail: • Primary CTA visually identical to secondary actions.
Accessibility Consideration: • CTAs must meet minimum target size and contrast requirements.
Rationale: Clear CTAs guide users efficiently toward task completion.

Title: Trigger data submission and state changes only through explicit user actions
Issue: • Users lose control due to auto-submission or unexpected state changes.
Advice: • Require explicit submit/confirm actions for all critical operations.
Examples – Pass: • “Delete” requires tap + confirmation dialog.
Examples – Fail: • Auto-submit on field change or screen load.
Accessibility Consideration: • Prevent unexpected context changes per WCAG 3.2.x principles.
Rationale: Explicit actions preserve user agency and prevent irreversible errors.

Title: Make webpage titles clearly accessible and recognizable
Issue: • Page purpose is unclear. • Users lose orientation across pages.
Advice: • Use meaningful, visible page titles consistently placed across pages.
Examples – Pass: • Clear H1 title like “Apply for Birth Certificate” at top of page.
Examples – Fail: • Missing, vague, or visually hidden page title.
Accessibility Consideration: • Titles must be programmatically associated (<title>, H1) for screen readers.
References: WCAG 2.1 SC 2.4.2; GIGW 3.0 3.2.3; BIS IS 17428:2020 8.1.4; DBIM Navigation
Rationale: Clear page titles support orientation, trust, and assistive navigation.

Title: Maintain a clear and logical navigation hierarchy
Issue: • Users cannot understand site structure. • Navigation feels cluttered or flat.
Advice: • Design a hierarchical navigation with clear parent–child relationships.
Examples – Pass: • Top-level categories with nested sub-menus (Services → Certificates).
Examples – Fail: • All links placed at same level with no grouping.
Accessibility Consideration: • Hierarchy must be conveyed visually and programmatically (lists, landmarks).
Rationale: Logical hierarchy reduces cognitive load and search dependency.

Title: Ensure primary navigation elements are clearly labeled and accessible
Issue: • Vague labels confuse users. • Icons without text reduce clarity.
Advice: • Use descriptive labels with optional supporting icons.
Examples – Pass: • “Track Application” with icon + text.
Examples – Fail: • Generic labels like “Info” or icon-only menus.
Accessibility Consideration: • Labels must satisfy link purpose in context (screen readers).
Rationale: Clear labels improve predictability and accessibility.

Title: Maintain consistent navigation patterns across pages
Issue: • Users must relearn navigation on each page.
Advice: • Keep navigation layout, order, and behavior consistent.
Examples – Pass: • Same header + breadcrumbs on all service pages.
Examples – Fail: • Navigation structure changes page-to-page.
Accessibility Consideration: • Consistency required for assistive tech landmark expectations.
Rationale: Predictability builds confidence and reduces navigation errors.

Title: Keep key navigation elements persistent across main screens
Issue: • Navigation disappears or shifts unexpectedly.
Advice: • Make primary navigation persistent across key screens.
Examples – Pass: • Fixed header (web) / persistent bottom nav (mobile).
Examples – Fail: • Navigation hidden after scroll or page change.
Accessibility Consideration: • Persistent landmarks aid screen reader orientation.
Rationale: Persistent navigation stabilizes user experience and reduces memory load.

Title: Place navigation elements in prominent, expected locations
Issue: • Navigation is hard to discover. • Users must search for primary controls.
Advice: • Place primary navigation at top (desktop) and bottom or hamburger (mobile). • Keep it visually prominent and fixed where appropriate.
Examples – Pass: • Desktop top navigation bar; mobile bottom tab bar.
Examples – Fail: • Navigation hidden mid-page or buried in footer only.
Accessibility Consideration: • Ensure landmarks (<nav>) and visible focus order.
Rationale: Predictable placement improves discoverability and reduces cognitive load.

Title: Ensure navigation elements meet minimum target size
Issue: • Users mis-tap navigation items. • Touch interaction errors occur.
Advice: • Use minimum 44×44 px touch targets. • Maintain spacing between items.
Examples – Pass: • Menu items sized ≥44×44 px with spacing.
Examples – Fail: • Small icons or tightly packed links.
Accessibility Consideration: • Required for motor accessibility and touch usability.
Rationale: Adequate target size reduces errors and frustration.

Title: Provide visual feedback on navigation interaction
Issue: • Users are unsure if action was registered.
Advice: • Implement hover, focus, active, and pressed states.
Examples – Pass: • Active menu item highlighted; pressed state visible.
Examples – Fail: • No visual change on interaction.
Accessibility Consideration: • Feedback must be perceivable beyond color alone.
Rationale: Feedback confirms actions and builds confidence.

Title: Use smooth, non-disruptive transitions between screens
Issue: • Abrupt transitions disorient users.
Advice: • Apply subtle, fast transitions (<300 ms).
Examples – Pass: • Fade or slide transition respecting reduced-motion settings.
Examples – Fail: • Abrupt page jumps or excessive animation.
Accessibility Consideration: • Must respect prefers-reduced-motion.
Rationale: Gentle transitions improve continuity without distraction.

Title: Support standard back navigation patterns
Issue: • Users cannot easily return to previous screens.
Advice: • Support browser back, gestures, and visible back buttons.
Examples – Pass: • Working browser back; mobile back gesture supported.
Examples – Fail: • Back disabled or causes data loss.
Accessibility Consideration: • Back action should preserve state where possible.
Rationale: Reliable back navigation reduces frustration.

Title: Use breadcrumbs for deep navigation paths
Issue: • Users lose sense of location in deep hierarchies.
Advice: • Implement breadcrumbs when depth >3 levels.
Examples – Pass: • Breadcrumb trail showing path with links.
Examples – Fail: • No path indicator in deep flows.
Accessibility Consideration: • Breadcrumbs must be programmatically associated.
Rationale: Breadcrumbs support orientation and efficient backtracking.

Title: Structure information architecture around user needs
Issue: • Important content is buried. • Navigation reflects org chart, not users.
Advice: • Base IA on user research, analytics, and demand.
Examples – Pass: • High-use services reachable within 1–2 clicks.
Examples – Fail: • Critical tasks hidden deep in menus.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear structure benefits screen reader navigation.
Rationale: User-centred IA improves findability and task success.

Title: Group related content logically
Issue: • Content appears fragmented. • Users struggle to understand relationships.
Advice: • Group content under intuitive, user-focused categories. • Use meaningful section labels and containers.
Examples – Pass: • Services grouped as “Employment”, “Health”, “Schemes”.
Examples – Fail: • Content grouped by internal departments or arbitrarily.
Accessibility Consideration: • Proper headings and grouping support screen reader navigation.
Rationale: Logical grouping improves comprehension and scanability.

Title: Keep information architecture shallow
Issue: • Users get lost in deep hierarchies. • Excessive navigation steps.
Advice: • Limit navigation depth to a maximum of 3 levels. • Flatten menus where possible.
Examples – Pass: • Key pages reachable within 1–3 clicks.
Examples – Fail: • Menus with 4–6 nested levels.
Accessibility Consideration: • Shallow IA reduces memory load for assistive tech users.
Rationale: Shallow structures reduce effort and navigation fatigue.

Title: Apply consistent structure to similar sections
Issue: • Users must relearn layouts repeatedly.
Advice: • Reuse templates, headings, and section order for similar content types.
Examples – Pass: • All scheme pages follow identical layout and hierarchy.
Examples – Fail: • Each scheme page structured differently.
Accessibility Consideration: • Consistency improves predictability for screen readers.
Rationale: Consistency reduces cognitive effort and learning cost.

Title: Provide multiple pathways to important content
Issue: • Users rely on a single navigation method.
Advice: • Offer access via menus, search, homepage links, and cross-links.
Examples – Pass: • Content accessible via menu, search, and in-page links.
Examples – Fail: • Content only reachable through one menu path.
Accessibility Consideration: • Multiple paths support WCAG “Multiple Ways”.
Rationale: Different users prefer different navigation strategies.

Title: Continuously refine IA based on user feedback
Issue: • IA becomes outdated or misaligned with user needs.
Advice: • Review analytics and feedback periodically and update structure.
Examples – Pass: • Menu labels updated based on search analytics.
Examples – Fail: • IA remains unchanged despite usage issues.
Accessibility Consideration: • Improvements benefit all users, including AT users.
Rationale: IA must evolve with content growth and user behavior.

Title: Structure list items for scanability
Issue: • Lists feel cluttered. • Users struggle to scan quickly.
Advice: • Use consistent information hierarchy (title, meta, CTA). • Avoid non-essential details.
Examples – Pass: • Card list with title, subtitle, status, action.
Examples – Fail: • Long paragraphs or mixed information per item.
Accessibility Consideration: • Proper structure supports screen readers and cognitive accessibility.
Rationale: Structured lists reduce cognitive load and improve efficiency.

Title: Maintain consistent list styling
Issue: • Visual inconsistency across list items.
Advice: • Apply uniform fonts, colors, spacing via design system.
Examples – Pass: • All items share same typography and spacing.
Examples – Fail: • Each item styled differently.
Accessibility Consideration: • Consistency improves predictability for AT users.
Rationale: Consistent styling improves learnability and trust.

Title: Use visual separators between items
Issue: • Dense lists appear merged.
Advice: • Use dividers, spacing, or background contrast.
Examples – Pass: • Clear divider between each row/card.
Examples – Fail: • No spacing or separation between items.
Accessibility Consideration: • Separators aid focus and reading order.
Rationale: Visual separation improves scannability.

Title: Ensure list items are easily clickable
Issue: • Touch errors due to small targets.
Advice: • Maintain ≥44px tap targets and adequate spacing.
Examples – Pass: • Entire card or row is tappable.
Examples – Fail: • Only text inside row is clickable.
Accessibility Consideration: • Meets WCAG target size for motor accessibility.
Rationale: Adequate target size reduces interaction errors.

Title: Provide visual feedback on selection
Issue: • Users unsure if action is registered.
Advice: • Use hover, focus, active, and selected states.
Examples – Pass: • Selected item highlighted clearly.
Examples – Fail: • No visual change on interaction.
Accessibility Consideration: • Focus visibility supports keyboard users.
Rationale: Feedback confirms interaction and prevents errors.

Title: Optimize performance for large lists
Issue: • Long lists cause slow load or jank.
Advice: • Use lazy loading, pagination, or “Load More”.
Examples – Pass: • Initial 30 items, load more on scroll.
Examples – Fail: • Entire dataset loaded at once.
Accessibility Consideration: • Progressive loading reduces cognitive and performance strain.
Rationale: Performance optimizations maintain usability at scale.

Title: Show loading indicators for dynamic lists
Issue: • Users unsure if content is loading.
Advice: • Display spinner, shimmer, or progress indicator.
Examples – Pass: • Skeleton loaders during fetch.
Examples – Fail: • Blank screen during loading.
Accessibility Consideration: • Status feedback supports WCAG dynamic content guidance.
Rationale: Feedback reduces uncertainty and abandonment.

Title: Place filters in prominent, accessible locations
Issue: • Filters are hard to discover. • Users overlook refinement options.
Advice: • Position filters top-left or top area on desktop. • Use chip ribbon or bottom drawer on mobile.
Examples – Pass: • Filter chips visible above list.
Examples – Fail: • Filters buried inside secondary menus.
Accessibility Consideration: • Logical focus order supports keyboard and screen reader users.
Rationale: Discoverable filters reduce effort and improve findability.

Title: Use collapsible filter sections for dense filter sets
Issue: • Filters consume excessive screen space.
Advice: • Group filters with headings and collapsible sections.
Examples – Pass: • Accordion-style filter groups (Price, Location).
Examples – Fail: • Long, ungrouped filter lists.
Accessibility Consideration: • Expand/collapse with aria-expanded supports assistive tech.
Rationale: Progressive disclosure reduces cognitive load.

Title: Use clear, jargon-free filter labels
Issue: • Users misunderstand filter meaning.
Advice: • Use plain, descriptive language with examples if needed.
Examples – Pass: • “Price Range”, “Department”.
Examples – Fail: • “Monetary Threshold”, “Org Unit”.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear labels improve comprehension for all users.
Rationale: Plain language reduces errors and hesitation.

Title: Support multi-select filtering where applicable
Issue: • Users restricted to single filter values.
Advice: • Use checkboxes or multi-select chips when logical.
Examples – Pass: • Multiple benefits selectable.
Examples – Fail: • Only one value allowed when multiple make sense.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear selection states support cognitive accessibility.
Rationale: Multi-select supports real-world decision-making.

Title: Apply filters efficiently with clear interaction model
Issue: • Users confused by delayed or automatic updates.
Advice: • Use real-time apply for lightweight filters. • Use “Apply” button for heavy operations.
Examples – Pass: • Instant update or clear Apply CTA.
Examples – Fail: • Full page reload without feedback.
Accessibility Consideration: • Predictable behavior reduces cognitive friction.
Rationale: Clear filter behavior improves trust and performance.

Title: Show visual confirmation of active filters
Issue: • Users lose track of applied filters.
Advice: • Highlight active filters and show count if needed.
Examples – Pass: • Active chips + “3 filters applied”.
Examples – Fail: • No indication of applied filters.
Accessibility Consideration: • Feedback helps orientation and reduces errors.
Rationale: Visibility of system state improves confidence.

Title: Provide clear option to reset all filters
Issue: • Users struggle to return to default state.
Advice: • Add visible “Clear All Filters” action.
Examples – Pass: • Single-tap reset restores baseline list.
Examples – Fail: • Filters must be cleared one-by-one.
Accessibility Consideration: • Supports error recovery and control.
Rationale: Easy recovery prevents frustration and abandonment.

Title: Persist user filter preferences across sessions
Issue: • Users must reapply filters repeatedly.
Advice: • Persist last-used filters using cookies or user profile preferences.
Examples – Pass: • Returning user sees previously applied filters.
Examples – Fail: • Filters reset every visit without user choice.
Accessibility Consideration: • Persistence must respect consent and privacy controls.
Rationale: Reduces repetitive effort and improves efficiency.

Title: Allow users to create and save custom filter presets
Issue: • Power users cannot reuse complex filters.
Advice: • Enable naming and saving filter combinations.
Examples – Pass: • Preset like “My Daily Schemes”.
Examples – Fail: • Filters lost after navigation.
Accessibility Consideration: • Saved presets must be clearly labeled and editable.
Rationale: Supports advanced workflows without cluttering UI.

Title: Provide relevant sorting options
Issue: • Users cannot reorder content meaningfully.
Advice: • Offer context-appropriate sorting (date, relevance, name).
Examples – Pass: • “Sort by Newest / Popular”.
Examples – Fail: • Single hard-coded order.
Accessibility Consideration: • Sorting controls must be keyboard operable.
Rationale: Sorting improves content findability.

Title: Define a logical default sorting order
Issue: • Initial order feels arbitrary.
Advice: • Default to most useful order (e.g., relevance).
Examples – Pass: • “Newest First” for updates.
Examples – Fail: • Alphabetical by default without rationale.
Accessibility Consideration: • Predictable defaults reduce confusion.
Rationale: Strong defaults reduce user effort.

Title: Allow ascending and descending sort toggling
Issue: • Users cannot reverse order.
Advice: • Enable ▲ / ▼ toggles for each criterion.
Examples – Pass: • Price ↑ / ↓ toggle.
Examples – Fail: • Fixed direction sorting.
Accessibility Consideration: • Controls must expose state to assistive tech.
Rationale: Supports flexible comparison.

Title: Enable combination sorting where contextually useful
Issue: • Single-criterion sorting insufficient.
Advice: • Allow secondary sort rules if relevant.
Examples – Pass: • “Price then Rating”.
Examples – Fail: • No multi-criteria control for dense data.
Accessibility Consideration: • Advanced controls should not overwhelm novices.
Rationale: Improves decision quality for complex data.

Title: Display clear indicators for current sort order
Issue: • Users unsure how content is ordered.
Advice: • Use arrows or icons to show direction.
Examples – Pass: • “↓ Price” highlighted.
Examples – Fail: • No visible sort indicator.
Accessibility Consideration: • Icons must have text alternatives.
Rationale: Visibility of system state builds trust.

Title: Highlight the active sorting option
Issue: • Active sort not visually distinguished.
Advice: • Apply selected state styling to active option.
Examples – Pass: • Bold or filled active sort button.
Examples – Fail: • All sort options look identical.
Accessibility Consideration: • Active state must be perceivable beyond color alone.
Rationale: Reinforces orientation and reduces errors.

Title: Limit forms to essential fields only
Issue: • Forms include unnecessary or redundant fields that increase effort.
Advice: • Request only task-critical data; remove optional or duplicate fields; use progressive disclosure where needed.
Examples – Pass: • Application form asks only name, ID, and required eligibility details.
Examples – Fail: • Long forms requesting unrelated demographic or optional data upfront.
Accessibility Consideration: • Fewer fields reduce cognitive load and support users with memory or attention impairments.
References: WCAG 2.1 SC 3.3.2; WCAG 2.2 SC 1.3.5; GIGW 3.0 Accessible Forms
Rationale: Minimizing fields directly improves completion rates and reduces abandonment, especially on mobile and low-bandwidth contexts.
Metrics Affected: Form completion rate; Drop-off rate; Time on task

Title: Use multi-step forms for long data entry
Issue: • Long single-page forms overwhelm users.
Advice: • Break forms into logical steps with clear navigation and backward movement.
Examples – Pass: • Form divided into “Personal Details → Address → Review & Submit”.
Examples – Fail: • Single scrolling form with 20+ fields.
Accessibility Consideration: • Step-wise segmentation supports focus and reduces cognitive overload.
References: WCAG 2.1 SC 3.3.2; SC 3.3.5; GIGW 3.0 Progressive Disclosure
Rationale: Chunking information improves comprehension and task success for complex workflows.

Title: Show clear progress indicators in multi-step forms
Issue: • Users are unaware of progress or remaining steps.
Advice: • Display persistent progress indicators like “Step 2 of 4”.
Examples – Pass: • Visible progress bar remains fixed during form completion.
Examples – Fail: • No indication of form length or remaining steps.
Accessibility Consideration: • Progress indicators improve orientation for screen reader and cognitive accessibility users.
References: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.3; SC 2.4.6; GIGW 3.0 Process Guidance
Rationale: Visibility of progress reduces anxiety and increases completion confidence.

Title: Ensure visible and clear field labels
Issue: • Labels are missing, unclear, or replaced by placeholders.
Advice: • Use explicit labels positioned above or beside fields; do not rely on placeholders alone.
Examples – Pass: • “Mobile Number” label displayed above input field.
Examples – Fail: • Placeholder text disappears when user starts typing.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear labels are essential for screen readers and cognitive accessibility.
Rationale: Proper labeling prevents input errors and supports assistive technologies.

Title: Use appropriate input types for data fields
Issue: • Incorrect input types increase typing effort and errors.
Advice: • Map fields to correct input types (tel, number, date, dropdowns).
Examples – Pass: • Numeric keypad opens for phone number field.
Examples – Fail: • Free-text field used for date or phone number.
Accessibility Consideration: • Optimized input types improve motor accessibility and reduce effort.
Rationale: Correct input types significantly improve speed and accuracy on mobile devices.

Title: Provide real-time input validation with guidance
Issue: • Users receive errors only after submission.
Advice: • Validate inputs inline with clear error messages and solutions.
Examples – Pass: • Email field shows error immediately with correction hint.
Examples – Fail: • Errors shown only after full form submission.
Accessibility Consideration: • Real-time feedback reduces memory load and frustration.
References: WCAG 2.1 SC 3.3.1; SC 3.3.3; GIGW 3.0 Input Feedback
Rationale: Immediate validation prevents cascading errors and repeated submissions.

Title: Optimize input fields for touch interaction
Issue: • Input fields and controls are too small or closely packed, causing touch errors.
Advice: • Ensure all interactive elements meet minimum touch target size and spacing; avoid dense clustering on small screens.
Examples – Pass: • Buttons and fields are ≥48×48 px with 8–12 px spacing on mobile.
Examples – Fail: • Small checkboxes placed too close together, causing accidental taps.
