Accessibility Consideration: • Adequate sizing and spacing support users with motor impairments and reduce interaction errors.
References: WCAG 2.1 SC 2.5.1; WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8; GIGW 3.0 Mobile Accessibility
Rationale: Touch-optimized controls are critical for mobile-first government services and directly impact task success and error rates.
Metrics Affected: Input error rate; Task success rate; Abandonment

Title: Enable autofill for repetitive or predictable inputs
Issue: • Users must repeatedly type commonly known or system-derivable data.
Advice: • Use standard autocomplete attributes and platform autofill APIs; support OTP autofill where applicable.
Examples – Pass: • Email, address, and OTP fields autofill automatically.
Examples – Fail: • OTP or address fields require full manual entry every time.
Accessibility Consideration: • Autofill reduces cognitive load and benefits users with motor or cognitive limitations.
References: WCAG 2.1 SC 1.3.5; WCAG 2.2 SC 2.2.1; GIGW 3.0 Form Efficiency
Rationale: Autofill significantly reduces effort and friction in high-frequency government transactions.

Title: Provide intelligent suggestions and predictive input
Issue: • Users must type full values even when options are predictable.
Advice: • Offer context-aware suggestions (auto-suggest, predictive text) without overwhelming users.
Examples – Pass: • City field suggests matching cities as the user types.
Examples – Fail: • Long dropdowns or free-text fields with no suggestions.
Accessibility Consideration: • Predictive assistance supports cognitive accessibility and reduces memory load.
References: WCAG 2.1 SC 1.3.1; SC 1.3.5; GIGW 3.0 Input Acceleration
Rationale: Intelligent suggestions accelerate form completion while reducing input errors.

Title: Use placeholder text only as supportive guidance
Issue: • Placeholder text is misused as a replacement for labels or validation.
Advice: • Use placeholders only to show examples or format hints; always retain visible labels.
Examples – Pass: • Placeholder shows “e.g., name@example.com” with a visible label above.
Examples – Fail: • Placeholder disappears and acts as the only label.
Accessibility Consideration: • Screen readers may not announce placeholders reliably; labels are essential.
References: WCAG 2.1 SC 3.3.2; GIGW 3.0 Forms; BIS IS 17802:2022 SC 5.6.3
Rationale: Proper use of placeholders prevents ambiguity and supports assistive technologies.

Title: Ensure every banner has a clear purpose
Issue: • Banners are used decoratively without serving an informational or task-related goal.
Advice: • Define a clear objective for each banner (promotion, guidance, alert) before design; remove purely decorative banners.
Examples – Pass: • Banner highlights an application deadline with CTA.
Examples – Fail: • Decorative banner with no message or action relevance.
Accessibility Consideration: • Meaningful graphics reduce cognitive load and help assistive technologies interpret content purpose.
Rationale: Purpose-driven banners prevent visual noise and keep users focused on primary tasks.

Title: Maintain contextual relevance of banners
Issue: • Banners are unrelated to the section or content they appear alongside.
Advice: • Ensure banners align with the local page context and user intent.
Examples – Pass: • Scholarship banner placed in Education section.
Examples – Fail: • Agriculture banner placed in Scholarship section.
Accessibility Consideration: • Contextual relevance aids comprehension, especially for users with cognitive disabilities.
Rationale: Contextual banners reinforce information scent and reduce user confusion.

Title: Ensure branding consistency in banners
Issue: • Banners use inconsistent colors, fonts, or styles.
Advice: • Apply approved brand colors, typography, and visual language consistently.
Examples – Pass: • Banner follows DBIM color palette and typography.
Examples – Fail: • Banner uses random fonts or non-brand colors.
Accessibility Consideration: • Consistent visuals support recognition and predictable navigation.
Rationale: Branding consistency builds trust and reinforces institutional identity.

Title: Use high-resolution, scalable graphics
Issue: • Low-quality or pixelated graphics reduce clarity and professionalism.
Advice: • Use scalable formats (SVG, WebP, 2x assets) for all banners and graphics.
Examples – Pass: • Retina-ready WebP banner renders clearly.
Examples – Fail: • Blurry JPG stretched beyond native resolution.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear visuals benefit low-vision users and prevent misinterpretation.
Rationale: High-quality graphics ensure readability across devices and resolutions.

Title: Balance visual appeal without overwhelming users
Issue: • Excessive visuals, animations, or colors distract from content.
Advice: • Use whitespace, limit elements, and avoid competing visuals.
Examples – Pass: • Clean banner with single message and ample spacing.
Examples – Fail: • Banner with flashing text, multiple CTAs, and clutter.
Accessibility Consideration: • Reduced visual noise supports users with attention or cognitive impairments.
References: WCAG 2.1 SC 1.4.3; SC 1.4.8; GIGW 3.0 UI Design
Rationale: Controlled visual emphasis improves comprehension and task efficiency.

Title: Prevent banners from obstructing core functionality
Issue: • Banners block navigation, content, or critical controls.
Advice: • Position banners in non-intrusive areas; use dismissible patterns for alerts.
Examples – Pass: • Top alert banner that can be dismissed.
Examples – Fail: • Banner covering form fields or navigation.
Accessibility Consideration: • Obstruction disproportionately affects keyboard and screen-reader users.
References: WCAG 2.1 SC 1.4.13; SC 2.4.7; GIGW 3.0 Usability; BIS IS 17802
Rationale: Non-obstructive banners preserve access to primary user tasks.

Title: Ensure responsive sizing of banners across devices
Issue: • Banners do not scale correctly across screen sizes, causing readability or usability issues.
Advice: • Use responsive layouts (fluid widths, media queries) so banners adapt without loss of clarity or hierarchy.
Examples – Pass: • Banner scales proportionally on desktop, tablet, and mobile with readable text.
Examples – Fail: • Banner text becomes unreadable or cropped on mobile.
Accessibility Consideration: • Proper reflow supports low-vision users and prevents horizontal scrolling.
References: WCAG 2.1 SC 1.4.10; SC 1.4.4; SC 1.4.5; GIGW 3.0 Responsive Layouts
Rationale: Responsive banners preserve content legibility and interaction across devices.

Title: Provide clear and prominent calls to action in banners
Issue: • Banners lack clear guidance on next steps or hide CTAs visually.
Advice: • Include concise, action-oriented CTAs with strong visual contrast and predictable placement.
Examples – Pass: • Banner with “Apply Now” button clearly visible and tappable.
Examples – Fail: • Banner text with no actionable CTA.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear CTAs help screen-reader users understand purpose and outcome of interaction.
References: WCAG 2.1 SC 2.4.4; SC 3.2.4; GIGW 3.0 UI Design
Rationale: Explicit CTAs convert attention into meaningful user action.

Title: Enable interaction for actionable banners
Issue: • Banners suggest action but are not interactive or lack clear affordance.
Advice: • Make actionable banners tappable with clear hit areas and accessible labels.
Examples – Pass: • Entire banner or CTA area is clickable with aria-label.
Examples – Fail: • Banner looks clickable but has no interaction.
Accessibility Consideration: • Interactive clarity benefits keyboard and assistive technology users.
References: WCAG 2.1 SC 1.1.1; SC 3.2.4; GIGW 3.0 Graphics Guidelines
Rationale: Aligning visual affordance with interaction prevents user confusion.

Title: Use animations subtly to draw attention
Issue: • Animations distract, overwhelm, or interfere with comprehension.
Advice: • Apply short, subtle animations (<500ms) only to emphasize priority content.
Examples – Pass: • Gentle fade-in on banner appearance.
Examples – Fail: • Flashing or looping animation competing with content.
Accessibility Consideration: • Reduced motion benefits users with vestibular disorders.
Rationale: Controlled motion improves focus without harming accessibility.

Title: Ensure animations do not degrade performance or battery life
Issue: • Heavy animations impact load time, performance, or battery usage.
Advice: • Use lightweight, GPU-friendly animations and test on low-end devices.
Examples – Pass: • CSS transform/opacity animation running smoothly.
Examples – Fail: • Large GIF or CPU-intensive animation draining battery.
Accessibility Consideration: • Performance stability supports assistive tech and low-resource devices.
Rationale: Efficient animations maintain usability without hidden user cost.

Title: Keep banner text concise and visually supported
Issue: • Banner text is verbose, dense, or hard to scan quickly.
Advice: • Limit copy to key message and reinforce with relevant visuals or icons.
Examples – Pass: • Banner headline under 20 words with supporting icon.
Examples – Fail: • Long paragraph text inside banner.
Accessibility Consideration: • Concise text improves comprehension for cognitive and screen-reader users.
Rationale: Short, focused messaging maximizes banner effectiveness in limited attention spans.

Title: Ensure readable text size and sufficient contrast
Issue: • Banner text is too small or lacks contrast, reducing readability.
Advice: • Use minimum 16px text on mobile, scalable units, and ≥4.5:1 contrast ratios.
Examples – Pass: • Banner text readable on all devices with strong contrast.
Examples – Fail: • Light grey text over white background.
Accessibility Consideration: • Supports low-vision users and users in bright environments.
Rationale: Readable banners ensure information is perceivable without strain.

Title: Provide alternative text for banners and graphics
Issue: • Images lack meaningful alternative text for assistive technologies.
Advice: • Add descriptive alt text for informative banners; use alt="" for decorative images.
Examples – Pass: • Banner image announced clearly by screen reader.
Examples – Fail: • Image announced as “image123.jpg”.
Accessibility Consideration: • Essential for screen-reader users and non-visual access.
Rationale: Alt text ensures non-text content is accessible and meaningful.

Title: Prevent banner overload and manage multiple banners
Issue: • Too many banners overwhelm users and distract from primary tasks.
Advice: • Limit to 1–3 banners; use carousels only with manual controls and pause.
Examples – Pass: • Single banner with optional carousel controls.
Examples – Fail: • Multiple competing banners visible at once.
Accessibility Consideration: • Reduces cognitive load and motion sensitivity issues.
Rationale: Controlled banner density preserves focus and usability.

Title: Keep banners updated and content current
Issue: • Outdated banners reduce trust and relevance.
Advice: • Define review cycles and archive expired or irrelevant banners.
Examples – Pass: • Event banner removed after deadline.
Examples – Fail: • Old campaign banner still displayed.
Accessibility Consideration: • Fresh content improves comprehension and credibility.
Rationale: Regular updates maintain user trust and relevance.

Title: Localize banners for language and cultural context
Issue: • Banners ignore regional language or cultural norms.
Advice: • Serve localized text and culturally appropriate visuals per region.
Examples – Pass: • Hindi banner shown for Hindi locale.
Examples – Fail: • English-only banner on regional portal.
Accessibility Consideration: • Improves comprehension and inclusivity.
Rationale: Localization increases relevance and inclusiveness.

Title: Ensure contextual relevance of banners
Issue: • Generic banners ignore user location or preferences.
Advice: • Use geo or preference signals to show relevant banners.
Examples – Pass: • State-specific scheme banner shown regionally.
Examples – Fail: • Irrelevant scheme banner shown universally.
Accessibility Consideration: • Contextual relevance reduces confusion and noise.
Rationale: Relevant banners improve usefulness and attention.

Title: Optimize images for fast loading
Issue: • Large, unoptimized images slow down page load.
Advice: • Use compressed formats (WebP/AVIF) and responsive images.
Examples – Pass: • Banner loads quickly on 3G network.
Examples – Fail: • Heavy JPG delaying page render.
Accessibility Consideration: • Faster load benefits low-bandwidth users.
Rationale: Performance optimization supports usability and access.

Title: Use lazy loading for non-critical banners
Issue: • Below-the-fold banners load unnecessarily early.
Advice: • Apply lazy loading for offscreen banners and graphics.
Examples – Pass: • Below-fold banner loads on scroll.
Examples – Fail: • All banners loaded on initial render.
Accessibility Consideration: • Improves initial load speed and efficiency.
Rationale: Lazy loading balances performance and experience.

Title: Make banner notifications clear and dismissible
Issue: • Notification banners obstruct tasks or cannot be dismissed.
Advice: • Use concise copy, clear hierarchy, and visible close controls.
Examples – Pass: • Top alert banner with × button.
Examples – Fail: • Modal banner blocking interaction.
Accessibility Consideration: • Supports focus, control, and accessibility.
Rationale: Non-intrusive alerts respect user control.

Title: Organize content into clear categories
Issue: • Content appears as long, unstructured blocks, making exploration difficult.
Advice: • Group content into logical sections using categories, tags, or filters (topic, user type, service type).
Examples – Pass: • Page divided into clear sections like “Eligibility,” “Benefits,” “How to Apply.”
Examples – Fail: • Entire page presented as continuous paragraphs.
Accessibility Consideration: • Proper structure improves navigation for screen readers and keyboard users.
References: WCAG 2.1 SC 2.4.6; GIGW 3.0 IA; DBIM 2.2; BIS IS 17802:2022
Rationale: Categorized content reduces cognitive load and improves findability.

Title: Recommend personalized content where appropriate
Issue: • Generic content ignores user context, reducing relevance and engagement.
Advice: • Surface contextual recommendations using location, session data, or usage trends without mandatory login.
Examples – Pass: • “Popular Services in Your State” section displayed.
Examples – Fail: • Same content shown to all users regardless of context.
Accessibility Consideration: • Must respect consent and avoid manipulative personalization.
Rationale: Contextual relevance improves engagement without increasing friction.

Title: Ensure content is easy to understand or simplified
Issue: • Content is written in complex language that many users cannot easily understand.
Advice: • Use plain language, short sentences, icons, and explainers; provide simplified summaries for complex topics.
Examples – Pass: • Plain-language summary with info tooltip for legal terms.
Examples – Fail: • Dense legal or bureaucratic text with no explanation.
Accessibility Consideration: • Supports users with cognitive disabilities and low literacy.
Rationale: Simpler language improves comprehension and completion rates.

Title: Tailor content to target audience demographics
Issue: • Content ignores users’ language proficiency or cultural context.
Advice: • Adapt language, examples, and structure based on user research and locale.
Examples – Pass: • Regional language content with culturally relevant examples.
Examples – Fail: • One-size-fits-all content across diverse audiences.
Accessibility Consideration: • Correct language tagging is critical for screen readers.
Rationale: Audience-aligned content improves trust and usability.

Title: Maintain consistent brand voice
Issue: • Content tone varies across pages, creating inconsistency.
Advice: • Follow a defined content style guide for tone, vocabulary, and phrasing.
Examples – Pass: • Consistent formal-yet-approachable government tone throughout.
Examples – Fail: • Casual tone on one page, bureaucratic tone on another.
Accessibility Consideration: • Predictable language supports comprehension.
Rationale: Consistent voice builds credibility and clarity.

Title: Adjust tone based on content context
Issue: • Same tone used for legal, help, and onboarding content.
Advice: • Match tone to purpose: formal for policy, supportive for guidance, encouraging for onboarding.
Examples – Pass: • Friendly onboarding copy; formal policy language.
Examples – Fail: • Casual language on legal disclaimer page.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear tone helps users interpret intent correctly.
Rationale: Contextual tone reduces confusion and anxiety.

Title: Use hierarchical headings and structured formatting
Issue: • Content lacks headings or logical structure, making scanning difficult.
Advice: • Apply proper heading hierarchy (H1–H3), bullets, and summaries for scannability.
Examples – Pass: • Clear headings with bullet lists under each section.
Examples – Fail: • Bold text used instead of semantic headings.
Accessibility Consideration: • Heading structure is essential for screen readers.
Rationale: Structured content improves navigation and comprehension.

Title: Highlight important information prominently
Issue: • Critical information such as deadlines, warnings, or mandatory steps is visually buried.
Advice: • Use visual hierarchy (bold text, highlight boxes, callouts, alerts) to surface key information clearly.
Examples – Pass: • Deadline shown in highlighted info box at top of page.
Examples – Fail: • Important notice embedded mid-paragraph.
Accessibility Consideration: • Visual emphasis must not rely on color alone; ensure semantic cues for screen readers.
Rationale: Clear emphasis reduces missed actions and user errors.

Title: Ensure grammatical correctness
Issue: • Grammatical errors reduce trust and comprehension.
Advice: • Use automated grammar checks and editorial review before publishing.
Examples – Pass: • Content passes grammar checks and human review.
Examples – Fail: • Frequent tense, agreement, or sentence errors.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear grammar improves comprehension for assistive technology users.
Rationale: Language quality directly impacts credibility.

Title: Eliminate spelling and typographical errors
Issue: • Typos and punctuation issues create friction and reduce confidence.
Advice: • Enforce proofreading workflows combining automated tools and manual checks.
Examples – Pass: • Error-free published content.
Examples – Fail: • Misspellings or inconsistent punctuation visible on live pages.
Accessibility Consideration: • Error-free text benefits screen readers and translation engines.
Rationale: Error-free content signals reliability and care.

Title: Break content into readable chunks with whitespace
Issue: • Dense text blocks discourage reading and scanning.
Advice: • Use short paragraphs, sub-headings, spacing, and adequate line height.
Examples – Pass: • Paragraphs ≤4 lines with clear spacing.
Examples – Fail: • Long unbroken text blocks.
Accessibility Consideration: • Adequate spacing improves readability for cognitive and low-vision users.
Rationale: Readable layouts improve engagement and comprehension.

Title: Provide clear instructions and guidance
Issue: • Users struggle to understand how to use features or complete tasks.
Advice: • Add step-by-step instructions, tooltips, inline guidance, and contextual help.
Examples – Pass: • Form includes clear steps and field guidance.
Examples – Fail: • Feature presented without explanation.
Accessibility Consideration: • Instructions must be programmatically associated with controls.
Rationale: Clear guidance reduces abandonment and errors.

Title: Ensure overall content accessibility compliance
Issue: • Content is not usable with assistive technologies or text resizing.
Advice: • Use semantic HTML, scalable text, accessible headings, and contrast-safe styles.
Examples – Pass: • Text resizes to 200% without loss of content.
Examples – Fail: • Fixed text sizes or broken layouts on zoom.
Accessibility Consideration: • Directly impacts screen reader and low-vision users.
Rationale: Accessibility compliance is non-negotiable for public services.

Title: Provide descriptive alternative text for non-text content
Issue: • Images lack meaningful alternative descriptions.
Advice: • Add context-aware alt text for informative images; use empty alt for decorative ones.
Examples – Pass: • Image describing process includes functional alt text.
Examples – Fail: • Alt text missing or generic (“image”).
Accessibility Consideration: • Essential for screen reader users and non-visual access.
Rationale: Alt text ensures equivalent information access.

Title: Keep content accurate and up to date
Issue: • Content becomes outdated as features, policies, or external conditions change.
Advice: • Establish periodic content review cycles; use CMS versioning, expiry flags, and ownership tags for time-sensitive content.
Examples – Pass: • Policy page updated after regulation change with visible “Last updated” date.
Examples – Fail: • Old instructions still referencing deprecated features.
Accessibility Consideration: • Outdated content can mislead assistive technology users relying on textual accuracy.
Rationale: Accurate, current content is essential for trust, task success, and legal compliance.

Title: Use feedback and analytics to improve content quality
Issue: • Content remains static despite user confusion or disengagement signals.
Advice: • Analyse search logs, exit rates, feedback forms, and revise unclear or underperforming content regularly.
Examples – Pass: • High-exit FAQ page rewritten based on search failures.
Examples – Fail: • No changes despite repeated user complaints.
Accessibility Consideration: • Iterative improvements enhance clarity for diverse cognitive needs.
Rationale: Continuous refinement ensures relevance and usability over time.

Title: Provide clear, accessible placeholder text
Issue: • Placeholder text is vague, misleading, or replaces proper labels.
Advice: • Use concise, descriptive placeholders that clarify expected input without jargon; always retain visible labels.
Examples – Pass: • Search field shows “Search services, schemes, or departments”.
Examples – Fail: • Placeholder reads “Enter here” or used as the only label.
Accessibility Consideration: • Placeholder text must meet contrast requirements and not be the sole instruction.
Rationale: Clear placeholders reduce errors while supporting accessibility.

Title: Keep tooltip text concise and task-relevant
Issue: • Tooltips are verbose, redundant, or unrelated to the immediate task.
Advice: • Limit tooltips to short, actionable explanations directly supporting the control or term.
Examples – Pass: • Tooltip explains field purpose in one sentence.
Examples – Fail: • Tooltip contains policy-length text or repeats page content.
Accessibility Consideration: • Tooltips must be accessible on hover and focus, and dismissible.
Rationale: Concise tooltips aid understanding without increasing cognitive load.

Title: Use system feedback to keep users informed
Issue: • Users are unaware of system status during loading, success, or error states.
Advice: • Use loaders, success confirmations, and error alerts consistently for user actions and background processes.
Examples – Pass: • Loader shown during data fetch; success toast after submission; inline error on failure.
Examples – Fail: • Silent delays or failed actions without feedback.
Accessibility Consideration: • Status messages must be programmatically announced to screen readers.
Rationale: Clear feedback reduces uncertainty and improves task completion confidence.

Title: Provide visual feedback for button states
Issue: • Buttons do not indicate hover, active, disabled, or pressed states.
Advice: • Implement visible state changes (color, elevation, opacity) for all button states.
Examples – Pass: • Button darkens on hover, shows spinner on submit, disables after click.
Examples – Fail: • Button appears static regardless of interaction.
Accessibility Consideration: • Hover and focus states must be keyboard-accessible and not rely on color alone.
Rationale: Button feedback improves interaction clarity and prevents errors.

Title: Highlight focused form fields
Issue: • Users cannot easily identify the active input field.
Advice: • Apply clear focus styles (border, outline, shadow) on focused form elements.
Examples – Pass: • Focused field shows strong border and label emphasis.
Examples – Fail: • No visible change when tabbing through fields.
Accessibility Consideration: • Must meet WCAG focus visibility requirements and support keyboard navigation.
Rationale: Focus indication supports accessibility and reduces form errors.

Title: Use tooltips for contextual help
Issue: • Interfaces become cluttered with explanatory text.
Advice: • Use hover/focus-based tooltips for secondary explanations only.
Examples – Pass: • Info icon reveals short tooltip on hover or focus.
Examples – Fail: • Long explanations embedded directly in UI.
Accessibility Consideration: • Tooltips must be dismissible, non-blocking, and accessible on focus.
Rationale: Tooltips provide just-in-time help without increasing cognitive load.

Title: Use skeleton screens for perceived performance
Issue: • Blank screens or spinners cause perceived delays on content-heavy pages.
Advice: • Use skeleton placeholders that resemble final layout during loading.
Examples – Pass: • Skeleton cards shown while list content loads.
Examples – Fail: • Empty screen or spinner only.
Accessibility Consideration: • Skeletons must not cause motion issues or confusion for screen readers.
Rationale: Skeletons reduce perceived wait time and maintain engagement.

Title: Provide textual updates for long processes
Issue: • Users are unsure whether a long-running process is still active.
Advice: • Show clear status text (e.g., “Processing…”, progress steps, ETA).
Examples – Pass: • “Processing application – step 2 of 3” displayed.
Examples – Fail: • Static loader with no explanation.
Accessibility Consideration: • Status text must be readable, persistent, and announced to assistive tech.
Rationale: Textual updates manage expectations and reduce abandonment.

Title: Place notifications consistently and non-intrusively
Issue: • Notifications appear inconsistently or block core content.
Advice: • Display alerts in a predictable location with clear actions.
Examples – Pass: • Toast appears top-right with “Undo” or “View details”.
Examples – Fail: • Modal alert blocks entire screen unnecessarily.
Accessibility Consideration: • Notifications must be focus-managed and screen-reader accessible.
Rationale: Consistent notification placement improves predictability and response time.

Title: Provide confirmation messages for completed actions
Issue: • Users are unsure whether actions such as form submissions or setting changes were successful.
Advice: • Display clear, contextual confirmation messages immediately after successful actions.
Examples – Pass: • “Your application has been submitted successfully” message shown after submit.
Examples – Fail: • Action completes silently with no acknowledgement.
Accessibility Consideration: • Confirmation messages must be announced to screen readers and not rely on color alone.
Rationale: Confirmation reduces uncertainty and builds trust in digital transactions.

Title: Allow users to undo recent actions
Issue: • Irreversible actions increase error cost and user anxiety.
Advice: • Provide undo or rollback options for destructive or critical actions.
Examples – Pass: • “Undo delete” toast available for 5–10 seconds.
Examples – Fail: • Item deleted permanently without recovery option.
Accessibility Consideration: • Undo must be keyboard accessible and time-bound with clear messaging.
Rationale: Undo mechanisms improve error tolerance and user confidence.

Title: Use consistent animations across similar elements
Issue: • Inconsistent motion patterns confuse users and reduce predictability.
Advice: • Standardize animation behavior using shared motion tokens or libraries.
Examples – Pass: • All cards use identical hover elevation and timing.
Examples – Fail: • Each card animates differently without rationale.
Accessibility Consideration: • Animations must respect prefers-reduced-motion settings.
Rationale: Consistent motion reinforces UI learnability and cohesion.

Title: Use accordions for secondary information
Issue: • Excessive information overloads primary content areas.
Advice: • Use expandable sections for secondary or optional information.
Examples – Pass: • FAQ answers hidden behind accordion toggles.
Examples – Fail: • Long explanations displayed inline by default.
Accessibility Consideration: • Accordions must support keyboard control and aria-expanded states.
Rationale: Progressive disclosure keeps focus on primary tasks.

Title: Use interactive maps for location-based information
Issue: • Static location information limits usability for spatial tasks.
Advice: • Provide interactive, zoomable maps with markers and controls.
Examples – Pass: • Map showing nearby service centres with tap-able pins.
Examples – Fail: • Static image of map without interaction.
Accessibility Consideration: • Provide text alternatives and keyboard controls for map interactions.
Rationale: Interactive maps improve spatial understanding and service discovery.

Title: Ensure all interactions are keyboard accessible
Issue: • Keyboard users cannot operate all interactive elements.
Advice: • Make all controls operable via keyboard (Tab, Enter, Space).
Examples – Pass: • Menu fully navigable using keyboard only.
Examples – Fail: • Dropdown inaccessible without mouse.
Accessibility Consideration: • Must meet WCAG keyboard and focus order requirements.
Rationale: Keyboard access is fundamental for accessibility compliance.

Title: Provide single-pointer alternatives for multi-touch gestures
Issue: • Multi-touch gestures exclude users with motor or assistive limitations.
Advice: • Offer visible, single-tap alternatives for all gesture-based actions.
Examples – Pass: • Zoom buttons provided alongside pinch-to-zoom.
Examples – Fail: • Functionality accessible only via swipe or pinch.
Accessibility Consideration: • Alternatives must be discoverable and operable with assistive tech.
Rationale: Gesture alternatives ensure inclusive mobile interactions.

Title: Provide a dedicated help centre
Issue: • Users cannot find guidance when stuck or unfamiliar with the service.
Advice: • Create a clearly labelled Help Centre with FAQs, tutorials, and guides accessible from header or footer.
Examples – Pass: • Central help page with searchable FAQs and task-based guides.
Examples – Fail: • Scattered help links or no central support location.
Accessibility Consideration: • Help content must be readable, keyboard accessible, and screen-reader friendly.
Rationale: A central help centre reduces support load and user abandonment.

Title: Provide context-sensitive help
Issue: • Users need to leave their task to understand form fields or features.
Advice: • Offer inline, contextual help linked to the current screen or input.
Examples – Pass: • “What is this?” tooltip beside complex field.
Examples – Fail: • Redirecting users to external help pages mid-task.
Accessibility Consideration: • Contextual help must be reachable by keyboard and announced to screen readers.
Rationale: Inline help reduces cognitive load and task interruption.

Title: Enable searchable help content
Issue: • Users cannot quickly locate relevant help information.
Advice: • Implement a searchable knowledge base within the help centre.
Examples – Pass: • Help search with auto-suggest and categorized results.
Examples – Fail: • Static FAQ list without search.
Accessibility Consideration: • Search must support keyboard navigation and clear result labelling.
Rationale: Search improves self-service resolution and efficiency.

Title: Provide easy-to-access feedback forms
Issue: • Users lack a simple way to report issues or suggestions.
Advice: • Add low-friction feedback forms accessible from key screens.
Examples – Pass: • Floating feedback button with short form and confirmation.
Examples – Fail: • Hidden or overly long feedback forms.
Accessibility Consideration: • Forms must have labels, error handling, and keyboard access.
Rationale: Feedback channels support continuous improvement and trust.

Title: Use short surveys or polls for experience feedback
Issue: • Lack of structured insight into user satisfaction.
Advice: • Trigger short, optional micro-surveys at appropriate moments.
Examples – Pass: • 2-question survey after task completion with skip option.
Examples – Fail: • Long mandatory surveys interrupting tasks.
Accessibility Consideration: • Surveys must be dismissible and not trap keyboard focus.
Rationale: Lightweight surveys capture feedback without disrupting flow.

Title: Provide customer support contact options
Issue: • Users cannot escalate issues beyond self-help.
Advice: • Expose clear contact options (email, phone, chat) under Help or Support, including availability and response timelines.
Examples – Pass: • Help page with helpline number, email ID, chat link, and service hours.
Examples – Fail: • No contact details or buried deep in legal pages.
Accessibility Consideration: • Contact links must be keyboard accessible and readable by screen readers.
Rationale: Human support is critical for exception handling and trust in government services.

Title: Display clear and actionable error messages
Issue: • Users do not understand what failed or how to fix it.
Advice: • Show human-readable error messages near the source with corrective guidance.
Examples – Pass: • “Enter a valid 10-digit mobile number” shown inline.
Examples – Fail: • Generic errors like “Invalid input” or “API error.”
Accessibility Consideration: • Errors must be announced to screen readers and not rely on color alone.
Rationale: Clear error messaging directly improves completion rates and reduces frustration.

Title: Allow undo or revert actions
Issue: • Users fear irreversible mistakes.
Advice: • Provide undo, revert, or confirmation before destructive actions.
Examples – Pass: • “Undo delete” toast or “Revert changes” option.
Examples – Fail: • Immediate irreversible deletion without warning.
Accessibility Consideration: • Undo actions must be keyboard operable and time-bound cues announced.
Rationale: Reversibility increases confidence and reduces abandonment in high-stakes flows.

Title: Provide guided walkthroughs for new users
Issue: • New users struggle to understand features.
Advice: • Offer optional, skippable onboarding walkthroughs or tours.
Examples – Pass: • First-time overlay highlighting key actions with skip option.
Examples – Fail: • No onboarding or forced, unskippable tours.
Accessibility Consideration: • Walkthroughs must respect focus order and be dismissible.
Rationale: Guided onboarding reduces learning curve and early drop-off.

Title: Use tooltips and hints for complex interactions
Issue: • Users are confused by unfamiliar controls.
Advice: • Attach concise, accessible tooltips to complex elements.
Examples – Pass: • Tooltip on hover/focus explaining a form field.
Examples – Fail: • Hidden explanations or jargon-heavy help text.
Accessibility Consideration: • Tooltips must persist on focus and be screen-reader friendly.
Rationale: Contextual hints reduce cognitive load without cluttering UI.

Title: Acknowledge user feedback immediately
Issue: • Users are unsure whether feedback was received.
Advice: • Show confirmation or thank-you message immediately after feedback submission.
Examples – Pass: • Confirmation screen or toast + optional email receipt.
Examples – Fail: • Silent submission with no acknowledgement.
Accessibility Consideration: • Status messages must be announced to assistive technologies.
Rationale: Immediate acknowledgement builds trust and closes the feedback loop.

Title: Keep users informed about feedback status
Issue: • Users submit feedback but receive no visibility into progress or resolution.
Advice: • Provide status updates via email/SMS and allow tracking using a reference ID.
Examples – Pass: • “Feedback #1234 – Under Review” email with ETA.
Examples – Fail: • No acknowledgement after initial submission.
Accessibility Consideration: • Status messages must be programmatically announced and clearly labeled.
Rationale: Transparency in grievance handling builds institutional trust and reduces repeat complaints.

Title: Communicate when feedback leads to improvements
Issue: • Users feel their feedback disappears into a void.
Advice: • Notify users when their input results in changes or enhancements.
Examples – Pass: • “Based on your feedback, we improved…” email or in-app message.
Examples – Fail: • Silent changes without user acknowledgement.
Accessibility Consideration: • Messages must be readable, concise, and accessible to screen readers.
Rationale: Closing the feedback loop increases civic participation and long-term engagement.

Title: Prevent data loss using auto-save
Issue: • Users lose data due to crashes, timeouts, or connectivity issues.
Advice: • Auto-save form data locally or server-side at safe intervals.
Examples – Pass: • Draft restored after refresh or login.
Examples – Fail: • Complete data loss after reload.
Accessibility Consideration: • Auto-save must not trigger unexpected context changes.
Rationale: Data loss in government services has direct real-world consequences.

Title: Provide recovery options for interrupted tasks
Issue: • Users cannot recover from session loss or interruptions.
Advice: • Offer “Resume”, “Restore session”, or recovery prompts.
Examples – Pass: • “Resume application” banner on return.
Examples – Fail: • Forced restart of long tasks.
Accessibility Consideration: • Recovery prompts must be clearly announced and dismissible.
Rationale: Recovery is essential for high-stakes, multi-step government tasks.

Title: Ensure graceful degradation during failures
Issue: • Entire product fails when a single dependency breaks.
Advice: • Design fallback modes and meaningful error states.
Examples – Pass: • Form submission via email during API outage.
Examples – Fail: • Blank screens or system crash.
Accessibility Consideration: • Failure states must expose system status without technical jargon.
Rationale: Government systems must fail safely, not catastrophically.

Title: Provide self-service knowledge base
Issue: • Users depend entirely on support teams for basic issues.
Advice: • Offer searchable FAQs, guides, and troubleshooting content.
Examples – Pass: • Knowledge base with filters and search.
Examples – Fail: • Scattered or outdated help content.
Accessibility Consideration: • Content must support keyboard navigation and headings.
Rationale: Self-service reduces support load and empowers users.

Title: Educate users with tips and tutorials
Issue: • Users misuse features due to lack of guidance.
Advice: • Provide tips, articles, and short tutorials.
Examples – Pass: • “Did you know?” tips or short explainer videos.
Examples – Fail: • Dense manuals or no guidance at all.
Accessibility Consideration: • Educational content must meet readability and captioning norms.
Rationale: Education improves digital literacy and reduces errors.

Title: Ensure accessibility of help and feedback features
Issue: • Help and feedback tools are unusable for users with disabilities due to missing keyboard support, labels, or roles.
Advice: • Design all help, feedback, and support components to meet WCAG requirements with semantic structure and ARIA support.
Examples – Pass: • Help center fully navigable via keyboard, screen readers announce form fields and status messages correctly.
Examples – Fail: • Feedback modal traps keyboard focus or lacks accessible labels.
Accessibility Consideration: • All interactive elements must expose name, role, and value; avoid focus traps and ensure contrast compliance.
Rationale: Accessibility of support is a non-negotiable baseline in government services.

Title: Provide multilingual help and feedback resources
Issue: • Support content is available only in a single language, excluding large user groups.
Advice: • Translate help and feedback resources into supported regional languages with consistent depth.
Examples – Pass: • User switches language and remains in same help article context.
Examples – Fail: • Language switch resets context or shows partial translations.
Accessibility Consideration: • Language of parts must be programmatically identifiable and switchable.
Rationale: Linguistic accessibility is critical for equity and reach in public digital services.

Title: Implement automated error and crash reporting
Issue: • System errors and crashes go undetected until users complain.
Advice: • Integrate automated error logging and monitoring with safe, anonymized reporting.
Examples – Pass: • Crash logged automatically and fallback UI shown to user.
Examples – Fail: • Silent crashes with no logging or user feedback.
Accessibility Consideration: • Error states must remain accessible and non-blocking.
References: GIGW 3.0 Website Monitoring; WCAG 2.2 SC 4.1.1; UX4G Error Intelligence
Rationale: Proactive error detection reduces downtime and user frustration.

Title: Identify relevant government services based on user needs
Issue: • Key government platforms are not evaluated or mapped to product objectives.
Advice: • Conduct a structured feature-to-service mapping to identify applicable services (e.g., DigiLocker, myScheme, Bhashini, UMANG).
Examples – Pass: • DigiLocker mapped to certificate retrieval; myScheme mapped to eligibility discovery.
Examples – Fail: • Services integrated ad-hoc without user journey relevance.
Accessibility Consideration: • Service discovery content must be readable and non-cognitive overload.
Rationale: Prevents unnecessary integrations and ensures citizen-centric value.

Title: Define clear use cases for each integrated service
Issue: • Integrated services lack documented user value or interaction purpose.
Advice: • Document user benefit, trigger point, and expected outcome for every service integration.
Examples – Pass: • “Fetch from DigiLocker” used only at document upload stage.
Examples – Fail: • Service exposed globally without task relevance.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear purpose reduces cognitive burden for assistive tech users.
Rationale: Ensures integrations are meaningful, not ornamental.

Title: Follow official API documentation and standards
Issue: • APIs integrated without adhering to official specifications or limits.
Advice: • Integrate strictly as per NIC / MeitY API documentation and API Setu guidelines.
Examples – Pass: • Authenticated calls via API Setu with documented payloads.
Examples – Fail: • Hard-coded or reverse-engineered endpoints.
Accessibility Consideration: • Improper APIs can break assistive flows unexpectedly.
Rationale: Prevents security, reliability, and audit failures.

Title: Ensure secure and compliant data exchange
Issue: • Data shared without encryption or regulatory compliance.
Advice: • Enforce TLS 1.2+, payload encryption, and NIC security standards.
Examples – Pass: • Encrypted API calls with secure token handling.
Examples – Fail: • Plain-text or partially encrypted payloads.
Accessibility Consideration: • Security failures disproportionately harm vulnerable users.
Rationale: Protects citizen trust and legal compliance.

Title: Obtain explicit user consent before data sharing
Issue: • User data shared with services without informed consent.
Advice: • Capture explicit, contextual consent before invoking service APIs.
Examples – Pass: • Checkbox with clear purpose explanation before DigiLocker fetch.
Examples – Fail: • Silent background data exchange.
Accessibility Consideration: • Consent must be perceivable and screen-reader accessible.
Rationale: Consent is mandatory for ethical and legal governance.

Title: Communicate role and benefits of integrated services
Issue: • Users do not understand why a service is used or how data is handled.
Advice: • Explain service purpose, benefit, and data usage inline or via help cues.
Examples – Pass: • “Powered by DigiLocker” info tooltip near CTA.
Examples – Fail: • Hidden or vague service attribution.
Accessibility Consideration: • Clear explanations aid cognitive accessibility.
Rationale: Transparency builds trust and reduces abandonment.

Title: Maintain UI consistency for integrated services
Issue: • Integrated services introduce foreign UI patterns or branding conflicts.
Advice: • Style all service-related UI using the product’s design system.
Examples – Pass: • DigiLocker button matches primary CTA style.
Examples – Fail: • Third-party UI embedded without adaptation.
Accessibility Consideration: • Consistency supports predictability for assistive users.
Rationale: Prevents fragmentation of experience.

Title: Ensure intuitive navigation to integrated services
Issue: • Service access points are hidden or context-less.
Advice: • Place service entry points exactly where the task requires them.
Examples – Pass: • “Fetch from DigiLocker” shown after document requirement.
Examples – Fail: • Service link buried in unrelated menu.
Accessibility Consideration: • Predictable navigation reduces cognitive load.
Rationale: Supports task-oriented journeys.

Title: Provide onboarding guidance for integrated services
Issue: Users are unaware of how or why to use integrated government services.
Advice: Provide first-time onboarding via banners, tooltips, walkthroughs, or contextual help explaining service value and steps.
Examples – Pass: First-time DigiLocker fetch shows a short explainer with steps and benefits.
Examples – Fail: Service invoked without any explanation or guidance.
Accessibility Consideration: Onboarding must be skippable, readable by screen readers, and non-blocking.
Rationale: Increases adoption and prevents early abandonment of integrations.

Title: Leverage Bhashini for multilingual access
Issue: Integrated services are usable only in limited languages.
Advice: Integrate Bhashini APIs to support content or real-time language translation with clear language switching controls.
Examples – Pass: User can switch interface language using Bhashini-powered toggle.
Examples – Fail: Language support limited to English despite multilingual audience.
Accessibility Consideration: Language switch must preserve context and be programmatically defined.
Rationale: Ensures linguistic inclusion at national scale.

Title: Ensure accessibility compliance of integrated services
Issue: Integrated services introduce WCAG violations.
Advice: Audit all service-related UI for WCAG 2.1 AA compliance including keyboard access, contrast, and ARIA semantics.
Examples – Pass: Integrated DigiLocker UI passes keyboard and screen reader tests.
Examples – Fail: Third-party UI blocks keyboard navigation.
Accessibility Consideration: Must comply with WCAG 2.1 AA across perceivable, operable, understandable, robust principles.
Rationale: Accessibility compliance is non-negotiable in government services.

Title: Communicate updates and changes in integrated services
Issue: Users are unaware of service changes, downtime, or security updates.
Advice: Inform users proactively via banners, alerts, or update logs when services change or are unavailable.
Examples – Pass: Banner shown during DigiLocker maintenance window.
Examples – Fail: Service fails silently or without explanation.
Accessibility Consideration: Status updates must be announced via ARIA live regions.
Rationale: Prevents confusion and loss of trust during service disruptions.

Title: Provide help and documentation for integrated services
Issue: Users lack support resources for service-specific issues.
Advice: Offer FAQs, guides, and troubleshooting specific to each integrated service.
Examples – Pass: Dedicated help section for DigiLocker and Bhashini usage.
Examples – Fail: Generic help content without service coverage.
Accessibility Consideration: Help content must be accessible and readable.
Rationale: Reduces support load and user frustration.

Title: Design architecture for scalable integrations
Issue: System cannot easily support new or growing service integrations.
Advice: Use modular, API-first architecture with service abstraction layers.
Examples – Pass: New service added via wrapper without UI rework.
Examples – Fail: Hard-coded integrations requiring major refactor.
Accessibility Consideration: Scalability issues can indirectly impact accessibility performance.
Rationale: Enables long-term sustainability and performance.

Title: Plan for future government service integrations
Issue: Product lacks forward-looking integration strategy.
Advice: Maintain roadmap tracking emerging government APIs and platforms.
Examples – Pass: Roadmap includes JanSamarth and future APISetu releases.
Examples – Fail: No awareness of upcoming services.
Accessibility Consideration: Future integrations must inherit accessibility and consent baselines.
Rationale: Prevents stagnation and ensures policy alignment.

Title: Identify and support critical offline use cases
Issue: Offline-critical user scenarios are not identified or supported.
Advice: Conduct research to identify low-connectivity contexts and design offline-safe workflows (drafts, partial completion).
Examples – Pass: User can fill forms and save drafts without connectivity.
Examples – Fail: Form becomes unusable when network drops.
Accessibility Consideration: Offline affordances must be announced via status messages and not rely on color alone.
Rationale: India-scale services must assume unreliable connectivity by default.

Title: Implement automatic data synchronization
Issue: Offline data is not reliably synced, causing loss or duplication.
Advice: Use background sync mechanisms with conflict resolution and deduplication logic.
Examples – Pass: Draft auto-syncs once connection restores.
Examples – Fail: User must re-enter lost data.
Accessibility Consideration: Sync status must be programmatically conveyed (ARIA live).
Rationale: Prevents data loss and trust erosion.

Title: Provide manual sync control
Issue: Users lack control over when data syncs.
Advice: Provide a visible “Sync Now” option when connectivity is available.
Examples – Pass: User taps “Sync Now” after reconnecting.
Examples – Fail: Sync happens silently with no user control.
Accessibility Consideration: Sync controls must be keyboard and screen-reader accessible.
Rationale: Empowers users in low-trust network conditions.

Title: Notify users about sync status
Issue: Users are unaware of sync success or failure.
Advice: Display clear success/failure notifications with retry affordances.
Examples – Pass: Toast shows “Sync completed successfully”.
Examples – Fail: Sync fails silently.
Accessibility Consideration: Notifications must meet WCAG 4.1.3 (Status Messages).
Rationale: Reduces anxiety and repeat actions.

Title: Maintain UI consistency in offline mode
Issue: Offline mode breaks UI patterns or flows.
Advice: Preserve layout and interactions; disable only network-dependent actions with clear states.
Examples – Pass: Same UI with disabled submit button + offline label.
Examples – Fail: Entire screen replaced with error page.
Accessibility Consideration: Disabled states must be announced to assistive tech.
Rationale: Predictability reduces cognitive load.

Title: Provide meaningful fallback content
Issue: Offline users see blank or broken screens.
Advice: Cache visited pages and show placeholders or last-known data with offline indicators.
Examples – Pass: Cached scheme details visible offline.
Examples – Fail: White screen with generic error.
Accessibility Consideration: Offline messages must be readable by screen readers.
Rationale: Ensures continuity of use.

Title: Show clear offline error messaging
Issue: Users receive generic or technical errors when offline.
Advice: Display contextual, human-readable offline messages with next steps.
Examples – Pass: “You’re offline. Submit when connected.”
Examples – Fail: “Network error 504.”
Accessibility Consideration: Error messages must follow WCAG 3.3.1 & 3.3.3.
Rationale: Improves error recovery and comprehension.

Title: Retry failed operations automatically
Issue: Users must manually redo failed actions.
Advice: Queue failed operations locally and auto-retry on reconnection with status feedback.
Examples – Pass: Form auto-submits when network returns.
Examples – Fail: User must resubmit manually.
Accessibility Consideration: Retry actions must be cancelable and announced.
Rationale: Minimizes user effort and frustration.

Title: Test product thoroughly in online and offline modes
Issue: Offline functionality breaks due to lack of systematic testing across connectivity states.
Advice: Validate all critical flows using offline simulations and network throttling to ensure caching, sync, retry, and error handling behave correctly.
Examples – Pass: Forms, drafts, cached pages, and sync flows behave as expected when switching between offline and online modes.
Examples – Fail: Features appear to work in production but fail silently when network drops.
Accessibility Consideration: Offline testing must include keyboard navigation, screen reader output, and status message announcements.
Rationale: Offline capability is unreliable without explicit testing under real network constraints common in India.

Title: Provide in-product documentation for offline usage
Issue: Users are unaware of how offline features work, how to sync, or what limitations exist.
Advice: Clearly explain offline behavior, manual sync steps, and limitations through help sections, tooltips, or inline guidance.
Examples – Pass: Help section explains offline drafts, auto-sync timing, and manual “Sync Now” action.
Examples – Fail: Offline features exist but users discover them accidentally or misuse them.
Accessibility Consideration: Documentation must be readable, concise, and accessible to screen readers (WCAG 3.1, 3.3).
Rationale: Transparency builds confidence and prevents data loss or misuse of offline features.

Title: Use simple and non-overwhelming visual design
Issue: Overly complex charts overwhelm users and reduce comprehension.
Advice: Prefer simple chart types, minimal colors, and flat visual styles to communicate data clearly.
Examples – Pass: Bar or line charts with limited colors and clear spacing.
Examples – Fail: Overloaded charts with gradients, shadows, and excessive annotations.
Accessibility Consideration: Predictable layouts reduce cognitive load and support WCAG Understandable principle.
References: GIGW 3.0 – Visual Design; WCAG 2.1 §3.2, §3.3; BIS IS 17802:2022
Rationale: Simplicity improves comprehension for diverse literacy levels common in public services.

Title: Provide text alternatives for charts and graphs
Issue: Non-text data is inaccessible to screen reader users.
Advice: Add alt text, long descriptions, or tabular equivalents for all charts.
Examples – Pass: Chart followed by an accessible data table or descriptive summary.
Examples – Fail: Chart presented only visually with no text alternative.
Accessibility Consideration: Mandatory for screen readers (WCAG 1.1.1).
Rationale: Ensures equal access to data insights.

Title: Ensure sufficient color contrast in data visuals
Issue: Low contrast makes data unreadable for many users.
Advice: Maintain ≥3:1 contrast for graphics and ≥4.5:1 for text.
Examples – Pass: Clearly visible labels and data points with strong contrast.
Examples – Fail: Pale colors blending into background.
Accessibility Consideration: Supports low-vision and color-blind users.
Rationale: Contrast failures are a common accessibility violation.

Title: Make charts screen-reader compatible
Issue: Charts are not announced meaningfully by assistive tech.
Advice: Use semantic HTML, ARIA labels, and accessible chart libraries.
Examples – Pass: <figure> with caption and aria-descriptions.
Examples – Fail: Canvas-only charts with no accessibility layer.
Accessibility Consideration: Required for WCAG Robust principle.
Rationale: Prevents exclusion of blind users from data.

Title: Maintain consistent color and typography
Issue: Inconsistent styling reduces trust and usability.
Advice: Apply design system tokens across all visualisations.
Examples – Pass: Uniform fonts and colors across dashboards.
Examples – Fail: Each chart uses different fonts and palettes.
Accessibility Consideration: Consistency aids predictability (WCAG 3.2).
Rationale: Visual consistency strengthens credibility.

Title: Use consistent scales, legends, and labels
Issue: Users misinterpret data due to inconsistent references.
Advice: Standardize axes, legends, and labeling for similar charts.
Examples – Pass: Same units and legend order across charts.
Examples – Fail: Different scales used for similar datasets.
Accessibility Consideration: Consistency supports understandability.
Rationale: Enables accurate comparison and analysis.

Title: Provide interactive exploration affordances
Issue: Static visuals limit insight discovery.
Advice: Add tooltips, hover states, and drilldowns with explanations.
Examples – Pass: Hover tooltip showing exact values.
Examples – Fail: Interactive elements without explanation or focus support.
Accessibility Consideration: Interactions must be keyboard accessible.
Rationale: Interactivity improves data literacy when accessible.

Title: Ensure responsiveness across devices
Issue: Charts break or become unreadable on small screens.
Advice: Use responsive SVG/canvas and test reflow behavior.
Examples – Pass: Chart resizes and reflows cleanly on mobile.
Examples – Fail: Horizontal scroll or clipped labels on mobile.
Accessibility Consideration: Required under WCAG Reflow.
Rationale: Mobile access is critical for Indian users.

Title: Use descriptive titles and labels
Issue: Users lack context for interpreting data.
Advice: Add concise titles and clearly labeled axes/series.
Examples – Pass: “Monthly Enrolments by District (2025)”.
Examples – Fail: Generic titles like “Chart 1”.
Accessibility Consideration: Supports WCAG Info & Relationships.
Rationale: Context is essential for correct interpretation.

Title: Minimize HTTP requests via bundling
Issue: Excessive HTTP requests slow page loads.
Advice: Bundle CSS and JS using tools like Webpack or Gulp to reduce request count.
Examples – Pass: Single bundled CSS/JS file per page.
Examples – Fail: Dozens of unbundled CSS/JS files loaded.
Accessibility Consideration: Faster loading benefits users on slow networks and assistive tech.
Rationale: Reduces latency and improves first paint time.

Title: Lazy load media assets
Issue: Large assets block initial render.
Advice: Use lazy loading for images, videos, and heavy media.
Examples – Pass: Images load only when scrolled into view.
Examples – Fail: All images load immediately on page load.
Accessibility Consideration: Reduces cognitive wait time and improves usability.
Rationale: Improves perceived performance significantly.

Title: Load JavaScript asynchronously
Issue: Render-blocking JS delays content display.
Advice: Use async or defer for non-critical JS.
Examples – Pass: Scripts loaded with defer attribute.
Examples – Fail: JS blocks HTML rendering.
Accessibility Consideration: Faster rendering helps screen reader flow.
Rationale: Improves first contentful paint.

Title: Use responsive image techniques
Issue: Oversized images waste bandwidth.
Advice: Implement srcset and sizes for adaptive image delivery.
Examples – Pass: Different image sizes served per device.
Examples – Fail: Same large image served to all devices.
Accessibility Consideration: Prevents zooming and reflow issues.
Rationale: Saves data and improves clarity.

Title: Compress images
Issue: Large images slow downloads.
Advice: Compress images using TinyPNG, ImageOptim, etc.
Examples – Pass: Optimized images under size budget.
Examples – Fail: Uncompressed high-resolution images.
Accessibility Consideration: Faster load aids users with cognitive load issues.
Rationale: Improves speed without quality loss.

Title: Use next-gen image formats
Issue: Legacy formats increase payload size.
Advice: Use WebP/AVIF with fallbacks.
Examples – Pass: WebP images served to modern browsers.
Examples – Fail: Only JPG/PNG used everywhere.
Accessibility Consideration: Improves speed on low bandwidth connections.
Rationale: Better compression efficiency.

Title: Leverage browser caching
Issue: Assets are repeatedly downloaded.
Advice: Set cache-control and expires headers.
Examples – Pass: Static assets cached for long durations.
Examples – Fail: No caching headers set.
Accessibility Consideration: Improves experience for repeat users.
Rationale: Reduces redundant network calls.

Title: Use CDN for static assets
Issue: Single server increases latency.
Advice: Serve static files via CDN.
Examples – Pass: Assets served from nearest CDN node.
Examples – Fail: All assets served from origin server.
Accessibility Consideration: Improves access speed across geographies.
Rationale: Reduces latency and improves resilience.

Title: Minify CSS, JS, and HTML
Issue: Unminified code increases payload size.
Advice: Minify code using build tools.
Examples – Pass: Minified production bundles.
Examples – Fail: Readable dev code shipped to users.
Accessibility Consideration: Faster load benefits all users.
Rationale: Reduces transfer size.

Title: Remove unused CSS and JS
Issue: Dead code bloats bundles.
Advice: Use PurgeCSS / tree shaking.
Examples – Pass: Only used styles/scripts shipped.
Examples – Fail: Large unused libraries included.
Accessibility Consideration: Improves performance on low-end devices.
Rationale: Keeps frontend lean.

Title: Inline critical CSS
Issue: Above-the-fold content loads slowly.
Advice: Inline critical CSS; defer rest.
Examples – Pass: Above-the-fold content styled immediately.
Examples – Fail: Full CSS blocks rendering.
Accessibility Consideration: Improves perceived speed.
Rationale: Faster first render.

Title: Optimize database queries
Issue: Slow queries degrade response times.
Advice: Optimize queries, reduce redundancy.
Examples – Pass: Indexed, efficient queries.
Examples – Fail: Full table scans for common queries.
Accessibility Consideration: Faster responses reduce user wait time.
Rationale: Backend performance is critical.

Title: Use appropriate database indexing
Issue: Missing indexes slow queries.
Advice: Index frequently queried columns.
Examples – Pass: Queries use indexed fields.
Examples – Fail: Queries scan entire tables.
Accessibility Consideration: Improves reliability and speed.
Rationale: Essential for scalability.

Title: Implement query caching
Issue: Repeated queries overload DB.
Advice: Cache frequent query results.
Examples – Pass: Cached responses for common queries.
Examples – Fail: Same query executed repeatedly.
Accessibility Consideration: Improves stability under load.
Rationale: Reduces backend strain.

Title: Enable HTTP/2
Issue: Legacy HTTP limits throughput.
Advice: Enable HTTP/2 for multiplexing and compression.
Examples – Pass: HTTP/2 enabled on server.
Examples – Fail: HTTP/1.1 still in use.
Accessibility Consideration: Improves performance on all devices.
Rationale: Modern protocol improves efficiency.

Title: Enable file compression (Gzip/Brotli)
Issue: Large payloads increase transfer time.
Advice: Enable Gzip or Brotli compression at server/CDN level. Prefer Brotli where supported.
Examples – Pass: Brotli enabled for text assets (HTML, CSS, JS).
Examples – Fail: No compression headers; raw files transferred.
Accessibility Consideration: Faster downloads benefit users on low bandwidth and assistive tech.
Rationale: Reduces payload size significantly.

Title: Implement load balancing
Issue: Single-server dependency causes latency and downtime.
Advice: Distribute traffic across multiple servers using load balancers.
Examples – Pass: Requests routed across healthy nodes.
Examples – Fail: All traffic routed to one server.
Accessibility Consideration: Improves availability for all users.
Rationale: Ensures reliability under load.

Title: Ensure full responsiveness across devices
Issue: Poor responsiveness breaks usability on small screens.
Advice: Use responsive layouts, media queries, and flexible grids.
Examples – Pass: Layout adapts correctly across devices.
Examples – Fail: Horizontal scrolling or broken layouts.
Accessibility Consideration: Supports WCAG reflow and zoom users.
Rationale: Core usability requirement.

Title: Optimize touch interactions
Issue: Small targets cause interaction errors on mobile.
Advice: Use minimum 48×48px touch targets and intuitive gestures.
Examples – Pass: Buttons sized for touch accuracy.
Examples – Fail: Tiny links close together.
Accessibility Consideration: Improves accessibility for motor impairments.
Rationale: Prevents mis-taps and errors.

Title: Use real-time performance monitoring tools
Issue: Performance issues go undetected.
Advice: Integrate GA, Firebase, or Clarity for live monitoring.
Examples – Pass: Dashboards track load and interaction metrics.
Examples – Fail: No monitoring or alerts configured.
Accessibility Consideration: Enables proactive fixes before user impact.
Rationale: Continuous optimization loop.

Title: Use feedback to guide optimization
Issue: User-reported issues ignored.
Advice: Analyse performance feedback and prioritise fixes.
Examples – Pass: Feedback leads to measurable improvements.
Examples – Fail: Feedback collected but unused.
Accessibility Consideration: Improves trust and perceived saying.
Rationale: User-centric improvement.

Title: Implement error logging tools
Issue: Errors remain invisible to teams.
Advice: Use tools like Sentry or LogRocket with alerts.
Examples – Pass: Errors logged with stack traces.
Examples – Fail: Errors only visible to users.
Accessibility Consideration: Faster fixes reduce user disruption.
Rationale: Essential for stability.

Title: Use crash reporting tools
Issue: Crashes cause silent failures.
Advice: Implement crash reporters (Sentry, Bugsnag).
Examples – Pass: Crashes auto-reported with context.
Examples – Fail: Crashes require manual discovery.
Accessibility Consideration: Improves reliability for all users.
Rationale: Prevents systemic instability.

Title: Preload critical resources
Issue: Late loading of fonts/scripts delays render.
Advice: Use <link rel="preload"> for key assets.
Examples – Pass: Fonts and hero CSS preloaded.
Examples – Fail: Fonts loaded late causing FOIT.
Accessibility Consideration: Improves perceived speed.
Rationale: Faster first paint.

Title: Load critical content first
Issue: Secondary content blocks main content.
Advice: Prioritise above-the-fold content; async rest.
Examples – Pass: Main content visible immediately.
Examples – Fail: Ads/scripts block rendering.
Accessibility Consideration: Reduces cognitive waiting.
Rationale: Improves perceived performance.

Title: Ensure animations are smooth (no jank)
Issue: Janky animations degrade UX and performance.
Advice: Use CSS transforms or requestAnimationFrame.
Examples – Pass: Smooth 60fps animations.
Examples – Fail: JS-heavy animations stutter.
Accessibility Consideration: Reduces motion-related discomfort.
Rationale: Maintains interaction quality.

Title: Provide processing feedback
Issue: Users unsure if action is working.
Advice: Show loaders, spinners, or progress indicators.
Examples – Pass: Spinner shown during submission.
Examples – Fail: No feedback during wait.
Accessibility Consideration: Supports cognitive accessibility.
Rationale: Reduces perceived wait.

Title: Monitor performance & reliability processes
Issue: Issues not addressed systematically.
Advice: Establish monitoring, alerts, and incident response.
Examples – Pass: SLA-based monitoring active.
Examples – Fail: No defined monitoring ownership.
Accessibility Consideration: Improves service continuity.
Rationale: Governance requirement.

Title: Ensure product reliability (no broken links)
Issue: Broken links reduce trust and task success.
Advice: Run periodic automated link and flow checks.
Examples – Pass: No broken links in audits.
Examples – Fail: Frequent 404s and dead ends.
Accessibility Consideration: Prevents navigation failures.
Rationale: Core quality bar.

Title: Optimize content delivery for slow networks
Issue: Heavy content penalises low-bandwidth users.
Advice: Optimize images, text, and delivery via CDN.
Examples – Pass: Lightweight pages on 3G.
Examples – Fail: Large images without optimization.
Accessibility Consideration: Supports inclusion in low-connectivity regions.
Rationale: Equity and reach.

Title: Preload essential content
Issue: Essential assets load too late.
Advice: Preload critical CSS, fonts, and first-screen data.
Examples – Pass: First screen interactive quickly.
Examples – Fail: Blank or unstyled first screen.
Accessibility Consideration: Improves TTI for assistive tech users.
Rationale: Faster task start.

Title: Integrate relevant analytics systems
Issue: Lack of analytics prevents evidence-based decisions.
Advice: Integrate analytics covering behaviour, engagement, and performance aligned with objectives.
Examples – Pass: GA4/Firebase capturing behaviour and performance metrics.
Examples – Fail: No analytics or partial tracking only.
Accessibility Consideration: Analytics should not interfere with assistive tech performance.
Rationale: Measurement is prerequisite for optimisation.

Title: Define clear KPIs aligned to objectives
Issue: Success cannot be measured without KPIs.
Advice: Identify KPIs aligned with service goals (usage, retention, task success).
Examples – Pass: KPIs documented and tracked regularly.
Examples – Fail: Metrics collected without linkage to goals.
Accessibility Consideration: Enables outcome-focused accessibility improvements.
Rationale: Ensures accountability and focus.

Title: Use heatmaps and session recordings
Issue: UX issues remain invisible without behavioural insight.
Advice: Use heatmaps/session recordings to identify friction.
Examples – Pass: Clarity/Hotjar reveals rage clicks and dead zones.
Examples – Fail: No behavioural visualisation tools used.
Accessibility Consideration: Must anonymise recordings and mask sensitive data.
Rationale: Reveals real user pain points.

Title: Track key user events
Issue: Critical actions are not measurable.
Advice: Define and implement event tracking for key actions.
Examples – Pass: Button clicks and form submits tracked.
Examples – Fail: Only pageviews tracked.
Accessibility Consideration: Events should not rely on inaccessible controls.
Rationale: Enables funnel and journey analysis.

Title: Segment users for deeper insights
Issue: Aggregate data hides meaningful patterns.
Advice: Segment users by behaviour, device, and usage patterns.
Examples – Pass: New vs returning user analysis available.
Examples – Fail: All users analysed as one group.
Accessibility Consideration: Helps detect accessibility issues across segments.
Rationale: Improves targeting and prioritisation.

Title: Obtain user consent for analytics
Issue: Data collection without consent violates trust.
Advice: Implement consent mechanisms before tracking.
Examples – Pass: Analytics fires only after consent.
Examples – Fail: Tracking loads before consent.
Accessibility Consideration: Essential for inclusive and ethical data use.
Rationale: Legal and ethical requirement.

Title: Anonymise user data
Issue: Identifiable data risks privacy breaches.
Advice: Enable IP anonymisation and avoid PII.
Examples – Pass: IP masking enabled; no PII stored.
Examples – Fail: Raw IPs and identifiers stored.
Accessibility Consideration: Builds trust with vulnerable users.
Rationale: Balances insight with privacy.

Title: Communicate data practices clearly
Issue: Users unaware of data usage.
Advice: Publish clear, accessible privacy policy.
Examples – Pass: Privacy policy linked prominently.
Examples – Fail: Hidden or outdated privacy notice.
Accessibility Consideration: Required for informed consent.
Rationale: Transparency builds trust.

Title: Use real-time analytics
Issue: Delayed insights slow incident response.
Advice: Enable real-time dashboards and alerts.
Examples – Pass: Live error spikes visible instantly.
Examples – Fail: Only historical reports used.
Accessibility Consideration: Faster fixes reduce accessibility regressions.
Rationale: Improves responsiveness.

Title: Integrate crash reporting
Issue: Crashes go unnoticed without reporting.
Advice: Use crash/error reporting tools.
Examples – Pass: JS crashes logged with context.
Examples – Fail: Users report crashes manually.
Accessibility Consideration: Prevents repeated failures for assistive users.
Rationale: System stability requirement.

Title: Analyse user flows and drop-offs
Issue: Drop-offs remain unexplained.
Advice: Use funnel and flow analysis.
Examples – Pass: Clear drop-off points identified.
Examples – Fail: No journey analysis performed.
Accessibility Consideration: Helps identify cognitive overload areas.
Rationale: Improves task success.

Title: Create custom dashboards
Issue: Raw data is hard to interpret.
Advice: Build dashboards for key KPIs.
Examples – Pass: Looker/Power BI dashboards in use.
Examples – Fail: Stakeholders rely on raw exports.
Accessibility Consideration: Clear dashboards support inclusive decision-making.
Rationale: Improves governance visibility.

Title: Generate periodic performance reports
Issue: Trends are missed without regular review.
Advice: Automate weekly/monthly reports.
Examples – Pass: Reports shared with teams regularly.
Examples – Fail: Ad-hoc, inconsistent reviews.
Accessibility Consideration: Enables sustained quality improvements.
Rationale: Supports continuous improvement.

Title: Conduct A/B testing
Issue: Decisions made without experimentation.
Advice: Run controlled experiments on key flows.
Examples – Pass: CTA variants tested with metrics.
Examples – Fail: Changes shipped without testing.
Accessibility Consideration: Tests must not reduce accessibility.
Rationale: Evidence-driven optimisation.

Title: Track usage of help & feedback features
Issue: Support issues not optimised.
Advice: Track interactions with help/feedback systems.
Examples – Pass: Search terms and drop-offs analysed.
Examples – Fail: Help usage unmeasured.
Accessibility Consideration: Improves inclusive support quality.
Rationale: Closes feedback loop.

Title: Thumb-zone optimised menu placement
Issue: Menu placement reduces reachability for single-handed use.
Advice: Place menu trigger in thumb-friendly zone with platform conventions and sufficient target size.
Examples – Pass: Menu icon reachable with one thumb and ≥48dp touch target.
Examples – Fail: Menu icon too small or unreachable on large screens.
Accessibility Consideration: Target size ≥48dp; contrast ≥4.5:1.
Rationale: Improves mobile ergonomics and discoverability.

Title: Display personalised user identity
Issue: Lack of identity reduces trust and context.
Advice: Show user name, avatar, and account metadata clearly.
Examples – Pass: Name + avatar + status visible at top.
Examples – Fail: Generic placeholder or missing identity.
Accessibility Consideration: Proper labels for screen readers.
Rationale: Builds user confidence and orientation.

Title: Logical grouping of navigation items
Issue: Poor grouping increases cognitive load.
Advice: Group items by user tasks and mental models.
Examples – Pass: Clear sections: Profile, Services, Support, Settings.
Examples – Fail: Flat list with no grouping.
Accessibility Consideration: Heading hierarchy must be programmatic.
Rationale: Improves findability and comprehension.

Title: Clear, action-oriented menu labels
Issue: Ambiguous labels reduce usability.
Advice: Use concise, action-based, user-friendly labels.
Examples – Pass: “Edit Profile”, “View Transactions”.
Examples – Fail: Vague terms like “Profile”, “Info”.
Accessibility Consideration: Labels must be screen-reader friendly.
Rationale: Reduces ambiguity and errors.

Title: Maintain shallow navigation depth
Issue: Deep nesting increases cognitive burden.
Advice: Limit menu depth to 2–3 levels.
Examples – Pass: All items reachable within 3 taps.
Examples – Fail: Multiple nested sub-menus.
Accessibility Consideration: Focus order must remain logical.
Rationale: Supports quick access and clarity.

Title: Prioritise high-frequency actions
Issue: Important actions buried in menu.
Advice: Place frequent actions prominently.
Examples – Pass: Notifications and logout easily accessible.
Examples – Fail: Logout hidden deep in menu.
Accessibility Consideration: Multiple ways to access key actions.
Rationale: Improves efficiency and satisfaction.

Title: User identity at top of menu
Issue: Context missing before navigation.
Advice: Place avatar and name at top of menu.
Examples – Pass: Profile header visible before items.
Examples – Fail: Identity shown at bottom or hidden.
Accessibility Consideration: Semantic grouping required.
Rationale: Establishes context immediately.

Title: Comprehensive account management options
Issue: Missing essential account functions.
Advice: Provide profile, security, accessibility, support, and logout options.
Examples – Pass: Full account management available.
Examples – Fail: Partial or fragmented options.
Accessibility Consideration: All options must be keyboard accessible.
Rationale: Ensures completeness of service.

Title: Easy access to support resources
Issue: Help content hard to find.
Advice: Surface FAQs, contact, and guides in menu.
Examples – Pass: Dedicated Help section visible.
Examples – Fail: Support buried deep or external.
Accessibility Consideration: Help content must meet WCAG AA.
Rationale: Reduces user frustration.

Title: Display organisational metadata
Issue: Lack of transparency about app ownership.
Advice: Provide About section with org and version info.
Examples – Pass: About screen with version and ownership.
Examples – Fail: No app or org information.
Accessibility Consideration: Readable text and clear labels.
Rationale: Builds institutional trust.

Title: Privacy controls and consent management
Issue: Users cannot manage privacy preferences.
Advice: Provide granular privacy and consent controls.
Examples – Pass: Privacy dashboard with toggles.
Examples – Fail: No privacy controls available.
Accessibility Consideration: Must comply with WCAG & DPDP Act.
Rationale: Legal and ethical requirement.

Title: Re-authentication for sensitive actions
Issue: Sensitive actions insufficiently protected.
Advice: Require password/biometric for critical actions.
Examples – Pass: Step-up auth for security changes.
Examples – Fail: Sensitive actions without verification.
Accessibility Consideration: Authentication flows must be accessible.
Rationale: Prevents misuse and fraud.

Title: High-performance menu interactions
Issue: Slow or janky menu degrades UX.
Advice: Ensure sub-300ms open/close with smooth animations.
Examples – Pass: Menu opens smoothly under 200ms.
Examples – Fail: Laggy or stuttering menu.
Accessibility Consideration: Motion must respect user preferences.
Rationale: Maintains perceived quality.

Title: Multi-lingual support
Issue: Content unavailable or inconsistent across languages.
Advice: Provide fully translated, equally updated content across Indian languages.
Examples – Pass: Language toggle with parity across all pages.
Examples – Fail: Partial translations or mixed languages in one section.
Accessibility Consideration: Use correct lang attributes per page/section.
Rationale: Ensures linguistic accessibility and inclusion.

Title: Sufficient text–background contrast
Issue: Poor contrast reduces readability.
Advice: Maintain minimum contrast ratios for text and UI elements.
Examples – Pass: Text contrast ≥4.5:1 (normal text).
Examples – Fail: Light grey text on white background.
Accessibility Consideration: Required for low-vision users.
Rationale: Improves legibility and reduces eye strain.

Title: WCAG compliance (overall)
Issue: Partial or inconsistent WCAG adherence.
Advice: Ensure WCAG 2.1/2.2 AA compliance across UI.
Examples – Pass: Fully operable via keyboard and screen reader.
Examples – Fail: Content inaccessible without mouse.
Accessibility Consideration: Covers perceivable, operable, understandable, robust principles.
Rationale: Legal and policy compliance requirement.

Title: Assistive technology compatibility
Issue: Screen readers or ATs cannot access UI correctly.
Advice: Implement semantic HTML, ARIA, and proper focus order.
Examples – Pass: Login form usable with NVDA/VoiceOver.
Examples – Fail: Screen reader skips form fields.
Accessibility Consideration: ARIA roles must not override native semantics unnecessarily.
Rationale: Enables independent use by disabled users.

Title: Keyboard navigation support
Issue: Mouse-dependent interactions block access.
Advice: Ensure full keyboard operability for all controls.
Examples – Pass: Entire flow navigable using Tab/Enter.
Examples – Fail: Focus trapped in modal.
Accessibility Consideration: Visible focus indicators mandatory.
Rationale: Critical for motor-impaired users.

Title: Ease of use for low-experience users
Issue: Complex UI overwhelms novice users.
Advice: Use simple layouts, guidance, and confirmations.
Examples – Pass: Step-by-step flows with clear feedback.
Examples – Fail: Dense UI with unclear actions.
Accessibility Consideration: Plain language and predictable behavior required.
Rationale: Improves digital inclusion.

Title: Accessible list items
Issue: Screen readers cannot interpret list structure.
Advice: Use semantic lists or ARIA list roles.
Examples – Pass: <ul><li> with proper labels.
Examples – Fail: Div-based lists without roles.
Accessibility Consideration: Required for structural clarity.
Rationale: Preserves information relationships.

Title: Accessible sorting controls
Issue: Sorting state not conveyed to screen readers.
Advice: Implement aria-sort and descriptive labels.
Examples – Pass: Screen reader announces sort order.
Examples – Fail: Sort changes silently.
Accessibility Consideration: Required for non-visual users.
Rationale: Ensures data comprehension.

Title: Accessible form design
Issue: Forms lack labels or sufficient contrast.
Advice: Use programmatic labels and compliant contrast.
Examples – Pass: <label for> used correctly.
Examples – Fail: Placeholder-only labels.
Accessibility Consideration: Errors must be announced to screen readers.
Rationale: Prevents form abandonment.

Title: Keyboard-accessible form elements
Issue: Form controls unusable without mouse.
Advice: Ensure all form elements support keyboard input.
Examples – Pass: Complete form via keyboard alone.
Examples – Fail: Cannot submit via Enter/Space.
Accessibility Consideration: Focus order must follow visual order.
Rationale: Enables independent completion.

Title: ARIA landmarks usage
Issue: Page structure unclear to screen readers.
Advice: Use semantic regions or ARIA landmarks.
Examples – Pass: Proper use of <main>, <nav>, <header>.
Examples – Fail: Entire page built with <div>.
Accessibility Consideration: Landmarks must be unique and meaningful.
Rationale: Improves navigation efficiency.
